Woman at centre of Cornell rape inquiry was 'failed' by officials, says New York governor

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 17:44:08 GMT

New York Governor Kathy Hochul has said the woman at the centre of the Cornell University rape case was "failed" at "every turn".

The woman, known as Jane Doe in legal documents, alleges she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house in 2024.

The case was investigated at the time but no charges were laid. It recently reopened after the woman filed a civil lawsuit last month that thrust the allegations into the national spotlight.

At a news conference on Friday, Hochul said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled. She has now appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to lead the case.

This appointment was made after Hochul said she "lost faith" in the local prosecutor's ability to oversee the investigation.

Expressing outrage that local prosecutors did not interview the accuser themselves, Hochul on Friday said: "This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable, and then at every turn she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her."

She has also vowed to close a "loophole" that prevents prosecutors from pursuing rape charges in cases when the victim has voluntarily consumed drugs or alcohol. Jane Doe is believed to have voluntarily taken drugs and alcohol on the night of the alleged gang rape.

"If someone is too intoxicated to consent it should not matter if they chose to use drugs or alcohol," said Hochul, adding: "Voluntary intoxication is not a licence for gang rape."

James, who is the state's chief legal officer, appeared alongside Hochul at Friday's news conference, pledging to "lead a process guided by the facts and the law".

She said her office would interview witnesses and pursue prosecutions if warranted.

District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who previously led the investigation, has defended his office's previous decision not to file charges in the case, arguing they were not given enough evidence to meet the legal threshold.

Van Houten said much of the information released in recent weeks about the case was not passed to his office.

In a statement on Friday, he said he supported James' investigation, adding: "It has become clear that we were not provided the full picture by the university."

Cornell has said it provided evidence to the district attorney's office from its own investigation, including a Snapchat group chat in which fraternity members discussed a "free" sexual encounter with Doe on the night of the alleged assault.

Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university in September.

Speaking to CNN on Friday, her lawyer Thomas Giuffra said she is "not doing well".

"She's under siege on social media, where people are trying to identify her; some false court postings, attempting to identify her," he said.

Survivor and victim advocates say current state law on sexual assault makes it difficult for charges to be brought against perpetrators if the victim voluntarily took drugs or drank alcohol before the alleged assault took place.

A bill to address what Hochul described as a legal loophole was already before the state legislature prior to this week's public outcry over how police and investigators handled the Cornell rape allegations.

People who have voluntarily become intoxicated to the point that they are unable to give consent are currently not protected by New York's rape laws, says state assemblyman Jeffrey Dinowitz, who first sponsored legislation to close the loophole in 2019.

"The real bottom line is that right now if you are voluntarily intoxicated, you will not get justice," he tells BBC News.

"Being voluntarily intoxicated, basically, is almost like giving somebody a get out of jail free card."

Dinowitz says that around half of US states have already changed their laws to say it makes no difference whether intoxication is voluntarily or involuntarily in rape cases.

Hochul said she will support the existing bill and that it could move forward as early as the next legislative session which reconvenes in January. As governor, she could also call lawmakers back for a special session before then.

Man City confirm appeal against guilty verdict

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 17:43:48 GMT

Manchester City were found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges against them

Manchester City have confirmed they have lodged an appeal after an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

In a short statement, the club said the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".

Asserting its innocence, the club added it had filed "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions" on Thursday evening.

Earlier on Friday, the Football Association said the verdict against City has "significant implications for the integrity of the game".

In a statement, English football's governing body added: "We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate."

It was confirmed on Tuesday that City were found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

"As proceedings between the Premier League and Manchester City Football Club remain ongoing, we do not intend to comment further at this stage," the FA added.

"We will, however, continue to monitor developments closely."

The overarching powers the FA has could see the governing body launch its own investigation into the matter with the threat of further sanctions.

Sources told BBC Sport that City were expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.

However, City's defence may be undermined by statements that major sponsor Etihad Airways gave to the United States government in 2015.

In response to the US Department of Commerce, Transportation and State during an investigation into state-owned airlines, Etihad Airways said: "The assertion that the Abu Dhabi government paid for Etihad's sponsorship of English Premier League football club Manchester City is false. In 2011, Etihad and Manchester City entered into a 10-year sponsorship agreement, which included naming rights for Manchester City's stadium. Etihad funded this sponsorship from its own liquidity."

Etihad Airways later stated: "We are and have always been clear that we do not receive any subsidies from the Abu Dhabi government."

The independent panel's findings decided that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The Premier League says City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

The independent commission which studied the case found City "utilised devices" to "disguise the true extent of certain club liabilities".

The findings have prompted the Treasury Committee, which is responsible for overseeing policies and administration of His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC), to ask whether the government department has requested the redacted documents contained within the commission's report.

Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the cross-party group of MPs, said she would "welcome reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in this case".

The letter follows a report from the Tax Policy Associates, external which claims City failed to pay as much as £12m in unpaid tax because of a "sham" contract with former manager Roberto Mancini.

In addition to unpaid income tax and National Insurance, the report claims City could face a penalty charge that would take their liabilities to £24m.

The Business, Innovation, Science and Trade committee has called for stronger action on corporate accounting in a letter to the government and the Financial Reporting Council.

Committee Chair Liam Byrne said the findings suggested a "serious failure of security" and that "clubs complying with the rules need confidence that those rules are enforced fairly".

Separately, it has emerged that City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak met with business secretary Jonathan Reynolds days before the club's guilty verdicts were announced.

The BBC has been told that the club was not mentioned and that Al Mubarak was visiting in his capacity as CEO of the Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund.

It is understood the pair's discussions focussed on the UK's relationship with the UAE including defence, security, intelligence and trade.

UK government sources argue it is "totally normal" for the business secretary to have these sorts of meetings.

The encounter was first reported by Bloomberg.

Additional reporting by BBC political correspondent Joe Pike.

The commission was made up of three people, each with many years' experience in the legal field.

The appeal will now be heard in private by a new, three-person independent commission panel, each with a similar expert background in law.

One section of the Premier League regulations says that an appeal hearing should conclude within 12 weeks of it being heard, and a decision communicated within 30 days of that.

Twelve weeks from Thursday – when City say they lodged the appeal – would be 24 December.

But this timeframe can also be disapplied if deemed necessary, meaning it remains uncertain how long the process will actually take.

The relevant regulation was only added to the rule book this summer.

Previous precedent suggests that sanctions against City will only be imposed after a decision on the appeal, though this is not guaranteed.

There could therefore also be a second appeal later down the line, against any sanctions imposed on the club.

City will claim as part of their appeal that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners.

Owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour - are said to have topped up the value of commercial deals as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of £830.69m.

This, it was argued, enabled the club to appear to comply with Premier League and Uefa financial rules.

Premier League rules allow state-owned bodies to sponsor clubs.

Etihad Airways has said it is considering legal action against the Premier League, claiming the release of the commission findings had "damaging implications… despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings".

The UAE's state-owned national airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".

Etihad is owned by sovereign wealth fund L'Imad which is chaired by the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, the son of the UAE president.

Greens can move Labour in the right direction, says Polanski

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 17:28:07 GMT

Zack Polanski has urged voters to back the Greens to force changes from Andy Burnham, arguing his party has the power to move Labour in "the right direction".

In his speech to the party's annual conference, the Green leader said that "sustained pressure" from his party had made forced Labour into changing its stance on issues including climate and its stance towards Israel.

He told activists in Brighton that Labour had failed to take action on housing, as he called for a three-year cap to limit rent rises in the private sector.

And he said that voting for the Greens would force changes from the government, telling members: "Vote Green, and watch Labour move".

Polanski arrived in Brighton facing questions over his leadership of the party amid signs the Greens' rise in popularity last year may have waned, and how he would respond to Labour's change of leadership under Burnham.

In his half-hour address, he did not mention the Conservatives or Reform UK but launched repeated attacks on Labour's record in office.

He criticised Labour for making "slogans without action" on the cost of living and vowed only his party would end "Rip Off Britain".

And he was particularly critical of Labour's record on housing, where he accused the party of failing to take on the "powerful vested interests of developers and big landlords".

Instead, he urged the government to enact an "emergency brake" on private rents, under which they would be prevented from rising above the lowest of consumer price index measure of inflation, wage growth or 2%, for three years.

He argued that pressure from the Greens in the face of government "inaction" had forced Burnham into calling an emergency Cobr meeting this summer amid record-breaking hot and dry temperatures.

The Greens, he added would not "hesitate" to tax "extreme wealth", as he repeated the party's call for a so-called windfall tax on back profits - an issue where the government has faced pressure from unions.

"Through our sustained pressure – and our historic wins – we have held the worst instincts of the Labour government in check.

"And we have started to move them in the right direction. But we can't wait for them to get there on their own."

He also sought to draw a clear dividing line with the government on the issue of oil and gas, ahead of looming decisions for the government on whether to approve the Rosebank oil field and Jackdaw gas field.

Burnham has stuck to Labour's manifesto commitment not to issue new oil and gas licences, but has left open the possibility of approving the two sites.

This summer's wildfires, Polanski told the conference hall, should prove the "final nail in the coffin for new oil and gas".

He began his address by celebrating his party's surge in membership since his election as party leader a year ago, and electoral successes including the hundreds of councillors it gained in May's local elections in England.

But his speech did not touch on an issue that could divide the membership over the weekend, ahead of a probable vote on a motion put forward by members that describes Zionism as a form of racism.

The motion defines Zionism as an ideology in support of "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and seeks to shift the party's position to supporting a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".

The current form of the motion has drawn criticism from senior figures, including deputy leader Rachel Millward, who earlier described it as "problematic".

Before the conference, Polanski declined to say whether he would support the motion in its current form but said he wanted to see it changed.

He has said he wants to see the motion amended to specify that it should not be used to discipline Jewish members attending synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.

He is also supporting a change that would replace the call for a single Palestinian state with backing for a "lasting settlement granting equal rights for all" to be "shaped and determined by Palestinians themselves".

Sabalenka 'trying hard to be easier on myself'

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:23:39 GMT

Aryna Sabalenka's last title came at the Miami Open in March

Aryna Sabalenka said she was "trying so hard to be easier on myself" as she began her China Open campaign with victory over Renata Zarazua.

The Belarusian needed just 63 minutes to win her first match since losing her world number one ranking and her US Open crown to Elena Rybakina in September.

The 28-year-old is bidding for her first title since completing the 'Sunshine Double' in March, when she won Indian Wells and the Miami Open back-to-back.

It has been a mixed year for Sabalenka by her high standards. She will finish without a Grand Slam trophy for the first time since 2022 and has often struggled to control her frustrations on court.

Asked about being so self-critical, Sabalenka said: "I think this is a good and a bad side of my personality, that I always ask and wait for more from myself.

"Sometimes it can drive me forward, but sometimes it can really drain my energy.

"Maybe this is something I have to finally learn. I'm really trying so hard sometimes to be easier on myself."

Sabalenka will face Czech 20-year-old Nikola Bartunkova - who came close to beating her at the Berlin Open in June - in the third round.

Top seed Rybakina begins her campaign at the WTA 1000 event on Saturday.

Earlier, Britain's Katie Boulter fell 7-6 (7-3) 6-1 to Wimbledon runner-up Karolina Muchova, while French Open champion Mirra Andreeva recovered to beat Chinese wildcard Yuan Yue 3-6 6-0 6-0.

In the men's event, sixth seed Daniil Medvedev produced 12 aces to beat Spain's Pablo Carreno Busta 6-4 6-2.

British pair Julian Cash and Lloyd Glasspool advanced in the doubles, beating Russia's Andrey Rublev and Karen Khachanov 6-3 6-4.

Novak Djokovic progressed to the third round of the men's tournament with a 4-6 7-6 (7-2) 6-2 victory over China's Bu Yunchaokete.

The six-time champion, who has never lost in Beijing in 31 matches, was given a scare by Bu after he dropped the first set.

Djokovic needed a medical timeout after giving back a break in the second set, accepting a time violation as he fought to regain his breath between points.

The 39-year-old Serb then consulted the trainer, as he had in his first-round win over Nuno Borges, but he dominated the tie-break.

Djokovic found his rhythm in the decider as he won four games in a row sealing victory after two hours and 52 minutes with a backhand winner.

He will face either US Open champion Alexander Zverev of Germany or China's Shang Juncheng on Saturday for a spot in the quarter-finals.

Will Warrington or Wakefield be Super League's sixth winner?

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:48:57 GMT

Warrington captain George Williams (left) and Wakefield skipper Mike McMeeken (right) are 80 minutes away from leading their respective sides to a first Super League Grand Final win

Just five sides have lifted the trophy at Old Trafford in a Super League Grand Final.

That exclusive club of Wigan, Leeds, St Helens, Bradford and Hull KR will gain a new member on Saturday as Warrington Wolves and Wakefield Trinity battle under the lights at the Theatre of Dreams for a spot at glory.

Whereas the Super League era has traditionally been dominated by the powerhouses of the sport with their heaving trophy cabinets, 2026 is the story of one side that has come close but not got over the line and another that has upset the odds to wedge themselves into the conversation.

But what is the mood like in either camp ahead of a box office Grand Final?

Wakefield's stunning semi-final win over Wigan set tongues wagging across rugby league and beyond, particularly given the nature of the demolition job delivered by Daryl Powell's side to the treble-chasers.

It was a performance which suggested Wakefield had the credentials to complete the job at Old Trafford, built on a marauding, metre-chomping pack and skilful, pacy backs capable of racking up points.

Head coach Powell has been around the block and knows just how difficult this one-off final is to get right even with a season's worth of momentum behind a team.

"We have to get the same performance level," Powell told BBC Sport. "When it really counts.

"I'm not saying it's going to be picture perfect, it's very rare there is but I think we have to be at a very high level to beat Warrington and we all know that."

'You could be legends' - inside unfancied Wakefield's rapid ascent

Will 2026 finally be Warrington Wolves' year?

This video can not be played

Wakefield stun Wigan to reach first Grand Final

While this is Wakefield's first final and the same for many of their players, like coach Powell a select few have sampled the unique atmosphere of Old Trafford for Super League's showpiece event.

Tom Johnstone begrudgingly left Wakefield for Catalans in 2023 and reached the Grand Final in his first season, before rejoining Trinity in 2025.

That night ended in disappointment with defeat by Wigan, so the 2026 final represents a second chance for the England winger to pick up the ring he so covets - although it will not be the most important ring in his life as he admits.

"It's going to be different in so many ways for me because as much as I loved Catalans, this is my team," Johnstone told BBC Radio 5 live.

"This has been my team for almost all of my career, and the team that gave me an opportunity 15 years ago as a youngster.

"So, this is special, this is the big one and it's probably going to be, if we get it done, the best night of my life. Sorry, after my wedding, my wife said. She said it has to be second to my wedding."

Wakefield shock Wigan to reach first Grand Final

'Pipe dream' to reality? Wakefield one win from title

Like Warrington, Wakefield have waited a long time to return to league glory, with a 58-year gap since their last title.

That narrative is one of many utilised by both clubs as inspiration for this Grand Final encounter, with several on both sides.

One story for Wakefield to thrive upon is the impending retirement of stalwart back-rower Jay Pitts.

Born in Ossett and a graduate of the youth set-up at Wakefield, the 36-year-old has amassed just short of 200 appearances for Trinity across two spells bookending his career which will end once Saturday's final is done.

Pitts has battled through this crucial period following a bicep injury, and his determination and leadership are integral to the spirit within the dressing room.

"After the Wigan game I just went into the changing rooms and said to him 'you know you get to play your final game at Old Trafford'. It's what dreams are made of," Powell added.

"While there's a few players leaving us for different reasons, for Pittsy retiring after his final game in rugby league - what better way for us all to do something special for him as a person?

"He's been a phenomenal player, a warrior, and I know all the boys love him. He gets a fair bit of stick for how old he is but that comes to us all so I won't worry about that too much."

Warrington reach Grand Final with Leeds win

It has been 71 years since Warrington last won a league title and it is their first trip to Old Trafford for eight years.

In the Super League era, the Wire have now reached five Grand Finals, but are yet to cross the line and write their name on the trophy.

For Ben Currie, he is acutely aware of the gap between trophies, having been with the club during their four other visits - albeit he is yet to actually a appear in a Grand Final.

"It's hard not to know about it when you've got the opposite fans singing about it every week," he told BBC Radio Merseyside.

"Obviously it's tongue in cheek and it's fun for the fans to do that.

"We'd love to give our fans the opportunity to sing back to them but there's no added pressure from anyone from above in the club, from the coaching staff or from the senior players.

"Everyone wants it just the same as everyone does at Wakefield."

One member of the Warrington team who could make an impact is 18-year-old Ewan Irwin.

Since making his debut in 2025, Irwin has gone on to make 21 appearances this season, scoring six tries and kicking 82 goals.

Matty Ashton, who himself was a bright young prospect for the Wire not so long ago, spoke highly of his team-mate, who has the chance to become the youngest player to ever score in a Grand Final.

"You see him day in and day out, his work ethic, he's probably the best I've seen in a young lad [and] obviously I've been at the club for seven years," Ashton said of Irwin to BBC Radio Merseyside.

"The way he's willing to learn when he speaks to leaders like George [Williams], it's just great to see.

"He's just got that something, you can see it. Obviously I don't want to put too much pressure as he's my team-mate, but he'll go all the way and he's got a big chance to do something like that."

Warrington name a squad with just one change in their line-up.

Jordy Crowther comes into the squad, with Max Wood dropping out.

First minister demands 'new deal' from Andy Burnham to make Wales equal to Scotland

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:40:31 GMT

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth has demanded a "new deal" for Wales from the UK government that would put the country on an equal footing with Scotland.

In a letter he said powers over policing, justice, rail and the Crown Estate should be transferred to Cardiff.

Speaking at Plaid Cymru's conference in Llandudno, the party's leader said Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised him he would not undermine Wales.

Ap Iorwerth is expected to meet the prime minister, along with the first ministers of Scotland and Northern Ireland, at the end of the month.

The UK government said it was "committed to building a stronger and fairer Wales in a stronger and fairer United Kingdom".

Plaid Cymru is gathering in Llandudno's Venue Cymru for the first time since it won a historic victory at the Senedd election in May.

The party had won power for the first time, ending Labour's 27 year control of the Welsh government.

Ap Iorwerth said the result amounted to a "new dawn" for Wales, and "the beginning of our work to give flight to a nation whose wings have been clipped for far too long."

But he warned that the upcoming Welsh government budget process would be "tough", and said he would have to "find savings where we can".

The Plaid leader said his meeting with Burnham at the Commonwealth Games "did leave me feeling positive - here we had an experienced devolutionist who wanted to bring power and people closer together.

"But as the weeks went on, it became increasingly clear that the prime minister's wave of new powers risked crashing against Offa's Dyke."

He accused Burnham of having a "devolution programme for England".

Speaking to party activists, ap Iorwerth said: "I've looked him in the eyes and said do not undermine Wales as a nation. Do not bypass our Senedd. And he looked me in the eyes and promised he would not. I will hold him to that."

Scotland's government and parliament has more control over the country's own affairs than Wales, where policing and justice are controlled in Westminster, and not Cardiff, and where rail is largely devolved.

Ap Iorwerth said his proposed "new deal" would "redress the historic unfairness of our fiscal and constitutional settlement and put Wales on an equal footing with Scotland as a bare minimum".

"It remains my hope that the prime minister will listen in a shared spirit, and that he'll see that the respect agenda between the Welsh and UK governments must work both ways," he said.

"If he fails, Wales will know again that our best interests will never be served by Westminster, and that it matters little whether who lives in Number 10 Downing Street is an Evertonian or an Old Etonian."

Ap Iorwerth has sent a 2,000 word letter to Burnham spelling out his requests.

Plaid Cymru won the largest number of seats at May's election, and since the defection of Sarah Cooper-Lessad it has 44 in the Welsh Parliament chamber.

It is five short of a majority, and needs the help of at least one other party group to pass its spending plans next year. It has been in talks with Labour, the Tories and Reform.

Ap Iorwerth acknowledged a "difficult economic and fiscal backdrop" and said it would be a "tight budget".

"There will be difficult decisions. The budget arithmetic requires us to be disciplined and resourceful."

He added there was a need for a "serious and collaborative approach with other parties".

"We'll have to drive efficiency, improve productivity and find savings where we can; through consolidating and streamlining services, avoiding duplication and focusing on outcomes."

But he said that had to be "free of the damaging approach of the parties on the right", accusing them of defining "savings" and waste by "ideology".

He said the UK government's forthcoming autumn budget was a chance to "reverse the planned-real terms cuts" to the Welsh government's own spending.

Plaid has long-called for Wales to receive substantial extra funds for rail. Ap Iorwerth said that should come "now, not the 2030s".

In another attack on rivals, he asked "others in sincerity to consider whose side they are on".

"Whose side are they on when it comes to protecting Wales from the poison of the far-right," he said.

The party leader paid tribute to fire services who fought the summer's wildfires, and said he would "not allow my government to burden my children and your children with the destructive legacy of complacency on climate change".

He said they had provided an "immediate cash injection to prioritise the longest NHS waits", and had moved "quickly to begin the rollout of the most generous childcare offer anywhere in the UK".

The party eventually plans to roll out childcare to children as young as nine months before the next election.

The first minister said his government was "determined" to tackle problems in the NHS, saying "too many aspects of the service are unfair on patients and on our brilliant staff" and are "unsustainable for the future", although he acknowledged he could not change the NHS "overnight".

He said he would not "shy away" from tackling child poverty "because of a difficult economic and fiscal backdrop".

Labour's Burnham has promised to end triple lock for pensions from 2030 to fund a new national care service. The idea appeared to win praise from Plaid ministers on Friday.

Social care is the responsibility of the Welsh government, and how it spends its money is up to its ministers. Both Plaid and Burnham would face elections before the policy would come in.

Plaid Cymru promised to "make progress" on delivering a national care service in its manifesto for the Senedd election.

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast, the Plaid leader suggested that he may spend extra funds that come to the Welsh government, if any came as a result of more social care in England.

Ap Iorwerth said Burnham's policy was a "good direction of travel", but he added: "We don't know what the consequentials will be."

At a conference fringe, the deputy minister for social care, Delyth Jewell, said Burnham's announcement was "very brave" and that a Plaid Cymru Welsh government would "have to work with the UK government on this".

But she said the building blocks were already being put in place in Wales.

Burnham had previously said he would be "open" to the idea of giving the Welsh government control over policing.

He has also said: "I have to respect the governments in the nations of the UK, and I will, and give a fair hearing to anything that is put to me."

A UK government spokesperson said: "This government is committed to building a stronger and fairer Wales in a stronger and fairer United Kingdom.

"That's why our focus is now on working with the Welsh government to empower local leaders and communities to deliver good growth and jobs in every postcode."

Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:30:12 GMT

Spain's Congress has rejected a series of measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis, in a defeat for the government of Pedro Sánchez that increases pressure on him to call a snap election.

Lawmakers voted on two decree-laws presented by the government in response to nationwide protests that have followed the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, from her home.

The decrees, which introduced a series of initiatives aimed at protecting tenants in the rental market, required parliamentary approval in order to remain in place.

MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.

Hundreds of demonstrators had gathered outside Congress as the debate took place and there were angry scenes.

Protesters chanted "shame on you" and "your profits, our misery", after the results were announced.

The government's defeat underlines the fact that Sánchez, a Socialist, does not command a congressional majority and it has heightened speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.

Sources told Spanish media that the government would spend the weekend deciding its next step, and whether to dissolve parliament.

Sánchez's beleaguered government had already been mired in a series of scandals and judicial cases affecting his Socialist Party and close allies.

Abascal was evicted after she was unable to pay a sharp rent increase introduced by Urbagestión, the company that owned her flat in central Madrid.

Hundreds of protesters gathered to oppose the eviction last week and the case triggered a broader movement across the country demanding affordable rentals, which have soared in recent years.

The social backlash has seen Urbagestión negotiate the return of Abascal to her flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued, with people occupying squares in Madrid and other cities, pitching tents in squares and with a series of marches scheduled for this weekend.

The Sindicato de Inquilinas (Tenants' Union) activist association which has been co-ordinating protests, announced during the congressional debate that it was abandoning the tent protest in central Madrid. It said it wanted to "take the struggle to all the neighbourhoods, residential blocks and homes of Madrid, wherever there are rental increases, expulsions and abuses each day, and turn the energy of the last few days into a permanent organisation".

Protesters are also calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.

The left-wing coalition government responded to the social anger by hurriedly drawing up the two decree-laws in an effort to defuse the protests.

The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds".

The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Sindicato de Inquilinas.

The conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.

However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.

Friday's debate was fierce and at times angry, as supporters and opponents of the decrees clashed in Congress.

"I don't ask you, I beg you to be brave and consistent," Sánchez said, moments before the two votes took place. "Because they are not just ambitious measures, they are necessary".

He appealed to lawmakers "to put order and humanity into [the housing] market, because if we don't, it will bring down our society".

Social Affairs minister Pablo Bustinduy, of the Sumar alliance, the junior partner in the governing coalition, presented the debate in dramatic terms.

"Today is about defending an international oligarchy which is extracting the rent from salaries earned with the effort of working classes of this country in order to share it out with dividends and they don't even pay taxes in Spain," he said.

"Voting against these decrees today means defending the interests of this oligarchy and turning your back on your own people."

However, Miriam Nogueras, of JxCat, said the decrees had been hastily drawn up and lacked rigour.

She said the decrees "will allow [vulture] funds to keep buying, keep speculating and evictions to keep happening… these two decrees would provoke the opposite effect of what they aim to achieve."

The political right has argued that the government's attempts to intervene will frighten homeowners, causing them not to put their properties on the rental market and pushing prices up further.

Juan Bravo of the PP said "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes".

Three reasons Middle East oil supply is nearly back to pre-Iran war levels

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:29:28 GMT

The volume of oil flowing from the Middle East region has almost returned to pre-war levels, data shows, despite the continued restrictions Iran is placing on vessels attempting to travel through the Strait of Hormuz.

Seven months after the US-Israel war with Iran led to the effective closure of the critical waterway, the maritime intelligence firm Kpler said that in the final week of September, daily oil flow from the Middle East reached 92% of its pre-war baseline.

Analysts attribute the rebounding flow of oil to three key factors:

But some experts have questioned the sustainability of these measures, given the risk of escalating Iranian attacks or a change in US policy.

About 40% of the total oil exported from the region in September bypassed the strait and exited via overland pipelines to ports on the Red Sea or the Gulf of Oman, up from 17% before the war, according to Kpler.

Oil exports from Iran, however, have ground to a halt after the reimposition of a US naval blockade in July.

The US military has been supporting ships as they pass through the Strait of Hormuz since at least mid-June and US Navy data shows the number of vessels assisted by US forces is up by a third in September compared with August.

Martin Kelly, senior intelligence analyst at security firm EOS Risk Group, told BBC Verify that US support is primarily in the form of "air support to ships", including through issuing warnings and intercepting incoming threats from drones, missiles or boats.

But ships moving through the US-recommended southern route of the strait near the coast of Oman, rather than seeking permission to use Iran's northern route, continue to be targeted.

September saw the highest number of successful Iranian attacks on commercial shipping since March, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data conflict monitor.

Naveen Das, a senior oil analyst from Kpler, said the market oil market "doesn't trust that we're going stay in this status quo" because of the risk of further Iranian escalation and the possible impact of the US midterm elections.

Most of the oil passing through the strait now moves via a "shuttle system" of more than 60 large oil tankers moving back and forth, according to Kpler.

More than 70% of the crude oil which passed through the strait in August was transferred from these "shuttle tankers" onto other vessels in the Gulf of Oman, Kpler said.

BBC Verify has analysed satellite imagery which appears to show these ship-to-ship transfers, seemingly more protected from Iranian attack, taking place off the coast of the Omani port city, Sohar.

But there is a "question over how long these ships can last", said Martin Kelly, particularly as attacks on them continue.

Imagery taken on 24 September shows six pairs of ships docked or paired together near the port.

An average of more than four million barrels of oil per day was transferred from ship to ship in the Gulf of Oman over in the week to 30 September, according to Kpler.

Overall, an average of 12 million barrels of oil per day passed through the strait over this period, compared with a pre-war baseline of 17 million.

Oil exporting countries in the Gulf have also responded to Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz by exporting more crude oil overland via pipelines.

Just under 20% of crude is now leaving the region from ports on the Red Sea at the end of Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, which is recording exports of more than four million barrels per day, according to Kpler.

Three weeks after an attack on this pipeline blamed on Iran-backed proxies in Iraq, Saudi Arabia is now exporting through the pipeline at "full stretch", according to Kpler.

Almost a quarter of all crude flowing from the region is now being piped past the Strait of Hormuz to terminals along the Gulf of Oman, particularly the city of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Kpler's data shows.

Naveen Das from Kpler said this increased use of pipelines is likely to become the "new normal" because "it seems very improbable that we live in a world whereby the Gulf countries and Iran go back to being relatively harmonious".

Oil exports from Iran have fallen almost to zero following the re-imposition of a US blockade in mid-July, down from 1.7 million barrels a day before the war began, Kpler data shows.

There are 20 empty Iran-flagged tankers currently off the coast of Sri Lanka, unable to return to the Gulf due to the US blockade, according to ship-tracking data and analysis from the US-based advocacy and monitoring organisation United Against Nuclear Iran.

While crude oil flow from the Middle East has resumed to almost normal levels, exports of liquified natural gas and oil products like jet fuel and have remained well below pre-conflict volumes.

Fewer than a million barrels of processed oil products passed through the Strait of Hormuz on average in the last week, down from 3.5 million per day before the war began.

Additional reporting by Rob England and Richard Irvine-Brown, graphics by Tom Shiel

Intensified Russian strikes are tearing Kyiv apart, warns mayor

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:26:37 GMT

Intensified Russian drone and missile strikes are "tearing Kyiv apart", the mayor of Ukraine's capital has warned.

Vitaliy Klitschko said the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.

He was speaking after Kyiv's defence council held a crisis meeting, following new Russian strikes on a key bridge that caused traffic chaos. The city's data centres have also been recently hit, resulting in internet outages.

President Vladimir Putin earlier said Russia was acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks.

"We're talking about survival," Klitschko said at Friday's defence council meeting with Kyiv's top military, security, emergencies and police officials.

Russia's aim was to "sow panic", he said, stressing that the capital would "prevail - but only through the joint efforts of those who love it and care for it".

The mayor was speaking just hours after Kyiv's key Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was hit in an overnight Russian drone attack. On Friday evening it was struck again - the fourth time in two days.

The bridge is one of the main transport arteries across the Dnipro River dividing western and eastern parts of Kyiv.

All metro and automobile traffic is now suspended across the bridge, causing major delays across the city. Restrictions are also in place on Kyiv's two other key bridges.

Kyiv's current population is estimated to be about three million, and many residents rely heavily on the city's metro network.

One person was killed in the capital when a multi-storey residential building was hit overnight, Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Putin had decided in early September that "there are no rules now" when attacking Ukraine.

In a published excerpt from his interview with the Financial Times, Zelensky said: "The Russians have failed to occupy us. So now they are carrying out massive attacks and mass killings.

"They want to destroy our bridges... our data centres, the internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities - everything. They want people to flee their cities."

Putin insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea.

"Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," Putin said after a wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum on Thursday.

Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helps the Kremlin finance the war.

Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.

The families of two teenagers who died when the car they were in ended up in a river have paid tribute to their kindness and "zest for life".

"He always knew the most up-to-date Sunderland football news and shared it with us immediately. Sunderland will miss its number one fan," they said in a tribute.

"Luke loved spending time with all his friends and family. As a family we did everything together from football to holidays, shopping trips and spending time with Wilf our dog.

"Luke is our life, we miss him so bad. Our hearts will ache forever."

Zara's family said she had "come into this world with a fight, and we know you left it doing the same".

She had previously attended The Drama Lab in Sunderland.

"You had a zest for life and life loved you," her family said in a tribute.

"Created as a companion for your sister, Olivia, who loves you deeply and unconditionally. You made us proud from day one, you studied and learnt new skills and made life time friends.

"Having fun along the way with your dance videos, infectious laugh and smile, you have always been our beloved daughter, sister, granddaughter, niece, cousin, girlfriend and best friend.

"To everyone who has been in Zara's life we thank you from the bottom of our hearts. You made her what she became."

Sunderland College also paid tributes to the teens.

It said Luke was a "charming, approachable and genuinely lovely lad", whose "kindness, enthusiasm and character" touched all at the sixth form.

In a tribute to Zara, it said her "friendliness, warmth, kindness and beautiful smile made an instant impression" and she was always willing to support other students.

The college added Jackson, who played for Hebburn Town Juniors and the club's U18s team, was a "polite, kind and funny young man", whose presence lifted others.

Tories aim to be election-ready ahead of party conference

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 14:09:25 GMT

When Kemi Badenoch arrived for her first Conservative conference as leader last year, a member of her entourage overheard somebody wonder aloud: "Who's that?"

This baffled member of the public was actually working at the Conservative conference. Badenoch had been the party's leader and the leader of the opposition for almost a year.

It is an anecdote which underlines the scale of the challenge Badenoch faced at that conference, an event her allies are now with distance willing to acknowledge was make or break for her leadership.

And it is an anecdote which also underlines that, far from break her, that conference represented the start of a major turnaround for Badenoch.

Twelve months on, Badenoch will arrive in Birmingham this weekend in total command of a party whose leading lights are beginning to permit themselves the occasional flicker of optimism after years of misery preparing for, and then experiencing, a brutal election defeat.

Yet for all that Conservatives now believe their leader is an electoral asset, they still face an existential threat from Reform UK and the challenge of how to adjust their strategy to face a new prime minister, Andy Burnham.

The answer to both those issues for Badenoch is a focus on the economy. "Stronger economy, stronger country" will be the party's conference slogan, with the two speeches Badenoch gives - one on Sunday, the other on Wednesday - building on announcements she has made in the past two weeks about cutting benefits for the long-term unemployed.

Welfare spending is increasingly seen by the Conservatives as a core battleground with Labour.

During Labour conference they derided the event as the "Welfare Party Conference". Whereas Sir Keir Starmer sought to cut welfare spending before backing down in the face of a rebellion by his own MPs, Burnham has made clear that he believes the way to reduce the benefits bill in the long-term is more up-front investment in support for those out of work.

This is a clear ideological difference which both parties are happy to embrace. Conservative strategists believe there is a broader lesson there.

"The differences between the parties have been quite muddled for a while," one says. "Now that Burnham is prime minister we have a more traditional left-right split."

Another area where Badenoch will embrace that divide in the coming days is the pensions triple-lock.

The policy currently guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% – whichever is the highest.

Badenoch will make clear that the Conservatives continue to support that policy in its current form, breaking with some generally supportive think tanks and policy experts who believe Badenoch should follow Burnham's lead.

In his conference speech on Tuesday, Burnham set out plans to end the existing triple lock from 2030, so the state pension increases at least by inflation or 2.5% - but remove the automatic annual link with average earnings.

The Conservatives hope the sharpening left-right split leaves Reform UK in a strategic bind, occupying a less obvious place on that spectrum.

A year ago some senior Conservatives feared being usurped by Reform as the leading party of the right was a near-inevitability, but now they are optimistic that Nigel Farage's party is on an inexorable slide.

That bullishness is fuelled in large part by the difficulties Reform has faced over Nigel Farage's £5m gift from Christopher Harborne and the fallout - including a police inquiry - from the recent Channel 4 News investigation.

"I find more and more voters raise concerns about Reform with me - people who weren't previously giving us the time of day," one MP said.

"These are successful people with big garages and good jobs who do not necessarily pay that much attention but want a small-c conservative government.

"They were switching to Reform because they were fed up with us and thought Farage was now the main option on the right. But they are starting to come back."

Others are less positive, pointing out that Reform still often record higher shares than the Conservatives in the polls — and more importantly have now won far more votes than them in successive years of local and national elections.

Whether or not there is indeed a long-term trend of the Conservatives regaining ground at Reform's expense, Badenoch may not have long enough to wait.

She has told her team to prepare for this conference as if it is the last before the general election. While not all of her aides agree, Badenoch is convinced that Burnham will go to the polls within the next year.

Party high command started weekly election planning meetings shortly after Burnham succeeded Starmer.

Neil O'Brien, a member of Badenoch's shadow cabinet, has begun work on a manifesto alongside the party's head of policy. It is intended to be a more concise set of pledges than the usual sprawling manifestos.

Also with an eye to the election, the Conservatives will present new faces at the conference who have applied to be candidates at the next election.

Badenoch's ambivalence in some cases, and opposition in others, to ex-MPs who lost their seats in 2024 standing for the party again has attracted some controversy, especially when it comes to the high-profile former cabinet ministers Grant Shapps and Penny Mordaunt.

The leader's supporters are unrepentant, arguing that the party "needs to show we have changed".

Things have certainly changed since last year, at least. That may prove the easy part.

I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 14:01:09 GMT

Reporter Michael Graczyk has covered nearly 500 executions carried out in Texas, continuing even after his 2018 retirement from The Associated Press.

He remembers two instances where needles popped out before reinsertion for successful execution - but never one in which an inmate survived.

That's what happened this week in Tennessee, when 50-year-old inmate Christa Pike remained breathing and audibly snoring after two separate doses of pentobarbital, the barbiturate used in the state's lethal injection protocol.

Graczyk, 76, says he wasn't entirely surprised to hear of the anomaly - and had actually thought about the possibility during his decades-long career as a Texas journalist.

"It seems to me it was just a matter of time," he told BBC News.

Tennessee's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of pentobarbital-filled syringes in case the person being put to death does not die after the first set, according to AP, but does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.

Governor Bill Lee halted executions in the state after Wednesday night's failure, ordering an independent review into procedures. Botched executions have come under scrutiny over the past decade, since a shortage of the drugs used led some states to change the formula, or procure drugs from more questionable sources. Some states even brought back death by firing squad as an alternative.

Pike is now in hospital where she is receiving "life-saving care", according to her lawyer.

It's not uncommon for lethal injections - the most frequently used form of capital punishment in the 27 US states where the penalty is legal - to be "botched". The Death Penalty Information Center, a think-tank that does not take a stance on the death penalty, describes a botched execution as one with "unanticipated problems or delays that caused, at least arguably, unnecessary agony for the prisoner or that reflect gross incompetence of the executioner". The organisation has compiled a list of 64 botched executions since 1982, 51 of them lethal injections. In at least seven of those cases, the executions were halted because the IV line could not be set.

But Graczyk has never seen an execution fail after the injection was delivered.

"That has never happened here," Graczyk said of the Lone Star State.

Graczyk, who covered a wide range of topics for the AP during his 46 years with the news service, considers his prolific attendance at executions to be an important part of the job.

"There is no [greater] authority, power, or whatever you want to call it, that state or federal government has over us than the power to take our life," he said.

There have been 1,683 executions in the US since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre, which is when the US Supreme Court re-instated the death penalty. Texas has carried out by far the most of any state, with 602 executions. In 1982, it became the first state to use lethal injections to execute people.

"I always thought it was important for someone who has no stake in the outcome of a case to be there and to see the law being carried out and to make certain that it is done properly," Graczyk said.

"That someone is there to see it and tell others: Here's what I saw. Here's what happened."

Although he is technically retired, he still works freelance for AP covering executions in his home state.

He feels a particular responsibility to remember victims in his coverage and it's especially disheartening when he writes a story about an execution that doesn't make big news.

"I feel bad for the victims in the case," he said. "They are the forgotten folks. They always have been."

"Today, all the emphasis is on the inmate in Tennessee," he said. "No tears are being shed, other than the victim's immediate family, for the victim … and I understand that's the business we're in, but it doesn't mean it's right."

Pike's victim was Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old originally from Florida who loved to roller skate, smile and help others, according to descriptions given by her friends and family. Slemmer was tortured and killed by Pike, then 18, and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, after they met her at a job training camp.

Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was present in Tennessee on Wednesday for the execution attempt, telling NBC News afterwards that it "was a mess".

Texas, where Graczyk lives and works, does not allow observers in the execution chamber when the IV is being inserted, he said.

"So when we get into the chamber, the inmate's already hooked up."

In a lethal injection execution, the IV would typically be inserted in the crook of the person's arm, Graczyk said. But if that didn't work, sometimes it would go into the top of their hand, their leg, neck or other sites.

During successful executions, Graczyk said inmates become "visibly unconscious after just a few seconds". They are usually pronounced dead 20 to 40 minutes after the fatal dose is given, he said.

He still remembers the death of Jonathan Nobles, who was executed by lethal injection in Texas in 1998. He'd been handed the sentence after his conviction for the brutal 1986 stabbing murders of two Austin women, Kelley Fraquhar and Mitzi Johnson-Nalley.

Nobles sang "Silent Night" as his last words.

"He gets to 'Round yon virgin' and he stops talking," Graczyk told BBC News. "That's how long it took for the drug to kick in so he wasn't conscious anymore."

That scene has stuck with Graczyk for nearly 30 years.

"To this day, when I'm in church on Christmas, and the choir is singing Silent Night, and all the congregation is joining in Silent Night and they're all, you know, in the spirit of the season and the joy of the season, and I'm thinking of this execution, I'm sure I'm the only one in that congregation that is having that kind of recollection."

When people hear about his career covering executions, he said, they are usually curious.

"Most people don't get to watch someone die," he said.

But when people ask him about what he has witnessed, he tells them "it's not the only thing I did or do or have done".

How Gordon became one of England's main men

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 13:15:44 GMT

Anthony Gordon has made 27 appearances for England, scoring six goals

Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Declan Rice, Jordan Pickford and now Anthony Gordon.

All have become guaranteed starters and reliable stars for England, with the Barcelona winger the latest to look, according to captain Kane, like one of the Three Lions' "main men".

Gordon was one of England's standout players at the World Cup and earned a big-money move to European giants Barca in the summer, while his good form has continued into his country's Nations League campaign.

He scored the opening goal in England's 2-0 win against the Czech Republic on Tuesday night, after also netting in a 3-2 defeat by world champions Spain at Wembley on Saturday.

In fact, the 25-year-old's England form has been building since the knockout stage of the World Cup began - his run of averaging a goal contribution every 69 minutes started with assisting both Kane's efforts in a 2-1 last-32 victory over DR Congo.

The former Newcastle player has scored three goals and provided three assists in his past six England matches, while he also won the penalty in England's dramatic last-16 victory over Mexico at Azteca Stadium.

And after a positive start in Spain, where he has already picked up five assists in La Liga, Gordon looks to be joining boss Thomas Tuchel's "undroppable" bracket.

Tuchel likes to give his players clarity on their role and makes clear who they are up against in the squad and for a starting position.

When asked whether Gordon is getting to be one of the first names on the team-sheet, he said: "He's getting there. He's defending his shirt, he's defending his position - an excellent performance again after his performance against Spain.

"He was very decisive [against the Czech Republic] and had an excellent goal. It was very, very difficult but the technique and finishing was excellent.

"He scored against Spain so he has decisive actions and he's defending his shirt and his position. He does it on the highest level and he's a very important player."

Gordon linked up well with his former Newcastle team-mate Lewis Hall on England's left and combined with right-back Trent Alexander-Arnold, who was making his first start for the Three Lions in nearly two years, for the opening goal.

Gordon said he had been "dying" to link up with Alexander-Arnold, who is also playing in Spain for Barcelona's rivals Real Madrid.

"It's a great compliment and it's great to play with him," Alexander-Arnold said of Gordon.

"I tried to get the ball, and try and see what the best play is and try and play forward and create something. And I was able to get the pass."

Captain and record goalscorer Kane is a guaranteed starter in England's biggest matches but the position to the left of Kane has been a problem area for the team, with no player able to make it their own.

Gordon looks to have secured that role and Kane said the winger is "showing that he belongs at the highest level, for Barcelona and England".

"His performances in the last couple of games have been some of his best that he has played in an England shirt," Kane said.

"I think he is just relishing putting the shirt on and being one of the main men in the team. He is an important player for us and he showed that during the World Cup."

It has not always been a straightforward route into the team for Gordon.

Marcus Rashford, Eberechi Eze, Phil Foden and Noni Madueke have all featured for England from the left in the past couple of years.

Gordon started to emerge as a clear option during Lee Carsley's time in interim charge, but said himself last October that he had only shown "50%" of what he can do for England.

Now that seems to be coming to fruition. Against the Czech Republic he attempted four shots, more than any England player and more than any of his team-mates against Spain too.

Gordon is ranked in at least the top four of England players for expected assists (0.9), expected goals (0.9), passes into the box (14), touches in the opposition box (29), chances created (eight), and shots on target (five), since the start of the World Cup knockout stage.

His importance is underlined by the fact he has contributed the same amount of goals and assists, six, as Bellingham since England faced DR Congo.

There has been an interesting subplot with Gordon and Rashford competing for a left-wing space for England and effectively Barcelona.

Rashford was on loan at Barcelona last season but they opted to not make his move permanent, instead he returned to Manchester United while the Catalan club splashed out £69m to sign Gordon from Newcastle.

Gordon has the ability to take on his full-back on the inside or beat them for pace on the outside before putting in a cross.

"People raised eyebrows when Anthony Gordon went to Barcelona for the money that he did and Marcus Rashford came back to Manchester United," former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"He has become a key part of the England team. There were certain games in the World Cup where he was substituted and he shouldn't have been - I think others should have come off instead of him.

"Gordon [when he is] full of confidence running at pace like he does, he can go either way and he's causing full-backs all kind of problems."

Gordon says that since his move to Spain he has changed people's perception of him being a player who is only quick and presses well, even if they are two of his best attributes.

"I always felt in England, people respected me because I was fast and I pressed but they never actually respected the quality and IQ that I play with," Gordon told ITV.

"Only the players I play with ever seem to notice that. I think now I'm at Barcelona and I play a different style, those qualities are highlighted much more and people are actually starting to take notice that I'm not just quick.

"In England, it was never really respected because people just see me as really quick and really aggressive.

"In Spain, they really appreciate my IQ and quality because at Barca, if you're not technical, if you're not smart, you're going to stand out like a sore thumb."

Tuchel is starting to build a team he thinks can challenge and win the Euros in 2028.

But first he wants to win the Nations League, and if England are to do that, it is likely Gordon will have played a huge part.

School protests send shivers down French government's spine

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 12:43:02 GMT

It is a piece of wisdom that all French leaders take care to heed: young people on the street equals trouble.

Since the student protests of May 1968 – memorably described by President De Gaulle as chienlit (bed defecation, in other words chaos) – every government has run scared of angry French youth.

Why? Because youth movements are unpredictable and shapeless, often with no clear structure to negotiate with. Because when they protest, other groups join in.

Also: because as they're young, the public tends to sympathise. And because if the police mess up and cause injury or worse, then the consequences are incalculable. And presidential elections are only months away.

For all these reasons, when la jeunesse en colère (angry youth) is at the barricades governments tread very carefully indeed.

Right now, French teenagers are at the barricades and if they are not visibly angry (the mood is more excitement), they certainly have the government of President Emmanuel Macron in what Le Monde called on Friday "the cold sweats".

A movement that started nearly two weeks ago in the low-income Seine-Saint-Denis area of northern Paris has in the last few days spread across the country.

On Thursday – the high point so far – hundreds of lycées (where 15-18 year-olds finish their schooling) were being blockaded. On Friday, the situation had improved but around 400 lycées were closed in order to protect staff and students. Universities are beginning to join in.

Violence has erupted. On Thursday the main hall of a lycée in Nantes was destroyed by fire. Smaller fires too numerable to mention were lit at school entrance gates around the country. The cost of the damage is millions of euros.

According to Education Minister Édouard Geffray, 65 teaching staff including 40 school heads have been injured. "Most of the staff who were hurt said that the people they were facing… were not their own pupils," he said.

In addition, the government says that around 300 police and firefighters have been treated for injuries, and some 2,000 people – mainly minors – taken into custody. For their part, student groups say they have a long list of people injured by police. Two teenagers have serious eye injuries and one has lost many of his teeth.

The problem would be hard enough if it was just a question of meeting the protesters' demands. But there is another dimension – a political and social one – which makes this student crisis far more dangerous than in the past.

The demands do exist, even if they remain vague. They are about money – the lack of it – and the need for more teachers, smaller classes and better buildings.

On such matters, many in France would agree with the teenagers. Certainly using protest to demand money from government is such a national habit that even governments agree it's legitimate. And of course, things are indeed getting worse in the education system – because money is so tight.

This week Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu published his draft for next year's budget. The motif is "More cuts – and this time we're serious!"

Whether or not he manages to remove €54bn (£46bn) from state spending, as he promises, remains open to question.

But it is surely obvious that the era of public largesse to defuse social unrest in France is now in its twilight. Students demanding an extra school nurse or insulation in the dining-block are likely to be disappointed.

But that is the lesser of the worries.

The far greater fear is that these student protests are being manipulated by the hard left – and that the violence of recent days is a foretaste of what awaits a dangerously polarised society in the year of elections that is coming.

For the right and centre, there is no doubt that behind the student trouble lies the cunning hand of the France Unbowed party (LFI) and its popular presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

LFI leaders have regularly appeared next to the students – notably in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis whose mayor Bally Bagayoko was criticised for saying that "violence can sometimes be legitimate."

An internal report prepared for the Paris police department which was leaked to the media analysed the opening of the movement in Seine-Saint-Denis. It concluded that students were being "egged on by far-left elements from students unions… and political groups such as… LFI."

It said the tensions "could be part of a flame-kindling strategy… aimed at imposing their ideas ahead of the national elections".

In support of its conclusion, the report's writers cited the presence of protesters who are not themselves lycéens, the vagueness of the demands, the flying of Palestinian and Algerian flags, and the use of tactics – like calling for supplementary protests at police-stations - that come from the radical-left playbook.

The LFI strongly denies doing anything more than lending its natural support to a movement it regards as legitimate. On Thursday Mélenchon called on students to avoid violence "which only serves our enemies' interests".

But his opponents believe that the 75-year-old veteran – who stands a good chance of making it to the second round of the presidential elections in May, probably against the hard-right's Marine Le Pen – knows exactly what he is doing.

Polls show he has massive support – some 40% -- among 18-24 year-olds in France, and that this is concentrated in the populous, high-immigration city suburbs where his talk of a "new France" and "creolisation", to reflect France's changing language and population, are highly appreciated.

But young people are also the biggest abstainers in French elections, so the strategy – as the elections approach – will be to give constant reminders to this part of the population that the LFI is at their side, and that their vote can count.

Whether this will be enough to ensure victory for Mélenchon is another matter. He must surely take seriously the polls which all show him losing massively in a run-off against Le Pen.

If that happens, France will be in very unstable territory - for which the young people's protests of recent days will indeed have been a harbinger.

Woman who killed abusive partner has murder conviction overturned

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 11:52:00 GMT

A west Belfast woman who stabbed her abusive partner to death while he slept has had her conviction for murder overturned.

The Court of Appeal ruled that jurors were misdirected on Julie Ann McIlwaine's loss of control defence to the killing of James Joseph Crossley in March 2022.

Senior judges quashed the guilty verdict and gave the prosecution two weeks to decide if it is to seek any retrial.

"We cannot be satisfied that the conviction is safe," said Lady Chief Justice Dame Siobhan Keegan.

McIlwaine, 35, who has been serving a minimum 12-year jail term, wept on the videolink from Hydebank Prison as the ruling was delivered.

She admitted killing her partner but denied murder, claiming to have suffered a temporary loss of control as a victim of domestic abuse.

Crossley, 38, was stabbed up to 10 times in the chest and abdomen as he lay sleeping beside the couple's young child at McIlwaine's former home in Dunmurry.

The pair had been in a relationship marred by emotional manipulation and coercive control.

At the time of his death, Crossley was on bail for an alleged assault against McIlwaine and subject to a restraining order prohibiting any contact with her.

Despite a period of separation, they had re-established their relationship by the night of the killing.

The court heard Crossley took medication and went to sleep after arguments in which he issued an ultimatum for McIlwaine to choose between him and her family.

During police interviews McIlwaine stated that she had considered taking her own life.

She described taking a knife from the kitchen, returning to the bedroom and moving the child before repeatedly stabbing her sleeping partner.

Prosecutors argued that she made rational choices which demonstrated being in control of her actions.

In October 2024, a jury rejected McIlwaine's case and unanimously found her guilty of murder.

Defence lawyers argued on appeal that they had been misdirected and reached a verdict which went against the weight of expert evidence.

Central to the appeal was how the trial judge advised jurors on the legal test for the loss-of-control defence.

Instead of asking them to decide if someone of similar characteristics to McIlwaine "might" have reacted similarly, the question posed was "would" that person have acted in the same way.

Dame Siobhan, sitting with Lord Justice Colton, backed defence submissions that the wording used wrongly imposed a higher threshold for establishing probability.

Two consultant forensic psychiatrists had also concluded that a properly directed jury could find McIlwaine met the criteria necessary to establish loss of self-control.

Both witnesses highlighted the psychological impact of prolonged abuse and the recognised behaviour responses of victims in coercively controlling relationships.

"The misdirection we have identified was highly material, given the uncontradicted expert evidence," said the Lady Chief Justice.

"The appeal succeeds… and the conviction for murder will accordingly be quashed."

Adjourning the case until 16 October, she told prosecution counsel: "You have to come back to court on what steps you want to take."

How to see the Orionid meteor shower this weekend

BBC News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 07:16:45 GMT

One of the best-known meteor showers is now active until 7 November.

The Orionids are particularly fast and can leave trails in the sky that last a few seconds after the meteor itself has gone.

The display occurs at around the same time each year when the Earth passes through a trail of dust and debris left behind by Halley's Comet.

The showers peak overnight from 21 to 22 October.

The Orionids are particularly fast, entering the atmosphere at around 41 miles per second.

As tiny particles from Halley's comet enter the Earth's atmosphere they heat up and produce streaks of light across the night sky that we see as meteors.

Halley's Comet is one of the most famous comets in our Solar System and has been observed from Earth for centuries. It takes around 76 years to complete one orbit of the Sun and was last seen from Earth in 1986.

Halley's Comet is not expected to be visible from Earth again until 2061, but its debris will continue to produce meteor showers each year.

In fact, the Earth encounters material left behind by it twice a year, resulting in the Eta Aquariid meteor shower in May and the Orionids in October.

The meteors appear to radiate from the constellation of Orion, which is where the shower gets its name, but they can appear anywhere across the night sky.

Under ideal conditions, around 10 to 20 meteors can be seen each hour at the shower's peak.

The constellation of Orion is one of the most recognisable in the night sky identifiable by the large hour glass shape formed by some of its stars

For the best chance of seeing them, find a dark location away from street lights and with as wide a view of the sky as possible.

Allow around 15 to 20 minutes for your eyes to adjust. You won't need binoculars or a telescope; the shower is best viewed with the naked eye.

Five night sky events to look out for this autumn

Your pictures of the Harvest Moon shimmering across the UK sky

Viewing prospects will be rather mixed on Friday evening.

The best conditions are likely to be across southern and eastern parts of England where there should be long clear spells, albeit with a few areas of cloud drifting across the sky from time-to-time.

In Wales, the Midlands and Northern England it may be more of a struggle to see the meteor shower, with a slow-moving weather front providing cloud and outbreaks of rain.

The rain is likely to turn patchier later in the night with a few cloud breaks likely to develop.

For Scotland and Northern Ireland it will be a story of clear periods, patchy cloud and a few showers - but if the gaps between the showers are long enough you should get a view for at least some of the time.

The Moon could also affect how many meteors are visible at the peak of the Orionids later in October, as the Moon will be building to its full phase on 26 October. This means its light could make some of the fainter meteors more difficult to see.

Brighter meteors however should still be visible, particularly from darker locations away from artificial light.
