This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

6:29

'A knock on the door': How the sandpaper scandal kicked off

Reporter Chris Barrett revisits the nastiness, distrust and leaks behind Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa.

“Every Test match, we follow the ball,” SuperSport’s head of production Alvin Naicker told this masthead.

“We have more than 30 cameras, 18 are manned cameras, the rest of them are on angles. There are so many cameras, I don’t know how people think they’ll get away with doing anything wrong.”

The now infamous vision of Bancroft working on the ball with what he initially claimed was yellow tape that had caught granules off the pitch was actually not aired live. It had occurred moments earlier, before the second ball of the 22nd over after lunch on the third day.

“One of the replay guys, he was recording it,” Naicker said. “He turned around and said, ‘Hey Al, have a look at this’. I looked at it on preview and said, ‘What happened there?’ He said, ‘Just have a look’.

“I look at it and go, ‘Wow’.”

The scandal not only rocked the world game but triggered a mass exodus from leadership positions in Australian cricket’s biggest crisis since World Series Cricket.

More than eight years later, as the Australian team returns to South Africa for their first Test series in the country since the scandal, starting on Friday, current skipper Pat Cummins would like to draw a line under the episode.

“It was a long time ago, and I don’t think there’s much more to add,” he said. “We’re concentrating on the tour ahead.”

Steve Smith, who was stripped of the Australian captaincy and banned for 12 months for turning a blind eye to the plan when he could have stopped it, is the only one of the central trio who is still in the team.

Whatever Cummins’ views, there remains great intrigue over the events in Cape Town, what led up to them and what followed.

This masthead’s reporting draws on recent conversations with more than 20 members of the 2018 Australian touring party, administrators, player agents and commentators, who mostly spoke on the condition of anonymity, as well as previous discussions and on-the-ground observations eight years ago.

There are still differing versions of what went down in South Africa, and unanswered questions.

Who knew what and when? Were the teams tampering with the ball earlier in the series? Did the swift Cricket Australia investigation capture the full picture?

To gain a greater understanding of why and how the sandpaper scandal unfolded as it did at Newlands, one needs to first return to the previous match of the series, the second Test at St George’s Park, Port Elizabeth.

The teams convened there after a highly charged first Test in Durban won by Australia, but better remembered for a heated stairwell altercation between David Warner and Quinton de Kock.

Cricket Australia chief executive James Sutherland had phoned Smith in a bid to restore calm, and the Australian captain brought his teammates together for a players-only gathering in the Port Elizabeth dressing room before play started.

The temperature did not come down.

The Australians were furious at South African officials’ indifference towards crowd abuse directed towards Warner’s wife Candice, who was in attendance with their two daughters and her brother. At the same time, an underhanded game within a game developed as the ball swung dramatically over a dry wicket.

Reverse swing, which was usually generated by scuffing the ball on one side, had been a factor in the series from almost the outset and Australia grew suspicious about finger splints being worn by two of the South Africans, AB de Villiers and Dean Elgar, noticing they jogged off and on the field during play on several occasions.

The Australians had also been told that umpires had found a discarded finger splint during the previous Test at Kingsmead.

Warner, meanwhile, was increasingly agitated, believing the cameras of the host broadcaster, SuperSport, were following him in the field, looking up to see himself on the big screen time and again. His suspicions were well-founded.

One day after play he even made his way up to the office of the ICC match referee, New Zealander Jeff Crowe, to relay his frustrations at the focus on him.

Warner was wearing strapping tape on his left hand, fingers and thumb, which he had broken in the past, and with the cameras trained on him, the inference was that he must be doing something other than shining the ball.

There have always been questions about whether the Australians were ball tampering in Port Elizabeth, too, but no one has come out and said it, nor that the South Africans were taking their own shortcuts despite the visitors’ belief that they were.

The broadcasters were more than curious as to why wickets fell in clumps with an older ball.

“We knew the ball was reverse-swinging, but we didn’t understand why it was reverse-swinging so early,” Naicker said.

The spotlight on Warner at St George’s Park explained why it was Bancroft, and not Australia’s vice captain and regular ball manager, who was tasked with using a foreign object in Cape Town. Unwittingly, Warner drew more attention to himself by writing the names of his wife and daughters on his hand and finger strapping.

“It gave us reason to believe we should watch something,” Naicker said. “Why would he do that? He was distracting from the fact he wasn’t doing anything with the ball, it was actually someone else.”

After a fiery second Test in which South Africa speedster Kagiso Rabada was charged for making physical contact with Smith, Crowe and the umpires took the two captains aside to demand they clean up their act 10 days later at Newlands with the series at 1-1.

Again, the edict went out the window and Australia, feeling a sense of injustice as Rabada somehow escaped suspension, careered closer to disaster.

What transpired in Cape Town has been well documented. Bancroft was sprung by the broadcaster’s cameras after lunch on day three with a small yellow object – later revealed to be sandpaper – and all hell broke loose.

The scrutiny had been on Warner, but suspicions piqued when he was moved from his customary fielding position in the ring to the boundary.

Bancroft had not been a person of interest for the host broadcaster until vision of him working on the ball with what he initially claimed to be yellow tape that had caught granules came to the attention of producers in SuperSport’s trucks.

“Not at all, zero, nothing, we didn’t have a clue,” Naicker said.

“Bancroft’s pure mistake was putting the sandpaper in his pocket and the cameraman zoomed in. We were watching it from glorious high definition trucks – you can see the yellow thing sticking it out of his pants.

“We could see through his pocket.

“What happened in Cape Town, to be honest with you, was pure luck. It had nothing to do with us going out deliberately looking for something.

“When Bancroft got the ball, he didn’t shine it on his pants. He started rubbing the ball on the palm. The cameraman stayed on Bancroft, he didn’t follow the ball to the next guy. When Bancroft put something in his pocket, the cameraman zoomed in.”

While SuperSport provided pictures from its broadcast truck for the big screen, it has no say what gets shown to the punters. As the footage of Bancroft carrying out his ill-conceived plan to hide the foreign object down his trousers was shown to the crowd, Naicker sensed an immediate mood change in the Australian team.

“You could see their shoulders drop, their body language, they knew there was something going on,” Naicker said.

Though Naicker is adamant SuperSport would have also exposed the home side if they had uncovered foul play, there was widespread distrust from the Australian team and ex-players, including former Australia Test paceman Brendon Julian, who was commentating for the host broadcaster.

“In terms of SuperSport, there’s no doubt they were following David Warner on that particular day,” Julian said. “I knew they were doing that. I was working with Graeme Smith, and [Shaun] Pollock. You know what the Saffers are like? They’re onto you all the time, even if you’re commentating.

“They knew Davey Warner was up to something. They suspected he was even doing something in the first Test. He had a lot of tape on his hands. He was playing it up to the crowd and showing them his hands.

“As soon as he went down on the boundary, they started following the ball. They put one camera on the ball. They followed the ball all the way around for the whole session. I was oblivious to it.”

Before play during a day of the first Test, as players and the commentary team mingled on the field to inspect the pitch during the warm-ups, Julian had relayed his concerns about SuperSport’s motives to coach Darren Lehmann, though he did not have ball tampering in mind.

“Just be careful – they’re on you, they’re trying to stitch you up with something,” Julian told Lehmann.

Warner would be fingered as the chief conspirator and rubbed out with Smith for 12 months, while Bancroft copped nine months, after a fast-tracked Cricket Australia investigation.

In the full glare of the watching public, it was an extraordinary gamble to take sandpaper onto the field. It backfired so spectacularly that the umpires, on inspection of the ball, didn’t even feel the need to replace it.

A match official told two sources the umpires did not change the ball as they believed South Africa’s was in worse condition. That assessment was a reflection of how poor a job Bancroft had done.

A more well-worn mode of ball tampering in Australian cricket was to rough up one side of the ball in the moments after one of the umpires dropped it near the rope when walking out to resume play, before whisking whatever device was being used off the ground.

This masthead has also heard examples of sandpaper being used in Sheffield Shield cricket but in more subtle fashion, with a tiny strip taped onto a finger or thumb, crucially in the standard brown colour rather than bright yellow. Sandpaper was commonly used in dressing-rooms to fix bats.

Privately, match officials in Australia described ball tampering as an “arms race”. Scratching of the ball had “been going on forever” at all levels of cricket, according to a player on the tour, with all kinds of methods deployed, from dried superglue on wicketkeeping gloves, to bottle caps.

At least one touring team to Australia applied superglue over the logo of their trousers to rub the ball on once the transparent adhesive dried and hardened. Lolly snakes were also in demand to stimulate thicker saliva with which to shine the ball.

The ICC penalty for ball tampering was effectively a speeding ticket – a fine of a few thousand dollars or a one or two-match suspension.

South Africa’s captain Faf du Plessis had twice been found guilty of tampering, for rubbing a ball on the zipper of his pants against Pakistan in 2013 and using a mint to shine the ball against Australia in 2016. He escaped a ban on both occasions.

“I remember even trying to use a nail back then and my nail broke … it was just part of the game,” he said in a podcast with former teammate Vernon Philander in August.

Watching the broadcast closely from the dressing room as cameras zeroed in on Bancroft, du Plessis was one of the first to cotton on to the West Australian working on the rough side of the ball.

“When I saw [Bancroft] do that I was like … ‘He doesn’t know what to do, he doesn’t know how to get the ball to reverse swing’,” Du Plessis said.

“Because taking a piece of sandpaper out of your pockets, with cameras, it’s not the cleverest thing to do.”

One theory is that Bancroft was never meant to take the sandpaper onto the field but, urged on at lunchtime in Australia’s desperation to get the ball shifting sideways, had taken the plunge.

After Smith then ignored advice not to attend what would become an infamous press conference after the day’s play, alongside the opener, the blame game began. It was only added to by how Smith and Bancroft fibbed to the cameras that it had not been sandpaper, but yellow tape.

Back in Australia, Sutherland had turned his TV off before the scandal came to light, then was asleep and uncontactable until early the following morning, having left his phone in the study of his Toorak home.

“It was a serious ‘WTF’ moment there,” he said in 2018. “I’d like to think that my judgment, and possibly influence, would have meant that the media conference would have gone slightly differently. As we know, the penalty and the severity of the penalty, was to some extent related to not telling the truth, or not telling the whole truth.”

Some players, among them Usman Khawaja, made the case for collective responsibility, the argument being that “they’re not going to sack us all”. But as they closed ranks, unaware of the gravity of what was unfolding, they didn’t go down that path.

“I do remember ‘Uzzy’ saying everyone has just got to stick together, but a lot of other people had other views,” recalled one member of the touring group.

Australia’s bowlers insisted they had no knowledge of the Cape Town plot – and issued another statement to that effect following a headline-making Bancroft interview five years ago.

Other divisions emerged. In Johannesburg, where the final Test was played, one coach privately pointed the finger squarely at another member of the support staff.

Head coach Darren Lehmann initially tried to hang onto his job, but resigned tearfully at the Wanderers after watching how Smith broke down after a jolting trip home. As one player lamented of Smith that week, “the bloke’s made one mistake in his life and been shot for it”.

In 2021, former bowling coach David Saker hinted that culpability may have been shared more widely than it was.

“Obviously, a lot of things went wrong at that time,” he said. “The finger-pointing is going to go on and on, and on. There was a lot of people to blame. It could have been me to blame, it could have been someone else. It could have been stopped, and it wasn’t, which is unfortunate.

“Cameron’s a very nice guy. He’s just doing it [the media interview] to get something off his chest … he’s not going to be the last. You could point your finger at me, you could point your finger at ‘Boof’ [Lehmann], could you point it at other people – of course you could.

“The disappointing thing is it’s never going to go away, regardless of what’s said. We all know that we made a monumental mistake. The gravity wasn’t as plain until it all came out.”

The South Africans, who took a more carefree attitude to tampering, were puzzled by the scale of the blowback, particularly criticism from former players. “We were sitting there going, ‘Come on, guys, it’s not like you guys never did it’,” du Plessis said.

“Everyone has done it at some stage of their career.”

Manipulation of the ball had never occurred as brazenly, of course, as in Cape Town.

But eight years later, some on the tour and within the Australian cricket hierarchy at the time believe the full story wasn’t told.

As an incredulous prime minister Malcolm Turnbull conveyed his disappointment at the team’s behaviour to a shocked nation, CA’s integrity boss at the time, Iain Roy, was in the air bound for South Africa to conduct their inquiry.

Over the next few days, members of the touring party were called to a room at the Southern Sun Cullinan hotel in Cape Town to be quizzed over the events at Newlands. The exact number who were interrogated is contested, but not all players were questioned.

Some interviews were brief. Those who were central to the episode spent well over an hour with Roy, whose report has never been publicly released and is under restricted access inside Cricket Australia’s system.

Those who have read the report do not believe the public narrative would change if it was released.

But one former CA director, who deliberated on the sanctions, said there was a view privately held by other board members this was not the team’s first instance of ball tampering, and that Warner was the instigator in those previous occasions.

This director, who has read Roy’s report, accepts the board was not given the full story.

“We may not have been told everything, I suspect that’s the case, but we acted appropriately on what we knew,” the director said on the condition of anonymity.

“I’m firmly of the view Warner was the instigator.”

Another director told this masthead they believed members of the team were aware the ball was being tampered with but did not know sandpaper was being used.

Players were told by Cricket Australia there was a confidential hotline they could contact anonymously to give more detail about the events in Cape Town, but it was not taken up.

“No one talked,” this director said. “We’ll never know.”

Bath go top with Finn Russell to the fore in thrilling derby victory against Exeter

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 21:31:24 GMT

Prem Rugby: Bath 40-34 Exeter

Hosts made to fight all the way in 11-try thriller

Bath went to the top of the Prem after beating Exeter Chiefs in a pulsating West Country derby at the Rec but they were made to fight all the way in an 11-try thriller.

Exeter trailed 26-10 at the interval but rallied to lead 33-31 midway through the second half before a yellow card for scrum-half Stephen Varney eventually proved decisive.

Cam Redpath, Dan du Preez, Bernard van der Linde, Ted Hill and Finn Russell scored Bath’s tries. There was also a penalty try award with Russell converting four. The hugely impressive Immanuel Feyi-Waboso scored two tries for Exeter, with Jack Yeandle, Josh Iosefa-Scott and Varney also going over. Henry Slade converted three and Harvey Skinner added a late penalty.

Bath took control as first Redpath intercepted a Skinner pass to run 50m and score before Van der Linde slipped through a gap in the visitors’ defence for an individual try. Russell converted both to give his side a 14-0 lead at the end of the first quarter.

Exeter badly needed a response and they got one thanks to the strong running of Feyi-Waboso. First he evaded a tackle from Ollie Lawrence to put the defence on the back foot and when the ball was recycled he powered past another two coverers with Varney on hand to touchdown.

The hosts scored their third try when they capitalised on a favourable bounce on halfway. Van der Linde and Ewan Richards took advantage to give Du Preez the chance to force his way over from close range, but Bath bungled the kick-off so Yeandle was able to keep his side in contention with a try from a driving lineout.

However, with half-time approaching, Bath exerted a period of pressure that culminated in Russell dummying his way over for the bonus-point try before converting for a 26-10 interval lead.

Exeter began the second half strongly and were rewarded with two tries in quick succession. First Iosefa-Scott crashed over from close range before Feyi-Waboso took his opportunity in style by brushing aside two would-be tacklers. Slade converted both and his side were right back in the contest with just two points between the teams.

Exeter took the lead for the first time when former Bath player Will Butt carved the hosts apart to provide Feyi-Waboso with an easy run-in for his second try. The home side were soon awarded a penalty try with Varney given a yellow card for a deliberate knock-on and in the scrum-half’s absence, Hill battered his way over.

Slade missed badly with a penalty attempt so Skinner took over the goal-kicking and his success gave Chiefs two deserved bonus points from the match.

Brazil’s Lula says only he can stop rise of fascism under Bolsonaro’s son

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 21:12:29 GMT

President leads huge rally in Rio before election on Sunday seen as most important for decades

The Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has claimed he is the only thing standing in the way of far-right “fascists” reclaiming power, as he led a huge rally through the streets of Rio ahead of Sunday’s crunch election.

Speaking on the eve of the demonstration, the 80-year-old leftwinger said he had decided to seek a historic fourth term because he believed only he could prevent the family of his rightwing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, returning to government.

“If it weren’t for me standing up to these fascists they’d easily win another election. I’m the one standing in their way,” Lula told a popular podcast called Flow, before adding: “It’s either me, or it’s barbarism.”

Hours later, Lula flew to Rio, staging what his team called a “victory march” between two highly symbolic downtown locations that played an important role in Brazil’s fight for democracy during the 1964-1985 military dictatorship.

“What’s at stake is not the victory of one man, it is the victory of an idea, it’s the victory of democracy,” Brazil’s president said after the parade set off from the Candelária church. The church is the location where more than a million people, including Lula, famously gathered in 1984 to demand direct presidential elections.

Lula, who was among those who spoke at that historic demo when he was an up-and-coming politician in his 30s, added: “Either we consolidate democracy, or we will lose it.”

From Candelária, a sea of red-clad Lula supporters marched a mile south towards Cinelândia, the scene of an equally well-known pro-democracy protest in 1968 called the March of the Hundred Thousand.

“No gringo is going to lay a finger on Brazil’s things,” vowed Lula, in an indirect reference to claims Donald Trump’s administration is seeking to sway the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour with a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure.

The decision to hold Friday’s rally between two such politically charged places spoke to how this year’s election has stirred up renewed fears over the future of Latin America’s biggest democracy.

Election-eve polls suggest Lula holds only a slender lead over his adversary, whose father, the ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after Lula beat him in the 2022 election.

Many Brazilian democrats fear that if 45-year-old Bolsonaro wins this year’s election, he will move quickly to free his father and his fellow coup-plotters from jail – and then set about dismantling and co-opting the country’s democratic institutions, such as the supreme court.

“This is the most important election of our lives – and we have to do everything we can to win,” said Marcelo Freixo, a politician from Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) who is running for a seat in congress.

Freixo warned: “We spent 21 years living under a really harsh dictatorship. We fought so hard to attain our democratic institutions. And a victory for the Bolsonaro family – a family that always … openly defended the dictatorship and tried to stage a coup … would spell the end for our democratic process and institutions.”

Valmir Aleixo, a 55-year-old history teacher who was one of thousands of people who joined Friday’s pro-Lula demo, said: “This is [a choice] between democracy and the savagery of far-right fascism. This is perhaps the most important election since the return of democracy in the 80s.”

Noni Ostrower, 74, came to what was Rio’s largest leftwing protest in years carrying a homemade banner that read: “Democracy Is Valuable”.

“I’m the daughter of two refugees from nazism. They came to Brazil from Germany because of this,” Ostrower said. “I was born here in Brazil … and today I have grandchildren and I absolutely do not want to see fascism return to Brazil – it would be a tragedy for the country. That’s why I’m here today.”

During the campaign, Flávio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his 71-year-old father if elected, with some speculating Jair Bolsonaro could even become a minister. His brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, a radical former congressman with ties to Trump’s Maga movement, reputedly hopes to become foreign minister. Flávio Bolsonaro has announced plans to appoint five firmly conservative supreme court judges.

Luiz Eduardo Soares, a prominent anthropologist and writer, said he feared what might happen if the Bolsonaro clan managed to reclaim power.

“I think these elections could be the last ones in my life, for my generation … What was done over the course of 10 years in Hungary, [Bolsonaro] will do in two,” Soares predicted in reference to the European country’s transformation into an “electoral autocracy” under its former prime minister, Viktor Orbán.

Diogo Nogueira, a famous samba singer who came to the rally wearing his trademark panama hat, said: “We need to win in the first round so we don’t allow this type of people to get back into government. If they ​do get back in, it won’t just be a problem for four years, but for 10 or 20.”

Polls suggest the election is likely to go to a second round runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro on 25 October, with Lula expected to secure about 45% of votes on Sunday and Bolsonaro 40%, according to the Datafolha pollster. But at Friday’s rally Lula claimed he could pull off a shock first-round win by claiming more than 50% of the vote.

In an online broadcast, Bolsonaro insisted his campaign would prevail. “Brazil is a few hours from deciding its future … for the next 30, 40, 50 years. It’s the end of an era. It’s the end of the Worker’s party era,” he claimed, asking undecided voters to back him to achieve that aim, even if they didn’t like him.

Nations League: Italy earn draw against 10-man France, Northern Ireland stun Ukraine

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 21:11:15 GMT

League A: France 1-1 Italy, Belgium 3-0 Turkey

Northern Ireland boost promotion bid with 3-0 win

Zinedine Zidane’s first home game in charge of France ended with a 1-1 draw against Italy in the Nations League on Friday. Visiting keeper Gianluigi Donnarumma produced a string of saves to frustrate fans at Stade de France, while the hosts ended the game with 10 men after Dayot Upamecano’s late dismissal.

Michael Olise put France ahead in the 55th minute with a curling shot which went in off the crossbar, following a short free kick taken by Rayan Cherki. But poor defending midway through the second half allowed Italy defender Alessandro Bastoni to run through and clip a low shot inside the right post.

Moise Kean missed a close-range chance early on for Italy, shooting straight at goalkeeper Mike Maignan. Donnarumma made a double save from Ousmane Dembélé and Désiré Doué early in the second half, then produced a brilliant low save to deny Adrien Rabiot moments after Italy’s equaliser.

Upamecano was sent off late in the game for picking up a second yellow card, but the hosts kept pushing for a winner, and Donnarumma had to claw away Eduardo Camavinga’s shot in stoppage time to preserve a point.

“We would have liked to win for our fans tonight but I was obviously really touched and delighted to be back at the Stade de France,” Zidane said afterwards. “I am happy with the performance albeit not with the result. We had chances to score a second goal and we didn’t do it. But I am really proud of my players.”

The Italy manager, Roberto Mancini, was pleased with his side’s efforts. “I think this was a great performance tonight against one of the best teams in the world, with very positive aspects to it,” he said. “We are on the right road, and we need to keep playing this way.”

France stay top of Group A1, a point clear of Belgium who eased to a 3-0 home win over bottom side Turkey in Liège. The two neighbours meet again on Monday at the Stade de France, while Italy host Turkey in Bologna.

Kevin De Bruyne, in his 127th match for the Red Devils, scored the opening goal with a cool finish from the edge of the box, after a nice one-two with Dodi Lukebakio. Turkey posed the greater attacking danger after the Napoli midfielder’s opener but could not find a leveller and were punished just before the hour mark.

De Bruyne claimed his second goal in the 59th minute, curling a ball from the edge of the box past Turkey goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir into the top corner. Romelu Lukaku, Belgium’s all-time record goalscorer, added a third in the 76th minute, skewing the ball home from Charles De Ketelaere’s low cross.

In League B, Northern Ireland stunned Ukraine 3-0 in Slovakia to go clear at the top of their group and boost their hopes of promotion to the top tier.

Ciaron Brown, the only player in Michael O’Neill’s starting line-up over the age of 24, scored twice either side of Isaac Price’s goal in Trnava. The away win puts Northern Ireland on seven points from three games, and they are still yet to concede going into Monday’s clash with Georgia in Belfast.

Northern Ireland’s positive start was quickly rewarded as Kieran Morrison floated a corner to the back post where Ruairi McConville headed it back for Brown, earning his 33rd cap, to prod home despite the desperate efforts of Illia Zabarnyi on the line.

Georgiy Sudakov was the first Ukraine player to get a sight of goal but his 19th-minute effort was straight at keeper Pierce Charles, and moments later the hosts were 2-0 down. Morrison’s first-time ball into the box was met powerfully by Price at the back post – earning Morrison an assist in his first competitive international.

Brown’s second came in bizarre fashion just after the hour – the 28-year-old Oxford defender went up to flick on Pierce Charles’ free-kick from inside the Northern Ireland half, and Ukraine goalkeeper Dmytro Riznyk let the bouncing ball slip through his legs to wrap up a remarkable result.

The Liverpool full-back Milos Kerkez scored the only goal in the other Group B2 tie to earn Hungary a 1-0 win over Georgia, moving the Magyars level with Ukraine in second place with four points from three games.

Edin Dzeko brought the curtain down on his international career during Bosnia and Herzegovina’s 1-1 draw with Sweden. The 40-year-old was withdrawn after 63 minutes of his 152nd appearance, with the hosts trailing after Viktor Gyökeres had scored two minutes earlier. Kerim Alajbegovic ensured the spoils would be shared with an 80th-minute effort.

In the group’s other game, Poland thumped Romania 6-0 with Robert Lewandowski hitting a hat-trick. Radu Dragusin was sent off in the 22nd minute for bringing Lewandowski down in the area, and the veteran striker got up to convert the penalty. Lewandowski struck again in the 47th and 86th minutes, with Piotr Zielinski, Jan Bednarek and a Virgil Ghita own goal completing the scoring in Warsaw.

The Faroe Islands earned an impressive 1-1 home draw with Group C3 leaders Slovakia, Adrian Justinussen’s second-half goal cancelling out a Gunnar Vatnhamar own goal before the break. Moldova moved up to second in the group with a 2-1 away victory over Kazakhstan.

Elsewhere in the third tier, Vasilije Adzic scored twice as Group C2 leaders Montenegro won 2-1 in Latvia, while Cyprus beat Armenia 2-0 despite a second-half red card for Kostas Pileas.

War review – Sienna Miller and Dominic West’s hellish divorce drama is massive, massive fun

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 21:05:40 GMT

This brilliant piece of balderdash – packed with money, class warfare, sex and dastardly lawyers – is the perfect antidote to life right now. We need this!

War … what is it good for? At last, we have an answer: delivering eight hours of high-quality balderdash direct to your TV screens for your glorious delectation. Hurrah!

For War, you see, is the name of George Kay’s latest venture. As the creator of, among many other things, two series of the impeccably preposterous Hijack, you know you are in for a rollicking treat. And so it proves with this story of two horrible rich, famous people, divorcing in the public eye and battling it out in court via two teams of even more horrible, rich lawyers with everyone bent on doing as much harm to the other side as possible.

It’s a high-stakes drama you don’t need to invest in. A wonderful palate-cleanser. Who has any emotions left after a day of news headlines, scrolling and life any more? We need this.

Dominic West plays social media mogul and philanderer Morgan Henderson. I’m not sure West is so much cast in these parts any more as simply manifests in the role as soon as someone writes “wealthy cad” into a script, but his agent must be delighted either way. Sienna Miller plays his film star wife Carla Duval, who, after 10 years, has had enough and – against the advice of her lawyers – has found a legally and morally grey way of gaining leverage over him, involving a hot friend willing to do her a favour and her husband.

War is a “yes – but!” drama. Yes, there is a prenup! It says they both walk away with whatever assets they brought to the marriage. Is this is a problem? Yes, for Carla, whose earnings have lately nosedived. But! Prenups can be set aside if there has been a big enough change of circumstances. Yes, but what constitutes a big enough change in circumstances? Morgan becoming a squidillionaire and the beloved stepdad of Carla’s son Gabriel (Aran Murphy)? That oughta do it! But what would be a reasonable settlement in this situation – some millions? Yes, but what about the Manhattan apartment? But what about a monthly stipend?

Morgan retains the services of Cathcarts & Sons, an old-school outfit – offices oak-panelled throughout and Pip Torrens prowling through them as the scheming St John Smallwood, looking for weaknesses in opponents and occasionally snacking on rats and interns. Carla goes with younger, shinier firm Taylor & Byrne, recently created by married couple Serena (Phoebe Fox) and Nick (James McArdle). They are chrome and glass offices and eager new recruit Johnny (Archie Renaux), originally from the mean streets of Peckham and more recently from a prestigious US firm he left under mysterious circumstances, scampers through them.

So, we have money, class warfare, sex and more money. Let the legal and non-legal shenanigans begin! We have the lawyers strategising in seven dimensions. If they do this, will the other side guess that? If they really must abide by this requirement, despite having the most expensive tailoring in the business, how can they make it work for their client? Or against the other? Can they reconstruct a paper trail that will protect them, if not their client, from future liability? What matters more – having the better case or the better lawyers or the better press? Should they stop St John coming into court with a twitching rodent in his bloodied jaws? Or would that play well?

It’s massive, massive fun, with a ripped-from-the-headlines feel to it that only adds to the entertainment. Oh, the back-stabbing! Oh, the double-crossings! Oh, the last-minute aversions of disaster! Until the next one!

Kay keeps a firm hand on the tiller, and although War weaves through its intricate plot at speed you never get the sense that things are going to spiral out of control. It’s helped by great performances throughout, from the anchors West and Miller – venal but just likable enough, at least before a certain stripping scene involving Morgan, to keep our interest even if they don’t need our sympathy – through Torrens’ brilliant turn and on to Celia Imrie and Archie Panjabi as the barristers who are eventually instructed to represent the couple, and from everyone else in between. Soap opera with money, talent and plot to burn. What more could you ask at the end of a long, long day?

War aired on Sky Atlantic and is on Now.

Christa Pike remains on ventilator after failed execution in Tennessee

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 20:26:37 GMT

Attorneys say hospital staff are working to clear pentobarbital she was administered from her system

Christa Pike remained hospitalized, unconscious and on a machine helping her breathe after her failed execution in Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing Friday.

The attorneys said hospital staff were working to save Pike’s life and clear the pentobarbital she was administered from her system as of late Thursday.

Pike received two doses of the drug in a failed attempt by the state of Tennessee to execute her on Wednesday.

In the court filing, Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with intravenous lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.

“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike’s body,” they wrote.

They also wrote that instead of “remedying this failure” the execution team proceeded to prepare and administer a backup set of pentobarbital syringes.

In a statement reported on X by NewsNation journalist Brian Entin, Pike’s attorneys described her as “critically ill and … receiving medical care for the devastating effects of Wednesday nights events”.

“We are working close with those closest to Christa to respect her wishes, safeguard her privacy and protect her rights as a patient during this extraordinarily difficult time,” the statement also said. “We ask that the public and the media respect that privacy as well.”

Pike’s attorneys on Friday asked a state court to order Tennessee’s department of correction to preserve all evidence from her failed execution.

“Preserving this evidence is essential to understanding what happened, ensuring accountability and protecting Christa’s legal rights,” her attorneys’ statement said.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 at the age of 20 in connection with the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike and her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, killed Slemmer at a job training camp in Knoxville, Tennessee.

One grim detail about the case is that a pentagram had been carved into Slemmer’s chest.

After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, her attorneys said.

“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike had said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the last execution of a woman in Tennessee was in 1820, meaning Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in more than 200 years.

Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute Pike has prompted top lawyers, doctors and members of the faith community to call for a moratorium on the death penalty in the US.

The state’s governor, Bill Lee, has ordered a third-party investigation into Pike’s botched execution. He has also paused executions in Tennessee.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

Arsenal shelve plans for major expansion of Emirates Stadium

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 20:10:12 GMT

Club opt for improvements in hospitality and retail

An increase to 60,704 capacity had been considered

Arsenal have shelved plans for a major expansion of the Emirates Stadium, opting for a programme of smaller improvements as the club’s owners review the Premier League champions’ wider operation.

Arsenal set up a working group led by the chief executive, Richard Garlick, in 2024 to examine the feasibility of increasing the 60,704 capacity, with some reports they could temporarily hold home matches at Wembley. But the club has decided against major redevelopment and will concentrate on what it described as the “continued evolution” of their home since 2006.

Arsenal confirmed at a supporters’ meeting that improvements would focus on hospitality, retail, visitor facilities and the matchday experience – an area the co-chair Josh Kroenke previously highlighted.

“We shared a commitment to the continued evolution of Emirates Stadium, rather than a huge-scale masterplan, building on improvement we have made to date in partnership with our catering partner, Legends, the introduction of safe standing (this season in the Clock End, and next season in the North Bank), improving hospitality and retail experiences, and upgrading visitor experiences,” Arsenal said.

Mikel Arteta, who last season guided Arsenal to their first Premier League title since 2022, is believed to have expressed concern over the disruption that would have been caused by any temporary move. It is understood Arsenal did not apply to host matches at Euro 2028, with a potential redevelopment in mind.

The club’s owner, Kroenke Sports & Entertainment, which agreed a record $4bn deal to buy Major League Baseball’s Los Angeles Angels last month, is understood to have brought in Boston Consulting Group (BCG) to examine parts of the operations. The review is understood to be overseen internally by Garlick and to be ongoing.

There is no indication the review will necessarily result in job losses among Arsenal’s approximately 800 employees. Sources have suggested the work is principally focused on non-football operations and identifying ways to improve efficiency.

The decision over the Emirates comes amid competition from Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, which opened in 2019 with a capacity of 62,850 and was designed to host a wide range of sporting and entertainment events, including NFL games and concerts. Arsenal, despite a smaller capacity, have significantly increased their matchday revenue. Income has reportedly doubled over five seasons to more than £150m a season, helped by the club’s return to the Champions League and an expansion of corporate hospitality.

Rugby’s brain injury claimants face £2.8m legal bill to continue case

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 19:52:49 GMT

Costs partly due to delays caused by previous solicitors

Case still ‘in crisis’, fees need to be settled this month

Claimants in the ongoing legal action over brain injuries in rugby have been left on the hook for £2.8m in legal fees owed to the defendants, the majority of which will have to be settled by the end of October if the case is going to continue in anything like its current form.

The costs are a direct consequence of the delays that the court decided were caused by what the judge, Senior Master Cook, described in court on Friday as the “contradictory and misguided approach” of Rylands Garth, the solicitors’ firm who had been representing the players until earlier this year.

Hundreds of claimants currently stand as struck off from the action because they were found to be in breach of a court order requiring them to disclose to the defendants – World Rugby, the Rugby Football Union, the Welsh Rugby Union and the Rugby Football League – all the available documents relating to their neurological testing. Cook ruled that those cases will be allowed to continue only on the condition that the defendants’ legal fees are settled, and that KP Law, the firm that replaced Rylands Garth in July, is able to comply with the unfulfilled disclosure obligations by the end of October.

Paul Downes KC, representing the claimants, acknowledged that the case was still “in crisis” and that the players were now in “whatever watering hole lies beyond the last chance saloon”. Downes acknowledged that someone “was going to have put their hand in their pocket” to settle the £2.8m in costs. It is unclear who it will be. The claimants’ action is being funded by the legal finance firm Asertis, which has already met the multimillion-pound costs of the claimants’ legal work and all the neurological testing that has been done so far in the six years the case has been running.

Downes also warned that if the cases were struck off, the delays caused would mean that many of the claimants would never get the opportunity for justice. “I understand seven of the rugby union claimants are deceased,” Downes said. “The sort of delays we are talking about almost certainly mean there would be many more.”

Cook also raised concerns about the fact that the same legal team was working on a second large-scale litigation about brain injuries in football, and the effect this might have on the progress of the rugby cases. He was reassured that despite Rylands Garth having recently insisted that it intended to continue with the legal action in football, it has also applied to come off the record in that litigation and will no longer be acting on behalf of the claimants. It is unclear as yet who, if anyone, will take it over.

Two Iranian men charged over alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 19:46:59 GMT

The men were arrested on 20 September, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar

Two Iranian men have been charged in relation to an alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community.

Rahman Salehi, 35, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, have been charged with preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism.

Police say the two men wanted to use an improvised explosive device to carry out their attack.

In a statement, counter-terrorism police (CTP) said the charges will allege they used “encrypted applications to acquire components to assemble a homemade explosive device”.

Furthermore the charges allege they obtained video instructions on how to make an IED, and got the “liquids, components and equipment” to make an IED.

The charges also allege the men carried out internet research on targets, acquired “images, plans and maps of potential targets for attack” and carried out reconnaissance.

Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for CTP, said: “These are extremely serious charges and allegations, and have come about from a joint CTP investigation, working closely with our partners in the security services. This investigation has led to the disruption of what we believe to have been a plot targeting the Jewish community in Manchester.”

She added: “This week also brought into sharp focus some of the wider threats being projected into the UK from Iran. While this incident and the investigation into the RAF Fairford incident are not connected in any way, I want to reassure the public that CTP, working with our national security partners, are using the full range of our capabilities to protect the UK from any hostile acts.”

The men, both in their 30s, were arrested on 20 September, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

They were arrested in ​Newton Street, in the Northern Quarter area of the city centre, before being held in custody at a London police station.

Counter-terrorism police had been given more time to question the men, who were detained under section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said: “These recent events are a stark reminder of the threats posed against this country from both terrorists and foreign state actors.

“This news will be deeply distressing for our Jewish communities, coming so soon after Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. I know this will be especially true in Manchester, as we mark one year since the terrorist attack at Heaton Park synagogue.

“The fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago is a reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country. While numbers are down, I know there is more we must do.”

Salehi and Ahmadyan They are due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on 3 October.

Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “We have decided to prosecute Rahman Salehi and Salam Ahmadyan following a fast-paced counter-terrorism policing investigation in Greater Manchester in September targeting the Jewish community.

“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and we remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendants in this case are active and they have the right to a fair trial.

“We understand that this case may cause concern, particularly considering the arrests came on the eve of Yom Kippur. We want to assure the Jewish community that working with the police, their safety and that of the wider public is our highest priority.”

The Metropolitan police, who are leading the investigation, said searches had also been carried out at properties on Epworth Street in Liverpool and Lancaster Road in Salford.

At the time of the arrests, Evans said police officers were “doing everything we can to keep them [the Jewish community] and the wider public safe”, while counter-terrorism police and local forces were working together “to provide protective security support and advice for areas with Jewish communities, and particularly during the High Holy Day period”.

Last year, Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, was shot dead by armed police after launching a terror attack during Yom Kippur at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester.

Two men were killed during the attack, Adrian Daulby, 53, and Melvin Cravitz, 66, while three others were injured.

Ann Widdecombe murder suspect charged with planning terror act against Nigel Farage

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 19:15:01 GMT

Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, say police

The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has been charged with engaging in conduct in preparation of acts of terrorism including against Nigel Farage.

Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service on Friday with one count of preparation of terrorist acts. The charge relates to activity alleged to have taken place between 31 May 2024 and 8 July this year, counter-terrorism police said.

Vicki Evans, the head of counter-terrorism policing, said: “We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time. The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the counter-terrorism policing network.

“This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge.”

Kerry was due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on Wednesday, police said.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said the charge raised “serious questions” about the security of MPs.

She wrote on X: “I know the new charges made today will be extremely concerning. My profound sympathies are with Nigel Farage and his family.

“Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all.

“This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life. We must use this as an opportunity to reset. Once parliament returns, I will update on our work to strengthen protections for those who choose to serve.”

Widdecombe, 78, a spokesperson for Farage’s Reform UK party and a former Conservative minister, died in July after being hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, a court previously heard.

She was found lying face down on her kitchen floor by her gardener on the morning of 9 July and declared dead by emergency services shortly afterwards.

Kerry is accused of her murder. The suspect spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address during a hearing at Westminster magistrates court in July. He was not asked to indicate a plea.

Olivia Field, the chief executive of the Jo Cox Foundation, which was set up in honour of the Labour MP who was murdered in 2016 in West Yorkshire, said: “No one in public life should have to fear for their safety.

“Violence, abuse and intimidation not only endanger individuals and their families, but threaten our democracy and have no place in public life.

“We must do more to prevent the rising levels of abuse and intimidation in politics. That means looking across society – from education and political literacy to the safety of online environments – alongside ensuring that appropriate security and support are in place for politicians, their staff and families.”

In August, CTP reopened a year-long investigation into an alleged firebomb attack at Farage’s home in south London.

The Metropolitan police and CTP London said they investigated the incident as an “attempted burglary” but made no arrests before the case was closed pending any new lines of inquiry.

After its reopening, CTP London identified a line of inquiry that it said “may have been relevant” but had not been “identified and pursued by them at the time”.

Time to ditch the iron? I spent six months testing the best clothes steamers – here are my favourites

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 19:00:38 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Steam through the laundry pile with our expert’s top picks for smoothing creases on cotton, linen, silk and more

How to look after your knitwear

I grew up in a household where everything was ironed. And I mean everything: tea towels, pyjamas, bath mats. Perhaps as a result of watching my mother (and yes, it was always my mother) spend hours every week standing at an ironing board, I revolted. My heart sinks every time I have to go into battle with an iron. But how do we banish irons while still getting linen trousers to look crisp? I present the clothes steamer.

Clothes steamers use heat and moisture rather than pressure to smooth fabric. A small onboard tank heats water into a steady flow of steam, which you run over garments while they hang. Instead of pressing fibres flat like an iron, the steam causes them to swell and relax, releasing creases without the need for an ironing board.

Because the fabric isn’t pressed directly against the hot surface of an iron, steamers can be gentler on delicate materials such as silk, chiffon and wool. They’re also useful for refreshing garments between washes: a blast of steam can help reduce odours and restore the shape of fabrics that have been crushed in wardrobes or suitcases.

I was already a fan of them on a personal level, and now I’ve taken that enthusiasm professionally by spending the past six months testing to find the best clothes steamers for the Filter. Here’s what I found.

Best clothes steamer overallRussell Hobbs Genie VacuSteam

Best budget clothes steamerPhilips 1000 Series handheld steamer

Best clothes steamer for travelLakeland Foldable steamer

Fastest clothes steamerSteamery Cirrus 3 iron steamer

Best steamer for precisionPhilips 5000 Series handheld steamer STH5020/40

I’ve been a journalist for more than 20 years and have spent the past five specialising in hands-on product testing. In that time, I’ve reviewed everything from mattresses and trampolines to coffee machines and dining tables, testing each in real homes rather than controlled showrooms.

That experience has made me sceptical of marketing jargon and overblown claims. I test products as consumers actually use them and I measure what matters. For this feature, that meant timing heat-up speeds, tracking energy consumption, measuring soleplate temperatures and assessing durability alongside day-to-day usability.

I also use clothes steamers fairly regularly at home, so I’m interested not just in performance, but also in whether they genuinely save time and effort.

I tested 24 clothes steamers in my home, on my own clothes and bed linen. My three children have a steady stream of school shirts and trousers that need to be pressed every week, so this took care of testing how the clothes steamers performed on cotton – and whatever they’re making school-uniform trousers out of these days.

I also tested the clothes steamers on more delicate fabrics. Crumpled linen trousers, silk dresses and formal suits were all unearthed from the depths of my wardrobe to be de-creased. During testing, I looked at how easily creases were released while using the steamer according to the instructions. I was also keen to compare each unit’s ease of use: no dripping or overheated handles escaped my notice. I also noted the onboard tank capacity and how long it lasted before needing to be refilled.

Here at the Filter, we are geekily obsessed with the stats during product testing, so I got my trusted infrared thermometer and stopwatch out to measure how long each steamer took to heat up and the temperature the soleplate reached. I also measured each steamer’s run time: how long it could operate on a full tank of water before needing a refill.

On a practical level, I also wanted to see how durable the clothes steamers were – after all, many of us will be chucking them into suitcases. So I dropped each steamer from waist height on to a carpeted floor to see if they survived the impact.

I returned several of the clothes steamers to the brands that supplied them for testing. Any steamers that weren’t sent back were donated to the Salvation Army.

The VacuSteam stands out from the pack because it sucks fabric to the ceramic plate. While this might sound alarming, it’s actually brilliant. One of the few faffy things about steamers is that you sometimes find yourself chasing fabric around. The suction on this Russell Hobbs model eliminates this frustration. It also offers a decent tank size and run time, and has three settings (you can operate it without the vacuum function).

Why we love itThe suction function means anything you hang to steam – dresses, shirts, trousers, or curtains in my case – gets done much quicker. The amount of time faffing to get the steam on to the bit of fabric you want can be considerable, and I’m all about efficiency.

This steamer did a fantastic job of getting wrinkles out of pure cotton, releasing even stubborn dried-in creases in one easy swipe. It also coasted through linen trousers in minutes and is gentle enough to use on silk. It heats up quickly, with the soleplate reaching 107C in testing, and it’s simple to use. Russell Hobbs offers a two-year warranty on this product.

It’s a shame that … it’s quite heavy, and it’s loud when the suction function is on.

Tank capacity: 200mlWeight when full: 1.28kg Cord length: 3mRun time on test: 7mins 39secs

This simple clothes steamer is small but impressive. Despite having a limited onboard tank, it lasts long enough to steam a whole garment. This is a great model if you’re just dipping your toes into the iron-free life and aren’t ready to commit to a more expensive model.

Why we love itWhile I’d stop short of using the phrase “pocket rocket” about this steamer (there are a few drawbacks), it’s lightweight and reasonably powerful. There’s a small tank onboard, which with most steamers means the run time between refills is frustratingly short. However, the 1000 Series lasted a decent length of time, and even outlasted some other steamers with bigger tanks. I could get through a pair of blousy linen trousers in one go.

The Philips handheld worked well on cotton, gently releasing creases with only a few passes, and it was even quicker on linen. I did find this steamer a bit spitty, so I was worried about using it on silk – water marks are not a good look, after all. For the price, I was impressed that this model comes with a useful heatproof mitt – many more expensive models don’t.

It’s a shame that … there’s no auto-off function, so you need to remember to unplug it after use.

Tank capacity: 85mlWeight when full: 544gCord length: 1.6mRun time on test: 5mins 40secs

This budget-friendly steamer has a folding head, which is great if you’re short on storage space or want to chuck it in a suitcase for travel. The non-stick soleplate is great for getting out stubborn wrinkles, and the decent run time means you’ll be able to get through a few items from your suitcase without needing to refill.

Why we love itOut of all the foldable steamers I tried, the Lakeland was the best. The tank is large enough to get through a few garments at once, and it’s fairly lightweight.

The best thing about this steamer is its simplicity. There is just one mode, a light that shows you when it’s on and ready to go, and a lock button so you don’t have to pull the trigger constantly – and that’s it. Performance-wise, the Lakeland steamer excelled – it removed wrinkles from tough cotton and linen with one pass. You can clearly see how much water is left, and the soleplate got to 106C, which is low enough that I’d feel comfortable using it for silk too. Lakeland also includes a fitted brush to create some distance between the soleplate and delicate fabrics.

It’s a shame that … it makes a disconcerting fizzing noise when you stand it up before the auto-shut-off kicks in. It is bulkier than other folding models, too.

Tank capacity: 160ml Weight when full: 794g Cord length: 1.9mRun time on test: 8mins

Steamery claims the Cirrus 3 is a superior steaming experience, so I was keen to be the judge of that. It’s designed to combine functionality with aesthetics and has a wide elliptical soleplate for maximum surface area. There are just two buttons on the device: on/off and steam – so it shouldn’t prove hard to master. Another impressive claim Steamery makes about the Cirrus 3 is that it produces “dry steam” – steam with no liquid water droplets, meaning it doesn’t make the fabric wet.

Why we love itThere’s much to love about the Cirrus 3. It’s a simple design (and therefore simple to operate), but it has lots of features built into it. I loved that it’s freestanding, so you can put it down while you rearrange garments without burning a hole in your table. It’s also clearly well made, and durable, too. While some steamers feel flimsy, I suspect this is a steamer you’ll have for years or even decades. Plus, it comes with a year-long warranty if bought directly from Steamery.

It’s a shame that … there’s no lock button, so you have to press the button down the whole time.

Tank capacity: 90ml Weight when full: 722g Cord length: 2.3mRun time on test: 4mins 22secs

Although it comes in a range of finishes, the colour clash of pink and red on the Philips 5000 I tested puts the fun in functional. But colour aside, there’s plenty of design here to like. The active heat in the soleplate allows you to press fabric directly on to it, giving a crisper finish. This is complemented by the precision tip, a generous onboard tank and correspondingly healthy run time.

Why we love itThis is one of the few steamers I tested with a precision tip – a feature that made steaming billowy pleated linen trousers a bit easier. The Philips 5000 Series was also incredibly fast at getting rid of wrinkles from cotton. I even tried it on a pair of crumpled jeans, and it blitzed them in seconds. It’s great that you can directly apply the soleplate to the fabric, meaning it almost doubles as an iron.

The soleplate got up to 122C during testing – I was a bit nervy about pressing silk with it, but on steam alone, it did a nice job on my silk pillowcases. Other big ticks for me here are an easy-to-fill tank, a head that you can angle, an excellent run time (more than eight minutes on one tank), and the option of turbo or eco modes.

It’s a shame that … this has no flat base, so you can’t stand it up while you move garments around.

Tank capacity: 120mlWeight when full: 774gCord length: 2mRun time on test: 8mins 56secs

Best for: an upright clothes steamer

If you’re steaming a lot, you may want to invest in an upright clothes steamer. The Steamery Cumulus is designed so you can hang clothes from the hanger on top and then use the steam head to get garments from all angles. It comes with a brush attachment to protect delicates.

The water tank in the base is a voluminous 1.8l. It’s easy to fill and slot back in and, unlike on Steamery’s Cirrus model above, you can see how much water is in the tank while you work. It was really easy to use, with a simple dial to jump between two settings (though I found that all fabrics needed the second setting).

This steamer is big and bulky – you can disassemble it when not in use, but it’s a faff. I also found that while it was great on shirts, jackets and dresses, it wasn’t really possible to do trousers or curtains, as they won’t sit on the hanger. If you buy direct from Steamery you get a year-long warranty – definitely worth having on a purchase this expensive.

It didn’t make the cut because … it’s expensive considering its limitations.

Tank capacity: 1,800ml; weight when full: 6.8kg; cord length: 2.5m; run time on test: 44mins

Best for: single-stroke results

This Tefal steamer has the same brilliant suction function as the Russell Hobbs Genie VacuSteam – our overall king of steamers. This sucks fabric to the soleplate, holding it in place for a more even and thorough dewrinkle than without doing so. During testing, I was thoroughly impressed by the Tefal AeroSteam’s performance. It powered through all the cotton and linen I threw at it. The wrinkles were all gone with only one stroke down the fabric. I was delighted to find it got a crease out of a cotton dressing gown that had been there since I bought it.

The soleplate got up to 160C, which meant I was too worried about using it on silk. However, despite a small tank, it ran for more than six minutes. In terms of sustainability, Tefal says it provides technical spare parts at a fair price for up to 15 years after purchase.

There are a few issues to be aware of with the AeroSteam, though. There’s no lock button to keep it on during use, and it’s loud to use when you have the suction enabled (you can steam without it if you want, but why would you?). This meant it was too loud to watch TV at the same time – a major downside for me.

It didn’t make the cut because … it’s more expensive than the Russell Hobbs, which effectively does the same thing. And it’s very noisy.

Tank capacity: 100ml; weight when full: 1.4kg; cord length: 2.6m; run time on test: 6mins 30secs

Best for: a full steamer starter kit

The Fridja comes with plenty of – to use a technical term here – gubbins. Inside the box is a bag, folding hanger, delicates guard, a collar press and a clever bottle adapter for using a water bottle as your tank. During testing, the f10 performed pretty well in full-power mode, but the eco mode just didn’t cut it on cotton creases. It also performed well on silks and linen, gently releasing wrinkles in moments, but if you’re looking for some serious crease-zapping power, the Russell Hobbs Genie VacuSteam is a smarter choice.

I found the f10 easy to use during testing – there’s a light indicator on the back, and full-steam mode was ready in 53 seconds, although this was slower than many other steamers on test. You can see how full the tank is while you’re using it, and it has a strong, wide base that feels secure when you want to put it down. There’s also an auto-off function, which provides some peace of mind.

It didn’t make the cut because … it lacks the steaming gusto of the other models I tested. It’s a tad heavy and clunky, too.

Tank capacity: 260ml; weight when full: 949g; cord length: 1.95m; run time on test: 11mins 45secs

The 3000 Series is one of Philips’ cheapest steamers. During testing I was impressed by the whole Philips range, so I was keen to see what this mid-tier steamer was like.

First up, it’s lightweight and compact – a solid choice if you’re looking for a budget-friendly folding garment steamer. It heated up quickly (34secs) and quickly removed wrinkles from linen and silk. However, I found that it left a bit of water residue on garments, which can often leave marks after drying. Because of this, I’d be slightly nervous using this on silk or light-coloured linen.

I found it easy to use, with the tank on the back easy to fill and load in and a light on the top that shows it’s come up to temperature. It also comes with a two-year warranty.

It didn’t make the cut because … it spat and dribbled a bit – not ideal. And it wasn’t the best on any metric I tested.

Tank capacity: 100ml; weight when full: 662g; cord length: 2m; run time on test: 4mins 48secs

Although all models vary, there is one thing all steamers have in common: first, you’ll need to fill the tank. Every model I tested has a detachable tank with a fill line, which you can take to a tap to top up. After clicking the tank back in place, you plug in your steamer (I couldn’t find a decent cordless steamer for love nor extensive research during testing). Most steamers will then require you to switch it on manually, although a few will start heating straight away. For safety, I’d prefer a manual on/off button, which gives you more control over when to start steaming.

Depending on what you’re steaming, you then hang the garment from a hook or rail and swipe the steamer across the fabric. Make sure it’s hanging freely to give you better access to the garment and to ensure the fabric is hanging naturally as the creases release. This will help prevent you from steaming in new creases. For delicate fabrics or those with printed designs, you may want to steam it inside out. Steaming the reverse side can help protect the outer sheen on silk and preserve the colour of the dyes on printed designs, although always check the garment’s care label and the steamer instructions before you begin.

How close you should hold the steamer to the garment depends on the fabric and the power you’re working with. I’d start at 4cm out and then gradually move closer if the wrinkles aren’t relaxing. Use your free hand to hold the fabric taut as you glide the steamer head across it – this helps to relax the fibres.

You want to be continually moving rather than hovering in one place, and I recommend starting at the top of the garment and then moving down. The steam rises, so using downward strokes works best.

Irons and clothes steamers work in different ways and give different results. You apply irons directly to garments to press and reshape fabric, giving a crisp finish, which is great for pleats and pressing seams. But steamers use heat and moisture to swell the fibres in the fabric, which relaxes them and releases wrinkles. Some steamers do have a heated soleplate, which can be directly applied to the fabric to press it, but others rely on hot jets of steam.

Steaming might not make a shirt look as “polished” – for a particularly crisp finish or creases pressed into fabric, you’ll want to deploy an iron. But garment steamers can be useful for delicate fabrics that you might be hesitant to use direct heat on, such as silk and knitwear.

Another factor to consider is that irons require an ironing board and the space to store both items. Many steamers are a lot more compact and need no other equipment, except perhaps a regular clothes hanger.

While cotton generally tolerates higher heat and steam to release creases, other fabrics require different treatments – but always check the care label.

Linen seems to crease if you even look at it. It’s best to steam it when it’s still slightly damp. Linen fibres are strong, so the fabric generally handles higher heat and plenty of steam. You might find you have to steam both sides and pull the fabric taut for stubborn wrinkles.

Wool is super sensitive to moisture and heat, and it is liable to shrink. Use a low heat and plenty of patience, and the moisture should release the fibres nicely. Avoid placing the soleplate directly on the fabric.

Cashmere needs a low heat, and you only want to use a little bit of steam as the moisture will quickly distort the fabric. A light touch is the order of the day with this fine, delicate and expensive fibre.

Silk is super delicate, so heat can mark it. Keep the temperature low, turn your garment inside out, and keep the steamer head moving across the fabric rather than holding it still for too long.

Velvet should be steamed from the reverse wherever possible, so that the pile isn’t crushed or flattened.

Printed or embellished fabrics should be turned inside out, as heat can damage dyes, sequins and other embellishments.

Leaders of G7 nations are to release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel.

The French President, Emmanuel Macron, said ministers from some of world’s largest economies had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks on Friday.

Macron convened the leaders’ video call to discuss the global surge in diesel prices, and Trump’s threat to cut off US diesel exports unless Europe tapped their own stockpiles to help cool global markets.

Under proposals reportedly drawn up by Macron, the current G7 chair, members will release 50m barrels of diesel and 50m of crude oil into the global market to ease prices.

The agreement suggests European countries will avoid being cut off from vital supplies of US diesel after coming under pressure from the White House in recent days to release their emergency supplies or face a US diesel export ban.

Trump said he was considering a ban on diesel exports after the surge in sales to overseas buyers pushed US diesel prices to record highs in a blow to the economy before the US midterm elections in November.

Macron said G7 nations – which also includes the US, UK, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan – wanted to “work in a coordinated manner to help bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”.

He added that the G7 members and partners would front-load a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days and that ministers would discuss the “possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary” in the coming days.

“We have all committed together to releasing these strategic reserves in the proportions I mentioned, with a focus on diesel, and we are all committed to ensuring there are no export bans, and President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point,” Macron said.

Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that Europe had “agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil” and that the process would start “immediately”.

The threat of a US export ban presented a considerable challenge for Europe, which produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries but relies on imports to make up the shortfall.

The ongoing disruption to fossil fuel exports from the Middle East has limited output from the region’s refineries as well as those in China, which is a leading buyer of Gulf crude. Meanwhile, Russian refineries have come under attack from Ukraine, causing its fuel output to fall to 20-year lows.

In response, the US exported a record high of 1.9m barrels a week to overseas buyers in early August as the slump in global refining squeezed supplies across Europe and Asia.

The record exports caused the US’s own distillate stockpiles to fall to their lowest seasonal levels since 1996, causing diesel pump prices to climb above $5.85 a gallon (£1.18 a litre) for the first time in early September.

The proposed ban on US exports was expected to fuel greater competition for cargoes on the global market which would push prices in the UK and Europe well beyond current record levels.

In the UK, the average price of diesel at the pumps climbed to a record high of £2 a litre on forecourts on Friday, putting more pressure on motorists and the wider economy.

The cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, according to the RAC motoring group, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war. UK lorries, vans and farming vehicles are also typically diesel-fuelled, meaning the price rises will be felt in the higher cost of goods across the economy.

Brent crude oil was trading at just above $100 (£76) a barrel on Friday, compared with about $72 before the Iran war started. It fell to about $98 a barrel after news of the emergency stockpile release before returning to more than $102 a barrel by the end of the day.

Macquarie Group’s Walt Chancellor said Europe’s decision to rely more on its own emergency reserves than US imports would not address the underlying problem in the US or the global market.

“The core issue the US faces is not a diesel problem. Nor is it a refined product problem. It may not even be a petroleum problem. It is a global energy problem,” he said, according to CNBC.

“So what is the solution then? In short, more oil through the strait of Hormuz and out of the Middle East. Anything short of that is really just shuffling deck chairs,” he added.

The IEA, the world’s energy watchdog, ordered the largest release of government oil reserves in its history in March when it agreed to release 400m barrels of emergency crude, to help calm the oil price shock sparked by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.

The intervention represented a third of the group’s total government stockpiles and was more than double the release of 182m barrels of oil made in 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
