Etihad’s statements on funding appear to contradict Manchester City’s defence

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 17:58:20 GMT

Airline denied links to Abu Dhabi government in 2015

FA confirms it has powers to take disciplinary action

Manchester City’s defence in their appeal against the independent commission’s guilty verdict in more than 100 charges of financial rule breaches appears to be contradicted by previous statements made by their main sponsor, Etihad Airways, to the US government.

A key element of City’s appeal, which was confirmed by the club on Friday, is understood to be based on their claim that commercial contracts, which the commission concluded were part-funded by their owner, were in fact paid for by the Abu Dhabi government.

In a 2015 submission to the United States’ department of commerce, transportation and state as part of investigation into state-owned airlines, Etihad described suggestions that the government paid for its sponsorship of the club as “false”.

Etihad, the state-owned national airline of the United Arab Emirates, has been City’s principal shirt sponsor since 2009 and was the main source of the initial transformation of their revenue that followed their purchase by Sheikh Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group (Adug) the previous year.

In 2011 City announced a 10-year naming rights deal worth £400m for the Etihad Stadium, which was extended on improved terms in 2021.

The Etihad submission to the US department of commerce said: “The assertion that the Abu Dhabi government paid for Etihad’s sponsorship of English Premier League football club Manchester City is false. In 2011, Etihad and Manchester City entered into a 10-year sponsorship agreement, which included naming rights for Manchester City’s stadium. Etihad funded this sponsorship from its own liquidity.

“We are government-owned and have been since our founding. We are and have always been clear that we do not receive any subsidies from the Abu Dhabi government, and that we are financed through a combination of equity, shareholder and commercial loans.

“Our shareholder [the Abu Dhabi government]’s equity and loans are not subsidies under any applicable definition; they are the means by which the Abu Dhabi government has sensibly invested in a successful business model.”

City’s argument is also a departure from the position the club took in their successful appeal against Uefa’s charges of breaching financial fair play rules at the court of arbitration for sport in 2020, when they maintained that all their sponsorship income was provided by their commercial partners.

The commission dismissed City’s argument as “untrue” in its core decision published on Tuesday. Paragraph 77 of the judgment states: “We concluded that it was an ‘explanation’ that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the Disguised Funding Scheme.” City submitted their appeal on Thursday evening and insist they have “a body of irrefutable evidence” that will prove the commission’s findings to be untrue.

The Football Association has confirmed it has powers to take disciplinary action against City and key individuals at the club. The FA said the independent commission’s decision on City had “significant implications for the integrity of the game” and that it “will take action where appropriate”.

The FA will wait until the appeal process has concluded – which based on the Premier League’s rule book should be by the end of January – before deciding whether to take action but said it was monitoring the case closely.

The FA has powers to take action against individuals proved to have broken rules and/or acted dishonestly, which the commission concluded had been the case. The names of those involved were redacted in the 40-page core judgment published this week but the FA could ask the Premier League for an unredacted version.

“The Independent Commission’s decision has significant implications for the integrity of the game,” the FA statement read. “We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate.

“As proceedings between the Premier League and Manchester City Football Club remain ongoing, we do not intend to comment further at this stage. We will, however, continue to monitor developments closely.”

The FA’s standard practice is to wait for disciplinary proceedings conducted by leagues, such as the Premier League or EFL, to run their course before taking action.

In July the FA fined Chelsea £10m and imposed a suspended two-window transfer ban after the club admitted 74 breaches of its agent regulations, four months after the Premier League fined them £10.75m for the same offences, which related to unlawful payments to players and agents. The FA has additional powers to take action against individuals, although did not do so in the Chelsea case because those involved are no longer working in football.

Brydon Carse has been charged with improper conduct by the Cricket Regulator after his arrest on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly during a night out with his Durham ­teammates in Derby in August.

The fast bowler was subsequently interviewed by Derbyshire police, which investigated allegations of assault before closing the case without pressing charges a fortnight ago, as revealed by the Guardian.

Carse has been charged by the Regulator, however, and will face a disciplinary hearing in front of the independent Cricket Discipline Committee in the next few weeks.

The 31-year-old was dropped from England’s Test squad for the second and third Test matches against ­Pakistan in August in the immediate aftermath of his arrest, not picked for the white-ball team that played Sri Lanka last month and overlooked for a tri‑series in Pakistan this month, but is currently available for ­international selection.

The disciplinary proceedings are unlikely to be concluded before Stephen Fleming names his squad for England’s three-Test tour of South Africa in December, leaving a potentially difficult decision for the new coach. The white-ball captain, Harry Brook, said last month that Carse needed “time away” from international cricket after Joe Root, the Test captain, had expressed “frustration” at his decision-making.

Carse has 12 months left on his England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) central contract, but is not facing action from his employers for breaching the terms. The sanctions open to the CDC include a warning, suspension and financial penalties.

Brook and Jacob Bethell were both given warnings over their future conduct after bringing the game into disrepute when they were photographed drinking in a Wellington bar the night before a one-day ­international against New Zealand last November.

Josh Tongue, who was out with them, was also investigated but escaped without sanction as he was not named in the side, while Brook had already been fined £30,000 by the ECB after it emerged he had an altercation with a nightclub bouncer on the same evening.

The Cricket Regulator also conducted an investigation this summer into Ben Stokes’ and Gus Atkinson’s behaviour after they were alleged to have broken an ECB curfew by drinking in a Chelsea nightclub following victory in the first Test against New Zealand in June.

Neither were charged despite being stood down by the ECB for the next Test, with the resultant ill-feeling from the incident believed to have contributed to Stokes’ subsequent retirement from international cricket.

Olivia Dean accused of plagiarism on her I’ve Seen It track

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 17:25:35 GMT

Mattie Music Group, owners of Bill Withers’ back catalogue, contend the Grammy winner infringed on Just the Two of Us

Olivia Dean has been accused of plagiarizing the Bill Withers classic Just the Two of Us.

The owners of Withers’ back catalogue aimed that allegation at his fellow Grammy winner in a copyright infringement lawsuit filed on Thursday in US federal court in Los Angeles.

Mattie Music Group contended that Dean’s track I’ve Seen It stole “substantial” aspects of Withers’ 1981 collaboration with Grover Washington Jr, which ascended to No 2 on Billboard’s Hot 100 before enjoying a comeback much more recently on the TikTok social media platform.

“In early August 2026, upon listening several times to I’ve Seen It, representatives of plaintiff came to what they considered to be the obvious and inescapable conclusion that I’ve Seen It copied in large and significant part [Just the Two of Us], including without limitation repeated copying of the distinctively protectable melody, and clearly infringed plaintiff’s copyrights in and to the original work,” Mattie’s lawsuit said.

Mattie’s lawsuit recounted how the group hired musicologist Alexander Stewart to analyze I’ve Seen It and compare it to Just the Two of Us. Stewart “concluded that the works contain substantial similarities in protectable musical expression”, according to the plaintiff.

“The number, character, and arrangement of the shared musical features are so striking that they support an inference that the similarities did not result from coincidence, independent creation or reliance on common musical elements,” Mattie’s lawsuit continued.

The lawsuit does not list as defendants Dean or her I’ve Seen It collaborators, Bastian Langbaek and Max Wolfgang. But the lawsuit alleges the three “had a reasonable opportunity to encounter the original work before creating I’ve Seen It”, the last track on Dean’s 2025 album The Art of Loving.

Sony Music Publishing and Universal Music Group’s Capitol Records – Dean’s publisher and record label, respectively – were named as defendants by Mattie. So was Kobalt Music Publishing America, Wolfgang’s publisher.

Mattie’s lawsuit added the plaintiff provided “written notice to each defendant identifying the registration, the accused composition and the material musical similarities” on 17 August. But, the lawsuit said, “defendants continued reproducing, distributing, licensing, publicly performing and commercially exploiting” I’ve Seen It.

Beside damages, the lawsuit said it seeks an injunction that permanently would “restrain further ongoing acts of copyright infringement by [the] defendants”.

Representatives for Dean, Capitol Records and Kobalt did not immediately respond to requests for comment from the Guardian on Friday. Billboard reported that a Kobalt representative declined to comment on the lawsuit.

Dean, 27, won the Grammy award for best new artist in February. The London native had also won four Brit awards at the time of Thursday’s lawsuit – including for album of the year with The Art of Loving.

Furthermore, on 31 July, Dean and Sam Fender’s Rein Me In became the longest-running No 1 single in UK history.

Withers, meanwhile, was a three-time Grammy winner originally from Slab Fork, West Virginia. His and Washington’s Just the Two of Us won the 1981 Grammy for best R&B song.

Mattie Music Group administers the estate of Withers, who died in Los Angeles at age 81 in March 2020. The entity is named after the crooner’s late mother, Mattie, and run by his widow, Marcia Johnson.

At Brighton, Polanski raised his arms in triumph. It felt more like a wave goodbye

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 17:20:35 GMT

The Greens’ leader seems long on agitprop but short on ideas – and one byelection away from losing his job

The Chronicle of a Death Foretold. It must be weird to realise that you have in effect made yourself obsolete inside a year. Worse, that you have actively accelerated your demise. Even AI doesn’t work at that speed. But that’s precisely what it looks as if Zack Polanski has done. Maybe he should just look on the bright side. He’s managed eight Liz Trusses. Not to be sneezed at.

Polanski is partly a victim of his own success. A cautionary tale of being careful what you wish for. Like Nigel Farage, the leader of the Green party was one of Keir Starmer’s fiercest critics. Andy Burnham and Wes Streeting excepted. Keir wasn’t radical enough. Did not care enough about Gaza. Was too dull. And under Zack’s leadership, voters swarmed from Labour to the Greens. The party climbed to a record high of 18% in the polls and won the Gorton and Denton byelection against the staggeringly dim Matt Goodwin.

But then Keir was airbrushed out of history and Labour chose a prime minister that a lot of people in the country actually liked. Someone who could communicate. Even if they weren’t in love with Andy, voters were willing to give him a chance. Ever since, the Greens have tanked. Now they are down to 11%. Zack’s net approval rating’s almost as bad as Nige’s. Not content with this, Zack has almost certainly fatally holed his credibility by standing in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, which he is very likely to lose. Shares in brand Polanski have never been lower.

The Green party conference in Brighton could not have come at a worse time. Zack didn’t want it to go ahead because he wanted to concentrate on his byelection campaign. Senior members of the leadership were briefing that the whole conference was pointless.

But the conference did go ahead, and on Friday lunchtime it began with the local MP, Siân Berry, and Gorton and Denton MP, Hannah Spencer, doing their best impressions of a Duracell bunny. High energy, hyperactive enthusiasm. Like Blue Peter presenters on amphetamines. Everything was great. Never better. “Come on, everybody,” said Siân. “We think the best of everyone.” We’ll reserve judgment on that till Sunday when some of the more toxic issues are aired. Hannah was also rushing on her run. “We have forced the government to change course,” she said. Mmm. And that’s sort of the problem.

Siân and Hannah were just the warm-up acts for the main event. And with the arrival of Polanski to give his leader’s speech, almost all the excitement was sucked out of the room. The packed hall became like a dead zone. The slogan on the back of the stage said “real hope” but all you could feel was desperation. The sense that the Greens had had a fleeting moment in the sun and the long nights were drawing in.

It is customary for a leader’s speech to be punctuated with standing ovations. That’s the whole point of them. Even if the leader is talking pure bollocks. Zack got two. One for saying Palestine and the other for “green revolution”. In Brighton, everyone gets a standing ovation for saying Palestine and green revolution. It’s written in the city’s DNA.

Zack looked down from the start. Normally he’s an animated speaker, but today he just looked defeated. As if he was trying and failing to will himself to care. It was just too big an ask. And maybe you couldn’t blame him. His team had chosen this day to brief the media that if they could persuade 30% of Labour voters in Holborn and St Pancras to vote for Zack, he would lose by only four points. That’s a bit like walking into A&E and being told by the doctors they can give you a heart and lung transplant but you are going to die regardless.

“What a year,” he began. Indeed. Though maybe he didn’t need to spell it out so clearly. From fringe party to something more mainstream and back again. All over in a heartbeat. Zack couldn’t disguise the look of regret in his eyes. From time to time his head bobbed up and down, as if trying to get his brain to agree with him, but his body language spoke of an inner despair. Rather than the leader of a national political party, he came across as a rather shouty undergraduate student. Long on agitprop and soundbites. Short on genuine argument.

Sure, there were nods to taxing the rich more, imposing rent controls, Free Palestine and environmentalism. But these were just words to try to please the crowds. There was no sense of how much this would cost, how it would be done or where the money would come from. “I say to government, ‘Slogans aren’t enough’,” he said without a hint of self-awareness. You could only put it down as a man who knows his political career could be as good as over by this time next week.

There was something rather sad about it all. The Greens had wanted so much more than this. They had believed they had elected a man of substance – someone less polite and deferential than previous leaders such as Caroline Lucas and Carla Denyer – who would go toe to toe with the other mainstream parties. But he had turned out to be a chimera. Just another hollow man. Long on slogans, short on ideas. A leader who had briefly burned brightly but had fizzled out. A victim of his own success. A one-year wonder destined to become a man of absence. Losing the byelection would only hasten the end.

Most leader’s speeches last about an hour. Zack was done and dusted in just over half that. Even then, it felt far too fluffy, far too long. Come the end, Hannah and Sian came on stage to raise his arms aloft in triumph. It felt more like a long wave goodbye.

Palestine Action activists brandished whips, hammers and kebab skewers to intimidate security guards and keep them at bay during a break-in at an Israel-linked arms factory, a court has heard.

Five defendants are accused by prosecutors of being part of a “black team”, wearing black jumpsuits, whose role was to overwhelm security guards, so that a “red team”, wearing red jumpsuits, could break into the Elbit systems factory in Filton, near Bristol, and smash up equipment including drones.

Qesser Zuhrah, 21, Zahra Farooque, 26, Kamran Ahmed, 29, Heba Muraisi, 31, and Liam Mullany, 34, went on trial at Woolwich crown court on Friday charged with criminal damage and violent disorder over the raid during the early hours of 6 August 2024. They deny the charges.

The prosecutor Deanna Heer KC told the jury that an alleged plan of the raid, discovered by police, said: “Shut Elbit Down. This is our primary objective as Palestine Action. We can do that by sticking together and ensuring its destruction with our brains and muscle.”

Jurors were told that a security guard, Nigel Shaw, who had struck a member of the black team across the back of his legs with an umbrella, suffered a 4cm laceration to his head after being attacked.

Heer said: “The role of the black team was to overwhelm the security guards so that the red team could break into the factory. They did so by threatening, intimidating and, if necessary, assaulting the guards, by throwing fireworks at them and brandishing weapons, such as whips and hammers and large kebab skewers.

“When one of the black team was detained by a security guard, other members of the group attacked him, hitting him until he released their colleague, leaving the security guard with a laceration to his head.”

She told the court the break-in was carefully planned and a prison van, driven by a member of the red team, crashed through the first perimeter fence surrounding Elbit’s factory at about 3.30am.

The black team followed on foot shouting slogans including “Free Palestine” as the van was driven through a second perimeter fence at the site of the firm, whose parent company is based in Israel.

Heer said: “The footage shows that the black team used or threatened violence against the security guards that night. It is clear, the prosecution submit, that Nigel Shaw was physically attacked and [was] caused injury but violence was also used or threatened by the black team before then when they threw fireworks or smoke grenades or cracked whips and brandished skewers in order to intimidate the security guards and keep them away.”

She said the idea was for the red team to destroy “as much property as possible” before the police arrived and they used fire extinguishers filled with red paint to spray the walls and floor, crowbars and sledgehammers to smash apart computer equipment and drones and also damaged a disabled toilet.

The court was told that the plan for the break-in described the black team, who had their faces covered, as “coverts” because the intention was “to get away without being caught”, unlike the red team who were labelled “overts”.

The trial continues.

Patrick McCabe is instantly recognisable in the early autumn sunshine, his wheelchair surrounded by fellow pupils at Fallibroome Academy in Macclesfield, Cheshire as they move from lesson to lesson, chatting, laughing and joking around.

His extraordinary GCSE success this summer has become the stuff of legend. The 16-year-old has cerebral palsy and it took four months for him to complete his exams using eye-tracking technology. Now Patrick has started his A-levels – French, business and media studies – and fresh challenges lie ahead.

In person, Patrick is impish, thoughtful, articulate, witty, intelligent and honest. Using his augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) device, he tells the Guardian school has been a good experience overall. Born in Switzerland, his family moved back to England when he was six. Since then, he has gone to local mainstream schools, where he wanted to learn like everyone else.

“The best thing has been that, just like my big brothers, I’ve been able to learn and develop skills and gain knowledge of the world around me,” he said. “Even if some days I didn’t always want to go [to school], I think the opportunity to learn has helped me to grow and develop an independent mind.”

It has not been easy. “The most difficult things have been building meaningful relationships, and communication barriers do exist,” said Patrick. “People are not always familiar with Eyegaze technology and are not always willing or able to give it a chance in terms of friendships.”

In many ways, Patrick epitomises the Labour government’s ambitions for students with special educational needs and disabilities (Send). Forthcoming reforms are built on an inclusive approach, keeping children and young people in local – rather than special – schools with all the necessary expertise and support on hand.

But Patrick’s story also illustrates the scale of change required if education and assessment in England are to be truly inclusive. His experience shows that exams are far from accessible to all, his family and school say vital expertise is not always available and – crucially – funding is never enough.

“All we wanted was for Patrick to have the opportunity to demonstrate his knowledge and be given something resembling a level playing field compared to other students,” said the headteacher, Ross Martland. The school and Patrick’s mother, Jo, battled with the exam boards to try to ensure he was given a fair chance.

In the end, it doesn’t sound very fair at all. While his peers spent the first part of the year revising, Patrick’s exams got under way on 2 February and went on every morning until 5 June. It required a herculean effort from him, which left him exhausted, frustrated and sometimes ill.

A 30-mark question that might form just one element of an exam could take up to six hours. Patrick was supported throughout by CandLE, an organisation that helps students using AAC technology to access education across the UK. That he passed all seven GCSEs and achieved the grades he needed to continue into sixth form is testament to his determination.

“Revising for my GCSEs was very exhausting because it took extra time and effort to revise in the first place,” said Patrick. “I felt I had to work harder to express what I know, even when I understand the subject. This was tiring, both physically and mentally. I needed extra breaks to rest, but I still wanted to do my best to show what I had learned.”

after newsletter promotion

Martland is fully supportive of the government’s Send ambitions. “I think the plans are right. Morally and values-wise, it’s absolutely right.” The issue is funding, he said, adding: “I’m concerned it will add significant pressures to schools if it’s not resourced properly.”

Throughout his time at Fallibroome, Patrick has worked with a devoted team of teaching assistants who support him not only with his learning in class but also his personal care. “We are incredibly proud of Patrick and all of our Send students,” said Rachel Crew, one of the teaching assistants working with him.

Patrick says the transition to sixth form is going well. He’s shed the bottle green uniform in favour of a smart blue suit and he says the school is doing everything it can to support him.

He says his mum has been “amazing” and he thinks students with physical disabilities who use eye-tracking technology should be assessed in a more appropriate way, so they don’t face additional barriers. But it is not only exams that worry him. “My concerns remain around friendships, if I’m honest,” he says.

So what’s Patrick planning next? After A-levels, he wants to study media at university. “I find it interesting and I’d like to go into the industry.” His mum tentatively suggests nearby Salford. Patrick’s looking at Bournemouth, 200 miles away. Is he daunted? No chance. “I feel excited about the experience.”

‘I thought Brassed Off might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley’: the director of Andy Burnham’s favourite film on its 30 year anniversary

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:56:40 GMT

Ahead of a live performance in the Royal Albert Hall, the writer Mark Herman explains why he’s not surprised it’s one of the new Prime Minister’s favourites and a why film like this wouldn’t get made now

It is one of the prime minister’s all-time favourite films and has endured in the hearts of the British public since it was released in 1996. Ostensibly a story about a small town colliery band’s journey to the finals of Britain’s biggest brass band competition at the Royal Albert Hall, Brassed Off is unashamedly political.

“I think the people who went expecting a political film got the bonus of a bit of a comedy,” says its writer, Mark Herman, three decades on. “And the people who went expecting comedy got the bonus of the political message. I think anybody who went got a sort of bonus they might not have expected.

“On the face of it, a brass band film is not an easy pitch but word of mouth really rolled and suddenly it went on and on in places for months,” he recalls. “I thought it might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley for about two weeks,” laughs Herman. “So yeah, it’s amazing.”

Set in the fictional industrial South Yorkshire town of Grimley a decade after mineworkers brought themselves to destitution trying to save their livelihoods, it captures the hopelessness felt by former miners who struggled to keep themselves out of the dole queue during the slow and painful destruction of the mining industry by the Tory government.

Starring Pete Postlethwaite, Tara Fitzgerald and Ewan McGregor, it follows the Grimley Colliery Band as they await a judgment from British Coal as to whether their pit will be closed. A resounding success, Brassed Off went on to be number 85 in the BFI’s list of Top 100 British Films and spawned a popular stage play. To add to the plaudits, Andy Burnham recently named it as one of his four favourite films.

“How do I feel about that? It’s good!” says Herman. “It’s very flattering, but I’d have been more surprised if he’d have chosen Notting Hill.”

On its 30th anniversary, fiction and real life are set to collide when Grimethorpe Colliery Band – the group that inspired the film – heads to the real-life Royal Albert Hall to perform the music alongside a special screening.

The film’s success at the time was “surprising and very rewarding” but the enduring appeal, Herman believes, is because, “It’s not about a brass band in Grimley, it’s about the universal subject of being downtrodden.

“It’s really interesting hearing teens and 20-year-olds talking about the film, because it’s such an old film for them, but it really hits them. They get the message everybody got 30 years ago, because it’s still relevant and still plays.” But these films are a dying breed and Herman admits he is “fairly pessimistic” about the current state of the British film industry. “I feel like films like Brassed Off wouldn’t be made [now].”

“I’ve spent the last 10 years trying to get films similar to Brassed Off off the ground but can’t,” he says. “It seems to be blockbusters or micro-budget at the moment and there’s no space for mid-budget British films like those, films like I want to make.

“The studios are not as brave as they were,” he adds. “They’d stick their neck out, in what I call the old days. It was quite a risky film to make, Brassed Off, but now they seem to only want to put money behind dead certs.”

His favourite films of the last year were I Swear, the biography of a man with severe Tourette syndrome, and The Ballad of Wallis Island, an offbeat comedy drama written by and starring the comedians Tim Key and Tom Basden.

His path – from childhood in the East Yorkshire seaside town of Bridlington, to studying graphic design at Leeds Polytechnic (now Leeds Beckett University) and the National Film and Television School – would still open doors for youngsters in the industry, he thinks. But it is not an easy industry to break into, and now, in his early 70s, he thinks the advice he got when he was young – advice he took for a short while – to move to London, probably still stands.

“If I’d have [stayed in] London and networked I’d have probably done more films, but maybe not ones I care about as much,” he says.

Instead he wrote a powerful script, unashamed to spell out in no uncertain terms how the Conservative government destroyed communities and ruined lives, the effects of which continue. Higher mortality rates from suicide, alcohol and drugs developed – and persist to this day – in former pit towns and the shadow of Margaret Thatcher still lingers like an oil stain in these communities.

In a climactic scene in the Royal Albert Hall, Postlethwaite’s character, Danny, the band’s conductor, gives a memorable speech – later immortalised in the protest song Tubthumping by Chumbawamba – shouting: “I thought that music mattered. But does it bollocks. Not compared to how people matter.”

During filming, Birmingham town hall was substituted for the London venue, which was too expensive and “didn’t look anything like the Albert Hall”, Herman jokes.

Brassed Off Live will be a “strange experience … when our fake Albert Hall is on screen and you’re sitting in the Albert Hall. It’s a thrill. Thirty years ago would we ever imagine being in the Albert Hall still watching it? It’s amazing.”

Brassed Off Live is at the Royal Albert Hall, London, on Friday 2 October

The Guardian view on the Conservative conference: a party still searching for a purpose

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:51:19 GMT

Kemi Badenoch has a lot to say about Labour and Reform UK but none of it amounts to a coherent alternative programme for government

The Conservative party is far from the margin of British politics, but it has yet to recover the relevance to which it feels historically entitled. The Tories are flattered by their status as the official opposition in parliament. In the wider country, Reform UK has set the agenda on the right, overtaking Kemi Badenoch’s party in opinion polls and poaching MPs from her benches.

But Nigel Farage’s progress has stalled. Scrutiny of Reform’s finances has made its leader look shifty. Competition from Restore Britain, an extreme nationalist party, has denied Mr Farage the luxury of taking far-right votes for granted. Pandering to a hardcore audience makes it difficult for Reform to affect the moderation required to capture more Tory and Labour votes.

This creates an opportunity for Conservatives to reassert themselves as the mainstream opposition to Labour. Many Tories believe the available space has grown since Andy Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister.

Mr Burnham has a bolder agenda than his predecessor, and he communicates it well – qualities that have been rewarded with a poll-ratings recovery. It is also a programme with unapologetic left-liberal ambition – universal social care, free at the point of use; opening the door to public ownership of utilities; dissolving red lines in relations with the EU; electoral reform. Under new leadership, the party has risen out of the defensive crouch from which it fought the election, fearful of offending Conservative sensibilities. Conservatives are duly offended. The vision that Mr Burnham outlined at his party conference last week was a repudiation of Margaret Thatcher’s legacy, and there is no greater heresy in Tory doctrine.

Mrs Badenoch will not struggle to articulate a rebuttal at her party’s conference in Birmingham over the next few days. She is a devotee of the Conservative cult of the Iron Lady, committed to low taxes and a smaller state as axioms of political virtue. She believes there are voters who share that conviction, who will be repelled by Labour, and who are deeply wary of Mr Farage. This is the electoral audience she is targeting.

It isn’t an irrational strategy, but nor is it a well-developed one. Mrs Badenoch likes to debate the opponent she wants rather than the one she has. She accuses Mr Burnham of taking Britain back to the 1970s, without engaging with his analysis of what went wrong in the 1980s or considering that her own nostalgic ideology might need revision with reference to subsequent decades.

Her approach to Reform is even more blinkered. The Tories want voters to take a dim view of Mr Farage’s candidacy to be prime minister, but they are selective in their criticism. Mrs Badenoch joins the fray over opaque donations, but has less to say about Reform’s toxic rhetoric around immigration, largely because Conservative policy fits the Faragist mould. The traffic in defections has slowed, but the boundary between the two parties is porous.

To make her party competitive in British politics, Mrs Badenoch needs more serious arguments. She needs an answer to Mr Burnham that doesn’t retreat into lazy 20th-century political cliche. And she needs to reject Mr Farage’s brand of national populism in terms that give voters reasons to distinguish between their two parties on points of principle, when at the moment there are none.

The Guardian view on Barack Obama’s new podcast: all the president’s books

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:50:35 GMT

From Oprah Winfrey to Dua Lipa, there is no shortage of celebrity literary champions. But the former US leader is in a class of his own

At the Labour party conference Andy Burnham revealed that Hamlet, Joseph Conrad’s Heart of Darkness and Tony Harrison’s poem V are his favourite works of literature. The UK’s first prime minister with an English literature degree was not the only political figure sharing his book choices last week. Barack Obama, the US’s most literary president since Abraham Lincoln, launched a new podcast in which he discusses six books that shaped him with writer friends.

First up was the actor – and recently turned short story writer – Tom Hanks on Marilynne Robinson’s Gilead, a meditation on faith, fatherhood and forgiveness in the form of a letter written by a 76-year-old pastor to his son. It was an unabashedly highbrow start. With the exception of John le Carré’s cold war classic Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, Mr Obama’s selections are American: Toni Morrison’s Song of Solomon, Cormac McCarthy’s All the Pretty Horses, James Baldwin’s essays The Fire Next Time and Robert Penn Warren’s All the King’s Men. Questions of democracy, race, power and violence are all here.

The former president’s summer and end-of-year reading lists are known for having an “Obama effect” on sales. This season’s picks include the Booker-shortlisted The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout, of whom he has long been a fan. His podcast, A Great Book with Barack Obama, joins a crowded arena. Established celebrity book clubs include those run by Oprah Winfrey and Reese Witherspoon in the US and Richard and Judy in the UK. These are now competing with starry newcomers, such as Dua Lipa’s Service95, appealing to gen Z readers. The British singer’s conversations with bookish heavyweights have seen her hailed as “the best literary interviewer” of our time. Audiences can decide for themselves this month when she is curator and host of the London literature Festival at the Southbank Centre, with guests including Zadie Smith.

With reading for pleasure among young people at its lowest level in two decades, high-profile champions have an important role to play – even if celebrity endorsements are sometimes accompanied by a whiff of elitism. Back in 2001, Jonathan Franzen caused a furore by snubbing an invitation for The Corrections to be featured on Oprah’s Book Club, deriding her choices as “schmaltzy” and “one-dimensional”. The announcement that Lipa would give the Booker prize ceremony speech in 2022 raised eyebrows in the industry. Yet a recommendation from Winfrey or Lipa can catapult a novel on to the bestseller lists.

You don’t need to be a pop star or president to become a literary tastemaker. Online communities such as BookTok and Bookstagram have democratised the book world. Everyone can be a critic today. As the rise of romantasy novels shows, bookfluencers are a powerful new force in publishing.

But in a speeded-up world, books podcasts are a balm for the soul. They can boost debuts, resurface old classics and rescue forgotten treasures. The path from politics to podcasting is now a well-trodden one. But an in-depth literary podcast from a former US president is a first, and not likely to be seconded anytime soon. “There are jokes about the Trump library,” Robinson quipped in 2018. “Because there won’t be any books in there.” For Mr Obama, reading helps to create “a moral framework” and is “a way of understanding the challenges of the moment”. Rarely have literary-minded leaders been so urgently needed.

The Green party’s anti-Zionism motion is yet another attempt to tell Jews how we should think

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:40:45 GMT

The resolution shows little understanding of what Zionism is, who Jews are or how antisemitism works

Tomorrow I will be in synagogue to say Kaddish, the traditional mourner’s prayer, in memory of my father who died eight years ago this week. If I were a member of the Green party, I would have reason to believe that that simple act could soon see me expelled as a racist.

It sounds hyperbolic, but the warning comes from Green party activists opposed to a resolution declaring that Zionism is racism, which will be debated at the party conference this weekend. The motion, which if passed would instantly become party policy, holds that Zionism should be “treated as any other form of racism”. On that logic, given that the Greens do not admit members of self-described racist organisations, they could not tolerate members of self-described Zionist organisations – a category that includes almost every synagogue, or synagogue movement, in Britain and indeed the world. Which is why saying Kaddish could lead to expulsion.

All this sounds arcane, but the Greens are no longer a fringe party. They beat Labour in a byelection in February, one of the events that catalysed the eventual removal of Keir Starmer. The Greens’ leader, Zack Polanski, hopes to win Starmer’s former seat of Holborn and St Pancras in next Thursday’s byelection. But the row over Zionism has cast a cloud over his campaign. If he loses the seat, many will conclude that the Green surge is over – which would relieve a significant electoral headache for Labour and Andy Burnham. So the stakes are high.

The charitable reading is that this move originates in genuine, and widespread, horror at Israel’s bombardment of Gaza, followed by a series of unfortunate misunderstandings of what Zionism is, who Jews are and how antisemitism works.

That, I repeat, is the charitable reading, but let’s go with it. It’s worth saying that if the proposers of this motion had simply wanted to express their revulsion at the catastrophic devastation of Gaza and those who executed it, they could have denounced Israel and the Israeli government. But their admitted purpose is to go much further – to attack Israel’s very existence and the movement that led to it: Zionism.

As Polanski, who has been twisting in all directions on this subject, has tried to argue, Zionism means different things to different people. The great Israeli writer and peacenik Amos Oz used to describe it as a family name, an umbrella for a wide range of radically different worldviews. Before Israel’s founding in 1948, you’d have cultural Zionists slugging it out with religious Zionists, Marxist Zionists raging against rightwing militaristic Zionists, all of them wholly at odds with the dominant group: socialist Zionists. What they had in common was the simple belief that Jews had the right of self-determination in their ancestral homeland, the land they had for millennia called Eretz Yisrael, the Land of Israel, and which the rest of the world called Palestine.

To this day, that’s essentially what it means to be a Zionist – that you believe in a Jewish national home in some portion of historic Palestine. There are rightwing Zionists who think it should be in all of that land; there are leftwing Zionists who think it should be broadly within the much smaller boundaries that existed before the 1967 war and alongside a Palestinian state. But both groups are Zionists. The racist minister Itamar Ben-Gvir is a Zionist, but so are many of the Jewish and Israeli anti-occupation activists who volunteer to act as a “protective presence”, putting their own bodies between settler extremists and Palestinian villagers in the West Bank. To brand everyone under that one umbrella as a racist shows a deep ignorance of what the word Zionism means and the sheer range of people who identify with it.

It also reveals a wilful misunderstanding of Jews and Judaism. Social media has been full in recent days of supposedly progressive non-Jews telling Jews what Judaism is and what it is not – with an arrogance that, I suspect, they would find unacceptable iin a majority group addressing any other minority – and the same error recurs. Breezily, we are told that Zionism is merely a political ideology, wholly separate from Judaism, which means, happily, that one can denounce the former without expressing any animus towards the latter. If only it were so simple.

Take that Kaddish prayer I’ll be saying. It refers to “Israel” three times. The Jews were called Am Yisrael, the people of Israel, centuries before we were called Jews. What’s more, when I say the prayer, I will, following tradition, be facing east – towards Jerusalem. The prayer book in my hand will be full of references to Jerusalem and indeed to Zion, expressing in a hundred poetic ways a yearning to return. This is not some new, political thing. It’s what Jews have been saying and doing for millennia. Many, many centuries before Zionism was a political movement, it was a longing – the need to end a painful exile from the Land of Israel – enshrined in the very heart of Judaism.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Which is one reason why, incidentally, the language of “settler colonialism”, repeated in the Green motion, fits Zionism so badly. When, say, the French settled in Algeria, they were not returning to the land where the French people were born, where French had been spoken two millennia earlier, and to which the dispersed and lethally persecuted French people had longed to return for 2,000 years. It’s also why, though of course there are plenty of anti-Zionist Jews, you will struggle to find a synagogue beyond the fringes of ultra-orthodoxy that does not identify in some way with Zionism – not, I stress, with this or that Israeli government or policy, but with the idea, the dream, of the Jews’ return to their ancient home. That dream became a matter of basic human survival after a history of bloody persecution reached its climax eight decades ago, in the murder of 6 million Jews by the Nazis and their collaborators across Europe. It’s that need for a refuge from antisemitism – a racism that claimed so many lives, for so long – that the advocates of Sunday’s motion would declare to be racism.

A group of Jewish Greens tried to alert their comrades to these dangers, asking for an amendment that might allow Jews to go to synagogue, but they were rejected. When one committedly anti-Zionist Jew rose to speak at a party workshop last week, he was shouted down with cries of “Zionist”. Polanski, who is himself Jewish and has called for the motion to be amended, says there’s a simple solution: if Jews denounce Israel in the terms demanded, agreeing to condemn “the occupation … the apartheid … the genocide”, they should be left alone. But the resolution itself insists on more. For Jews to comply, they would have to deny all connection with their historic homeland. This has so often been a feature of antisemitism: century after century, Jews are told that if they only disavow this belief or that practice, if they only say these words, they will be admitted into polite society. Where once Jews were told to embrace Christ, now they are told to disavow the world’s only Jewish country. The specific demand has changed; but the impulse is the same.

In each generation, those making such demands of Jews believe they are acting in a righteous cause. The Christian persecutors of the Inquisition were sure that they were honouring Jesus; today’s Greens are certain they are advancing the cause of anti-racism, even as they would hound and defame and shame a tiny minority. Any Green party member voting for this motion should reflect on that history and consider the company they are joining. It will be full of people they despise – but they will fit right in.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Burnham to pass law scrapping pension triple lock before next election

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:39:11 GMT

Guarantee will remain until 2030 but MPs will vote on changes during this parliament, government says

Andy Burnham will pass legislation to scrap the state pension triple lock in this parliament, even though the guarantee will remain until 2030, the government has said.

The prime minister used his conference speech to announce a change to the policy, which guarantees that the state pension rises by the highest of 2.5%, inflation or earnings growth.

In future, the earnings element will be adjusted to avoid much larger pension increases in years when wages spike.

In his speech, Burnham said the triple lock would remain in place until 2030 – after the next election – keeping Labour’s manifesto promise to retain the guarantee.

However, guidance published alongside the speech shows that the government intends to legislate before then, requiring MPs to vote on the changes.

It means parties will go into the next election setting out in their manifestos whether to retain Labour’s changes or repeal them if they win power.

The guidance also shows that the government estimates that the adjustment to the triple lock would reduce state pension spending by £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s and by £50bn a year by 2050.

However, the Resolution Foundation said on Friday that it was extremely difficult to estimate the savings, with figures ranging from nothing to about £24bn a year depending on which recent decade was used as a model.

Ruth Curtice, the thinktank’s chief executive, wrote on Friday: “The adjusted triple lock saves most in a volatile world, and so saves nothing in the 90s or 00s, and £24bn in the 10s.

“Over the longer term, which will most likely deliver some mixture of all of these economic realities, the new mechanism should trend closer to earnings.

“If real earnings growth permanently disappoints then even the protections in the new mechanism could prove expensive. A new, if not the main, reason to fight to avoid stagnant wages.”

Since it was announced, the policy has been criticised by the Conservatives, Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats – although some Tory and Lib Dem MPs are unhappy with their leaders for campaigning to retain a policy they believe is too costly.

Sharon Graham, the Unite general secretary, said earlier this week that getting rid of the pension triple lock to help fund social care changes would be “electoral suicide”.

However, YouGov has published polling suggesting voters support Burnham’s plan by 48% to 28%.

In his conference speech, Burnham confirmed he would end the pension triple lock and use the savings to fund a national care service in England that would be free at the point of use.

He said his changes would still leave millions of pensioners better off and that they would benefit from the new care system, which is expected to follow the Scottish system by covering care costs but not accommodation.

Burnham also promised to exempt lower-income pensioners from income tax during this parliament.

Englishness is not defined by ethnicity

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:07:33 GMT

Maariyah Seedat wonders at what point does her family become ‘English’ enough, Mark James Slater has always regarded himself as British and not English. Plus letters from Dr Richard Seabrook and Alan Baker

Jason Okundaye’s piece on defining Englishness mirrored my own experiences as a member of an ethnic minority (Of course you can be English if you’re not white. So why can’t the right leave the question alone?, 26 September).

As a child, growing up in multicultural Leicester in the 1990s and 2000s, I was “corrected” by adults in positions of authority – the vast majority of whom were white – for wanting to call myself English. It was a descriptor that I could not claim and, implicitly, was not my right because of my skin colour. I learned very quickly that referring to myself as British was the better, less objectionable option.

It always rubbed me up the wrong way. At what point does my family become “English” enough? How many generations later? I love my country of birth, and when I am abroad my Englishness is never brought into question, so why can my country not accept me as I am?

I believe that lived experiences like mine indicate why ethnic-minority adults “prefer an identification with Britishness”: a potent mix of historically being put in one’s place, and a desire to avoid exhausting circular arguments with those who cannot see beyond the colour of one’s skin. Maariyah SeedatToronto, Canada

Given that my grandparents’ family names are a mixture of Norman French, Dutch and Huguenot French, and we have probably lived within the borders of England from arrival to today, and that I was born in London, is it strange that I have always regarded myself as British and not English?

My understanding of being English is either the staid and stuffy upper classes residing in rural isolation or having some background role in an embassy or assurance office or living in a working-class community of very similar people in the terraced streets around a (former) factory.

That isn’t me. I am as invested in the other British cultures of Scotland, Wales, Ireland, Cornwall, the West Indies, Pakistan, Australia, India, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Africa and the US, not to mention western Europe and more recently eastern Europe.

Simply being English is such a restrictive definition, and I am proud to be counted as British as any of my neighbours. Mark James SlaterHelston, Cornwall

Jason Okundaye asks “Can you be English and non-white?” The answer is no, according to the government’s own system of coding ethnicities for the 2021 census. English appears as a subcategory of white, and not elsewhere. Thus it is not possible using this coding scheme to describe oneself as, for example, Black English, whereas you can choose to declare yourself Black British.

So the racist implications of “Englishness” are baked into the coding scheme until such time as “English” is moved out of its colour category and treated as a cultural identity (whatever that is) rather than as a consequence of DNA. Dr Richard SeabrookBeckenham, London

While Jason Okundaye claims as a simple truth that “there is no single, historically fixed population from which today’s ‘English’ have descended”, he misses a more important general point.

While I am able to claim to be a personally responsible agent as a grandfather, father, husband, researcher and writer, I am unable to claim responsibility for the fundamental structure within which I have acted and continue to act. I was born in Canterbury, Kent and thus I am English. My birth certificate, dated 20 October 1938, records my “sex” as “boy”. I am simply not responsible for my nationality or gender.

I am accordingly neither proud nor ashamed to be an Englishman: that is just a matter of fact. And this in turn means that I cannot either adulate or castigate others of different nationality or gender on the grounds of those characteristics alone. The right’s fixation based on bloodlines and biological inheritance has no foundation: it is baseless and crass. Alan BakerCambridge

Utilities are public services – and should not be run as businesses

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:07:22 GMT

Readers respond to an article by Will Hutton and Andy Haldane suggesting that they could be run for the public benefit

Will Hutton and Andy Haldane advocate “turning [utilities] into public-benefit companies with a primary, constitutional objective of delivering high-quality services, with profitability subordinate to that broader aim” (Andy Burnham talks about ‘public control’ of the utilities but it’s a minefield. We can lead him through it, 25 September). So still companies, but with a public interest rather than a profit motive. This is still the wrong approach.

Utilities should not be run as businesses but as essential public services. They do not function in isolation, and business models are unsuited to their functioning in the public interest. They have social and environmental as well as economic responsibilities that have to be met. For 20 years, prior to the advent of the Scottish parliament, local government functioned well in Scotland within a framework of regions and districts. The regions had powers and responsibilities for the wide range of functions that had to be coordinated and operated strategically at the regional level. They included water and sewerage.

The present government appears to be edging sideways, through metro mayors and joint working, towards governance for city regions. This should be formalised and given a full portfolio of responsibilities, powers and resources for strategic planning, economic development, education, health, transportation, infrastructure and the environment. Infrastructure should include water and sewerage.

As an example, urban rainwater needs to be collected and recycled for cooling, which was normal practice for thousands of years in southern Europe. Such practice should be moving north to include water reserves for wildfire control. How could such provisions, urban cooling and wildfire control ever be met through the profit motive?

If the present water companies in England have liabilities that exceed the value of their assets, and cannot meet their legal responsibilities, then it is difficult to see why they should be rescued and maintained through public expenditure. Roger Read Former secretary general, Metrex

Will Hutton and Andy Haldane put forward a poor argument for maintaining private ownership of utilities. Instead of comparing the present situation with how things were when the water utilities were publicly owned – surely the fairest comparison – they cite spurious examples of the alleged failings of other nationalised industries.

We are alone in the world (apart from Chile) in having a wholly privatised water industry; is everyone else out of step?Sally ThompsonCardiff

Will Hutton and Andy Haldane give some interesting thoughts on the public control of utilities. These could also apply across the complete essential services sector, from water companies to dental practices. Few who experienced the performance of the old postwar nationalised industries would wish a return to this failed model. However, why not just keep it simple and legislate to force all essential-services operators to list as companies on the London Stock Exchange?

For each sector, further legislation could set maximums for yields and permitted borrowing: two key indicators of company activity. The public would then be more inclined to invest in the companies, just as they do at present with National Grid. Ian Graham Port Carlisle, Cumbria

Other countries learn from their elders’ wisdom – so could Britain

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:07:17 GMT

A German service matches retired professionals to firms that use their experience, writes Alan Coppin, responding to an article about a 90-year-old Japanese competitive bodybuilder

Your feature on the 90-year-old bodybuilder Toshisuke Kanazawa was a joy (‘I’m 100% natural’: how Japan’s 90-year-old bodybuilder is still winning titles, 25 September), but it’s also a useful provocation. Almost 30% of Japan’s 123.7 million people are over 64 yet, rather than being written off, people like Kanazawa are still contributing well into their 90s.

Britain does the opposite. Between 670,000 and 860,000 people drop out of the UK workforce annually, and by their 60s more than a third of people are economically inactive. The loss is a stock of judgment and knowhow that simply walks out of the door.

Germany offers one model. Founded in 1983, its Senior Expert Service has a pool of more than 14,000 retired professionals and has arranged more than 60,000 placements by matching engineers, accountants, former military and skilled tradespeople with the small firms, charities and schools that could use their experience. Nothing like it exists here. There’s a second potential beneficiary: the almost 1 million young people not in employment, education or training. It is hard to think of a better use of an elder’s time than helping one of them get a foothold.

Modest pilot schemes in one or two sectors, modelled on the German system, would quickly show whether it is worth scaling up.

Kanazawa’s story shouldn’t just prompt admiration for one exceptional man. It should trigger a serious look at whether Britain is wasting a resource it already has: the thousands of experienced people it puts out to pasture every year. Alan CoppinAuthor, The Human Capital Imperative: Valuing Your Talent

England school inspections to be overhauled again after barrage of complaints

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:00:11 GMT

Exclusive: Education secretary sends Ofsted back to ‘drawing board’ as teachers raise serious concerns about new system

School inspections in England will be overhauled for the second time in a year, after a barrage of complaints that the new system was dangerously stressful and damaging teachers’ mental health.

Lucy Powell, the education secretary, will tell the schools regulator Ofsted to “go back to the drawing board” after becoming concerned that inspection changes overseen by her predecessor, Bridget Phillipson, were creating problems for headteachers.

Sources say Powell does not want to scrap the new system of ratings, which score schools from “exceptional” to needing “urgent improvement” in six key areas, but she does want inspectors to take greater account of the social and economic background of each school and its pupils.

Powell’s changes, which will be communicated to Ofsted in the coming weeks, will be the second set of major alterations to the school inspection regime in just over a year, after Labour’s election manifesto pledge to replace the previous inspection framework in the wake of the death of the headteacher Ruth Perry.

One source said: “She wants Ofsted to go back to the drawing board when it comes to measuring inclusion in particular. That’s where most of the problems seem to lie.”

Powell’s changes will mean a significant shift from those carried out by Phillipson, who is now equalities minister and party chair.

The two MPs fought an occasionally bitter contest to become Labour’s deputy leader last year, during which allies of each traded insults and accusations. Andy Burnham promoted Powell, a long-term ally, to Phillipson’s job as education secretary when he entered Downing Street earlier this year.

Powell told an event at last week’s Labour party conference: “I want to see a much stronger emphasis in the current inspection regime on context, much stronger than it is at the moment.

“I think this is one of those areas that it’s not straightforward to sort of move the oil tanker around massively quickly, but we absolutely do need to see reforms there.”

Ofsted declined to comment. The inspectorate has commissioned its own independent evaluation of the new framework, with an interim report due out later this year.

Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said he was encouraged that ministers were listening to the criticism of inspections being raised by parents and experts as well as teachers.

Whiteman said: “We have serious concerns about fairness and comparability. Schools serve very different communities and face very different levels of challenge. Leaders working in areas of greater disadvantage, or with higher numbers of pupils with special educational needs (Send) and disabilities, must not be placed at a systemic disadvantage by an inspection framework that fails to properly reflect those contexts.

“Inspection should take account of the circumstances in which schools are operating, while recognising the tremendous work many are doing to support children facing the greatest barriers.

“There is a need for an inspection system that is rigorous and proportionate and which genuinely supports school improvement.”

The new “report card” system came into force last year, replacing Ofsted’s headline inspection grades of “outstanding” to “inadequate”, with a more detailed system intended to put less pressure on schools.

The new system was initially welcomed by teachers, though criticised by others who warned it would make it harder for parents to judge a school.

Since its implementation however, the regime has been met with a flurry of complaints from school leaders, who say it is harming their mental health and creating greater stress than the system it replaced.

Perry’s sister, Prof Julia Waters, said last month that she had been contacted by at least a dozen teachers left “feeling suicidal” by Ofsted inspections, and raised her concerns in a letter to the prime minister.

Amanda Hulme, the headteacher of Claypool primary school in Bolton, told the Guardian last month that her most recent Ofsted inspection was the most stressful experience of her career.

Unions have called for teachers to be given “urgent relief” from the new system, while some want Ofsted to stop grading their schools altogether.

A survey of school staff inspected under the new regime found that two-thirds said it was as bad or worse than the framework it had replaced. The survey of National Education Union members also found that three out of four said the inspections had negatively affected their mental health, with one primary school teacher describing it as “a circle of stress and fear”.

Powell is understood to be concerned that schools in more “challenging” contexts are doing worse under the new system.

A recent study by the former Ofsted inspector Steve Wren found schools with higher levels of children receiving free school meals (a key test of poverty) or Send support were receiving lower ratings than average.

Wren also found that ratings for secondary schools were closely correlated with how well pupils had performed before they joined the school, suggesting inspectors were not taking sufficient account of previous attainment levels.

Wren said in his analysis: “Do these grades represent the reality that secondary schools with lower prior attainment are doing a markedly worse job of educating their pupils, or is the framework biased against them, or are inspectors not skilled at spotting strengths in such contexts?”

Senior Green party figures privately fear a defeat in Holborn and St Pancras could severely damage Polanski’s leadership, amid concerns the party’s rapid rise in membership and polling has not translated into campaigning strength on the ground.

“I see this election as high-stakes for people in Holborn and St Pancras and high-stakes for the climate crisis,” Polanski said. “We know that … a decision on [drilling projects Rosebank and Jackdaw] has been delayed until after this byelection, because Andy Burnham literally wants to see whether he can get away with drilling for new North Sea oil and gas.”

The Guardian has reported that the Jackdaw decision is likely to be held until after the byelection, while a decision on Rosebank is still pending. Burnham has promised a more “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil and gas than his predecessor, as the government balances its climate commitments against pressure over energy security and jobs.

Suicide by plane or terrorism? Speculation over motive in flight 1073 attack

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:40:05 GMT

Experts sceptical flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life and say key question is means of radicalisation

At about 9.30 on Wednesday morning local time, Tali Manes was taking her six-year-old daughter, Nina, to the toilet on the regular flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when she heard a series of heavy blows against the cockpit door.

Manes, an Israeli bank executive, immediately told a flight attendant seated nearby that something was wrong. When he did not react, she shouted at him: “Something is happening in there!” Seconds later, the man “simply went to the [cockpit] door and opened it”, Manes told Israel’s Channel 12 TV.

Inside, the scene was the stuff of travellers’ nightmares: blood spattered over the cockpit walls and a brutal struggle in progress between the badly injured pilot and the co-pilot, who was armed with some kind of sharp weapon. There was no one at the controls of the Boeing 737.

Manes shouted again: “He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!”

Many of the details of what happened on flight FZ 1073 are still unclear, but what happened next is well documented by witness testimony and videos.

As the plane went into a steep dive, losing 16,000ft of altitude in about a minute, most of the 182 passengers screamed, prayed and tried desperately to reassure panicking children. But a small group rushed to the cockpit and overpowered the co-pilot. One, a plumber, copied an action seen on TV documentaries about plane crashes to pull the aircraft out of its dive.

Two off-duty pilots on the flight, both among the handful of non-Israeli passengers, then took over the controls of the now almost rudderless aircraft to guide it eventually to a landing 90 minutes later in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. In the meantime, Manes had helped truss the co-pilot with a telephone cord while a dentist treated the injured Indian pilot, Smit Machchhar. It was a “great miracle”, Manes said on eventually reaching Tel Aviv on an emergency flight 10 hours later.

In a video call with Narendra Modi, the Indian prime minister, broadcast live by TV networks, Machchhar, who is recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, said he had been “fighting for my life”.

The pilot successfully sent an alarm to air traffic control signalling the attack and then, as his strength ebbed, managed to unlock the cockpit security door.

“I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” Machhchar said. “At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”

For the moment, the identity of the co-pilot who attacked Machchhar is unknown, though regional sources said he was an Omani national who had joined flydubai – which is owned by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) government – between five and nine months ago.

In Israel, there is little doubt about the co-pilot’s intentions. “The co-pilot is a terrorist who tried either to hijack the plane or bring it down as a suicide. The worst scenario is he was trying to get into Israel,” said Arik Arad, the chair of the aviation cybersecurity consultancy Cyviation and El Al’s former head of security at Ben Gurion airport

Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, has claimed the co-pilot was exposed to “Islamist radical indoctrination”, saying Israeli investigators had found evidence on social media accounts that he wanted to “kill Jews”.

“The attacker, he calls out to the aircrew: ‘Kill me, kill me,’” Netanyahu told Fox News, adding it was “clear he was suicidal”.

Experts said there have been only a handful of instances of suicide by plane – cases where the pilot’s motivation is primarily to kill him or herself by crashing the plane, rather than using the plane as a weapon, as in the 9/11 attacks.

In 2015, the co-pilot of a low-cost German airline flight who had hidden evidence of psychiatric illness from his employers deliberately crashed, killing himself and 150 others. Suggestions that the crash of an AirIndia 787 in Ahmedabad last year was the result of a pilot deliberately cutting fuel to engines have been fiercely disputed.

Terrorism experts are sceptical that the flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life. “The odds that a pilot would decide to commit suicide and just happen to be flying a plane full of Israelis are pretty low,” said Colin Clarke, a terrorism expert at the respected Soufan Center in New York.

“Netanyahu has a big interest in this being terrorism, but the best explanation is probably the most obvious one [ie terrorism],” he said. “The question … is: was [the co-pilot] recruited by a group or an organisation … or was he radicalised alone? In which case, what was hyping him up, given he was flying a planeload of Israelis? Could that be Gaza?”

Security services have been warning of a wave of radicalisation across the Middle East prompted by the war in Gaza, which came to an inconclusive halt with a fragile ceasefire a year ago. But there has been limited evidence as yet that any violent Islamist extremist groups have gained support as a consequence of the conflict.

Terrorism experts said the most obvious group that might be involved in such an attack would be al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which is based in Yemen and has a history of efforts to bring down planes. They said AQAP had recently sought to launch or inspire violence internationally.

“Aviation remains the classic propaganda by deed,” Clarke said. “It’s been said that terrorism is theatre, and nothing is more theatrical than taking down an airplane. You get a body count, media coverage, you get your message across, and this makes a plane the ultimate spectacular terrorist attack.”

There are now many questions for aviation security. Changes made to plane design after 9/11, which allowed pilots to lock cockpit doors from the inside, have long been controversial among experts. If Machchhar’s desperate efforts to allow access to the flight deck had been unsuccessful, there is little doubt all onboard FZ 1073 would have died.

There are also questions about screening of pilots. This can be expensive for airlines and could deprive them of valuable crew if too many fail more rigorous efforts to expose psychiatric illness or extremist views. Pilots may be reluctant to fly routes where they undergo greater screening, and some may hide physical or psychological problems for fear of being grounded.

Arad said: “The important issue … is that obviously pilots are not being screened enough. Lots needs to be done.”

Dubai international airport, the world’s busiest airport for international passenger traffic, has built some of its appeal on a reputation for safety in a volatile region, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England.

“They are very conscious of the fact – a little bit like Israel in many respects – that they cannot afford to have a terrorist attack happening on a flight out of there,” he said.

The UAE has ordered investigators to “collect information and evidence to determine the truth of the incident, its circumstances, details and motives, and to verify the extent of its connection to any terrorist activity or purpose, or the existence of prior planning or direction for it,” its attorney general, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, said on Thursday.

Arad foresees growing threats to civilian aviation from cyber-attacks and the malevolent use of AI, which could allow the targeting multiple planes simultaneously. But other experts pointed out there was no need for such sophistication to pose a threat.

Clarke said: “Whether or not it involves an attacker who was self-radicalised or part of a group, keeping things simple is always the best way to carry out an attack, and this came pretty damn close.”

Mercedes put team first as Russell and Antonelli face off on F1’s return to Sepang

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:22:24 GMT

Title rivals bring upgrades to first Grand Prix in Malaysia since 2017 on a demanding but well liked circuit

While the byzantine nomenclature of this weekend’s “Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia” will have Formula One’s statisticians muttering darkly under their breath for years to come, the import of the sport’s return to the Sepang circuit remains all too straightforward at the sharp end. Complicated only perhaps by a Red Bull resurgence and an enthused Max Verstappen, determined to make his mark on the championship run-in.

The return to Malaysia for its first race since 2017 has been welcomed in F1. It is a much-liked circuit among drivers, albeit the high temperatures and humidity make for an enormous physical challenge.

However, this is no long-term return to Sepang. It is back, as its torturously titled branding suggests, as a one-off replacement for the Bahrain GP, which was cancelled earlier this year because of the war in the Middle East. The Bahrain GP it is then, right down to the Bahraini backing, a Bahrain GP trophy and Bahraini-themed activities at the circuit but the pole and the victory will most assuredly be earned in Sepang, leading to said statisticians deploying the asterisk on their keyboard.

For the title protagonists, however, the name is moot. What matters is the race and both the championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, and his rival and Mercedes teammate George Russell want to make a mark in Malaysia. Antonelli leads Russell by 66 points with eight rounds remaining. A handsome lead but he dropped 15 points to the British driver at the last round in Baku where Russell showed the best form of his season, dominant across the weekend.

Antonelli, who made a costly error in qualifying and finished fifth, declared it his “worst” weekend and vowed to re-establish the order in Malaysia, while Russell felt a confidence and ease with the car that he has not enjoyed all season. A platform, he felt, from which to build a late title tilt at Antonelli.

The prospect of a comeback from Russell, applying pressure to his 20-year-old teammate who is in only his second season in F1, might put Mercedes too under pressure in managing them. A process of which they are all too aware, as the last time F1 was in Malaysia it was the first year after the Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg relationship at Mercedes had come apart with rancour. Nonetheless the team insist they will continue to allow their current drivers to race one another.

“Does it [Russell finding form] change the dynamic? I think from the overarching philosopher’s standpoint, no,” said the team principal, Toto Wolff, this week. “Because we want to give both drivers equal opportunity and to go for a championship. But the team comes first. That has always been the Mercedes philosophy.”

To that end they have brought a swathe of upgrades to Sepang, only their second major developments of the season, including adaptations to the floor, rear suspension and rear bodywork. They have been long-awaited but as ever with the first year of new regulations there is no guarantee they will simply bolt on and find lap time.

Malaysia is the first test and fine-tuning will be required given it is something of a baptism of fire, with the circuit’s heat and its abrasive, high-degradation surface making for a far from normal run-out. Indeed, how the teams handle tyre degradation will probably define the race, a finely balanced test for the strategists of two or even potentially three pit stops.

For Mercedes, in Friday’s practice sessions finding the right set-up and operating window to make the most of potential downforce gains was proving tricky, with Russell and Antonelli seventh and eighth in the second session.

They will probably find more pace come Saturday at which point they may have to deal with Verstappen and Red Bull, whose car has come on in leaps and bounds after their upgrade in Baku. Verstappen has yet to win this year and, while the title is gone, he is fiercely competitive and still determined to take the flag. The Red Bull was well balanced out of the blocks in Sepang, and Verstappen declared it “positive” and a “decent start”. Such guarded judgment is praise indeed, given how often this season Verstappen has had to wrestle with a recalcitrant car from the off.

He was not quickest in second practice when Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, also showing strong form, took the top spot from Verstappen’s Red Bull teammate Isack Hadjar by a tenth. But the Dutchman, in fourth, did not set a time doing a qualifying simulation on soft tyres. Verstappen surely has more to come and will be hungrily eyeing a shot at a win that would make it two in a row separated by almost a decade since he took the flag when it was last held in Malaysia in 2017.

A point to prove then for the four-time champion but for Antonelli and Russell it is relative points that matter and perhaps most importantly in defining the championship, who asserts themself to the greatest effect in this one-off showdown in Malaysia.
