AI threatens to destroy so much of our culture. Our greatest loss might be our ability to listen

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:00:14 GMT

Australians are conversing less every year, with a recent study showing we lost an average of 338 spoken words each day between 2005 and 2019

We talk a lot about losing our ability to write as a result of AI. I’m convinced our greatest loss might be our ability to listen. Listening to different views and entering into different worlds is integral to our humanity.

But Australians are conversing less every year. While rapidly evolving AI tools and chatbots promise faster responses and so-called “empathetic” listening, a recent study showed we lost an average of 338 spoken words each day between 2005 and 2019. That adds up to a staggering loss of 120,000 spoken words per person, compared with the year before.

This matters immensely. Language is culture. It tells us who we are.

As an oral historian, I’ve spent much of my career studying the power of human speech and storytelling. Between 2018 and early 2024, I led a team at the National Library of Australia responsible for the largest oral history collection in the southern hemisphere, which began in 1957 and now consists of more than 58,000 hours of recording. More recently, I’ve immersed myself in listening to hundreds more hours of this collection, working on a new book and an accompanying podcast.

The depth of the library’s collection, much of which is available online through Trove, is extraordinary. It holds accounts of First Nations Australians speaking about deep history and first-person memories reaching back into the 19th century.

All up, I’ve now listened to thousands of Australians from different eras, places and backgrounds tell their stories in their own words.

This has helped me understand exactly what we lose when we stop listening. When I listen to an oral history, I immerse myself in the life of someone I mostly likely will never meet. In a world where our social circles are reducing due to distance, remote work and increasing time online, the gift of hearing from someone different is precious.

Dame Mary Gilmore, born in 1865, speaks of tallow candles and life before electricity. An Australian prime minister recalls being elected after their party spent 23 years in opposition. A mother who risked everything shares how she sought refuge here, crossing pirate-infested seas after the Vietnam war. A pioneer stationed in Antarctica reflects on challenges of distance. The next voice may be Dr Ella Stack, a Darwin doctor who survived Cyclone Tracy, stayed to help, recorded survivor memories, then ensured Darwin was rebuilt as mayor.

I often hear Australian accents from the past or words no longer spoken, along with many professions described that no longer exist. As I listen, I’ve sometimes cried with laughter because of the ability of some people to share memories with humour.

I’ve listened to people remembering times of great social disruption, such as the 1891 Queensland shearers’ strikes or the conscription debates of the first world war. I’ve been deeply moved by the courage of First Nations Australians who shared testimonies of being part of the Stolen Generations.

Listening to other people from diverse backgrounds and perspectives who may not hold the same views as us can improve our mental and physical wellbeing, foster the exchange of information, grow understanding and spark new ideas. It is also deeply linked to building empathy.

Empathy is the richest gift listening offers. That will be our greatest loss if we speak and hear less. By engaging with experiences of others without requiring instant gratification and artificial agreement, we enter into other’s lives. We grow to be patient and appreciate difference. We learn we can disagree but in ways not unnecessarily destructive.

Mostly we learn that, although a century or more of time may separate us as well as our diverse backgrounds and experiences, we can still connect through moments of shared humanity and experiences of love, loss, change, challenge, joy and resilience. These voices from the past can resonate as powerfully as ever in our present.

Dr Shirleene Robinson is an oral historian and visiting fellow at the University of Technology Sydney’s school of communication and social sciences. She edited The Memory Tapes: Voices from the Oral History Collection of the National Library of Australia and hosted the accompanying podcast

Richard E Grant has one hope of lasting on Celebrity Traitors: leaning into his eccentricity

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:00:10 GMT

Chats with inanimate objects, farting into Tupperware: this cornered animal must sell his confession as just another quirk

As we all know, The Traitors is a game of deception. The entire point is to conceal your true motivations in order to better carry out a series of murders undetected. This is the way it should be, and the way it always was. And then Richard E Grant came along.

Grant’s trajectory during the opening episode of Celebrity Traitors was as follows. Step one: be selected as a traitor by Claudia Winkleman. Step two: immediately tell everyone you are a traitor.

As a dumbfounded Joe Lycett pointed out in the aftermath of Grant’s revelation, nobody has ever done this in the history of The Traitors. The entire system works on a process of elaborate deduction based on a complex matrix of pattern recognition and gut instinct. This, as you will be aware, is much harder to do when the villain straight-up announces that he’s a villain without any form of coercion.

Immediately, you can see why Grant never starred in any episodes of Columbo. This is because his episode would consist of him walking up to Peter Falk, announcing “Hello there, I am a murderer,” and being arrested. It would be 30 seconds long. Nobody would watch it.

But let’s look at the positives here. By being so brazen about his identity, Grant has basically forced the game into a place it has never been before. Aside from Jerry Hall – a woman who I am beginning to suspect is wrong about everything – all the contestants this year believe Grant is a traitor. And so it is his job, and the job of his bewildered accomplice, Maya Jama, to frantically throw bodies in his path until suspicion drifts elsewhere. He’s a cornered animal, and they are often the most dangerous.

It also means Grant has to play into all his latent eccentricity, to make it seem that erroneously announcing himself as a traitor when he is in fact a faithful is just something he does. To sell it, he has to make everyone around him believe that this is just one bizarre character quirk in an entire ocean of them. From now on, he has to really sell his role as the mad uncle of the castle, by muttering to himself and having conversations with inanimate objects and farting into Tupperware. This is the only way he has any hope of lasting on the show.

The big question is how intentional this was, which is to say: was Richard E Grant a genius or an idiot for doing that? Certainly his horrified expression after admitting the truth seems to suggest the latter. And reactions on social media would reinforce that somewhat. Anyone who has watched The Traitors will know that drawing attention to yourself so early on is often a recipe for an early exit.

Anita Singh in the Telegraph called Grant “lord of chaos” while Emily Bootle in the i called his outburst “a cock-up”. “This is the only show that could be completely sabotaged in the first episode and for that to somehow make it even better,” Bootle added.

But if Grant can survive then he’ll have the freedom to move around knocking people off unbidden. For now, the spotlight is on him and him alone. Though who knows how long that might last.

More celebrities are embracing grey hair. For other women, it can come at a cost

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 14:54:37 GMT

Olivia Colman and Lisa Bonet are among the stars going silver – but workplace ageism means many women still fear ditching the dye

To dye, or not to dye. That is the decision many people, particularly women, face when their hair starts to grey.

This week Olivia Colman joined the growing ranks of women embracing grey hair and ditching the dye. Appearing at Zurich film festival, Colman had swapped her dark signature pixie cut for a grey, curly mane swept to one side.

Online, Colman was swiftly lauded for her new look, with Vogue describing her as a “silver hair muse”.

The 52-year-old joins fellow actors including Andie MacDowell and Lisa Bonet who have embraced the salt-and-pepper or all-out silver look.

However, for women outside Hollywood, escaping the tyranny of the hair dye bottle is not always so easy.

“Being able to embrace your grey hair proudly is a privilege,” says Stacey Duguid. In June, Duguid, a former fashion editor, began documenting her struggles to find a job aged 52 despite her decades of experience. She told her followers that she had downsized her house and was now on universal credit. She received thousands of messages from fellow middle-aged women also struggling to find employment.

“There is a reluctance for women who are trying to get back into the workplace to go grey,” Duguid says. “To do it, you are most likely already in a senior position in the workplace. As an unemployed, broke, single parent it wasn’t an option for me.”

Grey hairs start to emerge, on average, in the mid-30s for white and Asian people and around the mid-40s for Black people.

Louise Chunn, a former editor turned founder of the therapist-finding platform Welldoing, first stopped dying her hair when she became the editor of InStyle magazine in the UK.

She says: “I didn’t fear how bosses would view my grey hair, because the editor’s job offer came from New York. It was more important that you were well groomed, somewhat sophisticated.”

Chunn began dying her hair again in her 50s because she worried it made her look older, but stopped in her 60s.

Colman’s new look was created with extensions by the London based hair specialist Inanch Emir. Using four shades of grey, Emir mirrored Colman’s natural colour while adding volume and length.

Duguid describes Colman’s hair as “spectacular” but has all the trademarks of a much younger woman. “It’s a sort of fetishised version of grey hair,” she adds.

Sarah Bower, a grey-blending and colour specialist at Larry King salon in London, says clients considering embracing their grey hair are most concerned about looking older.

Bower says going grey isn’t as simple as calling it a day on hair dye. Much of her work involves blending the demarcation line – the visible difference between someone’s natural colour and dyed hair – to “try and make it look like they’ve already got their natural hair colour”. She says it can take up to three years to fully grow out grey hair.

According to the Office for National Statistics about 3% of people between the ages of 50 and 64 are unemployed in the UK. Despite the state pension age rising to 67, a recent study by the Centre for Ageing Better found that a job applicant is perceived to become undesirable to recruiters on average at the age of 55.

Research by Ian Burn, an economics professor at the University of Liverpool, found that age discrimination in recruitment against women in the UK starts at least 10 years earlier than it does against men. Once a woman hits 40, her chances of being called for interview begin to decline. For men, the decline does not start until their 50s.

Recent catwalks have been more age inclusive. In January, Stephanie Cavalli, a 50-year-old model, whose hair is peppered with greys, opened the Chanel couture show. Fifty-nine-year-old Evelyn Effrim-Botchey, who stopped modelling in her late 20s after work began to dry up, has spoken about how her grey-streaked hair has helped her comeback.

Sign up to Fashion Statement

Style, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solved

after newsletter promotion

But most older models continue to have dyed hair. Not one of Gucci’s glamorous sciura cast at its recent Milan show was grey, while 70-year-old Jerry Hall, still blond, fronts this month’s Grazia. Pamela Anderson, 59, has embraced going makeup-free since 2023 but remains blond.

Duguid has heard from older women who use filters during video interviews and calls to help mask their age. “It’s completely exhausting” she says. “Grey hair is different, though, because you can’t really hide it. If you are trying to find a job, you will go out and get a box dye.”

Alyson Walsh, a former magazine editor who now runs the style platform That’s Not My Age, says: “Despite the fact that older women have lots of experience and knowledge, there’s still the stereotype that you’re not allowed to look old,” she says. Walsh stopped dying her hair in 2015. “I feel empowered,” she says. “It saves me money. There is less maintenance and it’s in better condition. I don’t look older. I just look my age.”

Back in the distant days of Covid lockdowns, I obsessed over the 3in-wide streak of visible grey in my hair. I’d long stopped using box colours and hair salons were shut. Was it time to let nature take over from chemicals?

Working from home and in social isolation, going grey was liberating. My at-home defiance of societal expectations for a middle-aged woman even felt rebellious.

The prospect of a new job and new colleagues dented that defiance. Should I abandon my mini revolution and surrender to the salon – fork out for a beautiful toffee brown with caramel lowlights?

If I’d known Olivia Colman and other high-profile women were going to publicly raise a metaphorical finger to the expected norms of ageing, I might have held back on the hair therapy.

But I battled the toffee cravings and took up a new professional role.

My team members are younger than me, and years of messaging that grey equals old, and indicates an end of self-care, is difficult to escape.

But I stayed the course. I learned that my all-natural hair, while an integral part of who I am, is only a small part of how others see me. In short, no one I work with seems to care.

There is no doubt, a sexist-laden ageism exists. Stereotypical assumptions persist about how older women should age. Why else would we be talking about Olivia Colman’s “daring” grey hair?

But my grey hair – along with the lines on my face – tells my story. Both are, I have decided, life affirming. Donna Carton

‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 14:50:59 GMT

Mayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridge

Valeriya Tkachenko was dropping her son off at school in central Kyiv when the air raid alert sounded. Staff hurried the children and parents into the shelter, where the frightened lawyer spent the next two hours with her son.

“I’m scared to death all day about what could happen to my son,” she said as she emerged from the shelter, already late for work.

A day earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone had struck a school nearby. “And I can’t plan anything any more,” she said. “It’s not sustainable like this.”

Across the city on Friday morning, Artem Marchenko, an IT worker, was forced to abandon his car and walk for 20 minutes across the Pivdennyi Bridge on his way to work after repeated Russian strikes damaged the crossing.

He feared Russia would soon target Kyiv’s other bridges, paralysing movement across a city of about 3 million people, the two halves of which are divided by the Dnipro.

Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion, as intensifying Russian attacks reshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness.

For weeks, the main worry in the capital had been the coming winter, when Russia is expected once again to try to plunge Ukraine into darkness and cold. But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they had been bracing for is already here.

“The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime,” the Kyiv mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said on Friday. “The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”

This week alone, Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, datacentres, a school and hospital and one of Kyiv’s main bridges. Moscow has also started its attacks on Ukraine’s energy, targeting a thermal power plant and other energy facilities, leaving several neighbourhoods without power and water by morning.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy underlined the apparent shift in Russian tactics in an interview with the Financial Times this week, saying Vladimir Putin had recently ordered his commanders to abandon the rules of war.

“They want Ukrainians to leave the capital … and show that if you don’t have the capital you don’t have the country,” Zelenskyy said in separate comments to reporters.

Until recently, Kyiv had retained a deceptively normal rhythm, while cities closer to the front, including Kharkiv and Dnipro, absorbed the brunt of daily missile and drone attacks. Now, residents joke grimly that the balance is beginning to shift, with those cities at times feeling safer than the capital.

The city is confronting a particularly dangerous combination of an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles and a new generation of faster, jet-powered Russian drones that are harder to shoot down.

Kyiv is racing to fast-track a new generation of interceptor drones capable of taking down the jet-powered models. Several are already in use, according to three defence industry sources, though they said it could still take weeks or months to deploy them at a scale sufficient to provide meaningful protection for the capital.

At the same time, Russia’s advances on the battlefield remain relatively slow and are coming at enormous cost.

Moscow captured about 361 sq km in September, according to the military analyst Konrad Muzyka, an increase on recent months but still far short of the pace needed to seize the rest of the Donbas before winter, when offensive operations typically become more difficult.

Ukraine, meanwhile, has clawed back about 126 sq km in a series of counteroffensives in the east, being conducted under the codename Vivaldi. That slower-moving battle on the ground is increasingly at odds with what is happening far behind the front. The contrast reflects a broader shift in the war, as Ukraine’s major cities come under growing pressure.

“You can be quite successful in the land domain, but if you are vulnerable in the air, especially in the rear, that is the vulnerability your opponent is going to exploit,” said Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies.

Ukrainian officials have been warning their European counterparts about the scale of the looming threat. According to the New York Times, Ukraine’s energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, recently briefed European counterparts on an intercepted Russian plan to use as many as 1,000 missiles, drones and bombs against the country’s energy system. The targets included electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants and boiler houses, in what appeared to be an effort to plunge Ukrainian cities into darkness and cold and create a humanitarian crisis.

“Russia plans to freeze Kyiv out, to throw it back into the stone age,” said one senior western diplomat in Kyiv, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Western diplomats say publicly that they intend to remain in Kyiv, mindful that leaving would hand Moscow a propaganda victory and risk creating the impression that Ukraine was being abandoned. However, privately two senior diplomats said contingency plans were being drawn up to relocate embassies to Lviv or eastern Poland if Russia began deliberately targeting foreign missions.

“The situation is obviously deteriorating fast,” the diplomat said.

Feeling wired? The truth about ‘nervous system resets’

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 14:00:09 GMT

The internet is full of warnings about our ‘dysregulated’ nervous systems. But, experts say, you don’t need to reset yours – you might just need to make it more flexible. Here’s how (and no, you don’t need an acupressure mat)

Whether it’s tapping the side of your hand or standing on a vibrating plate, suggestions on how to “reset” your nervous system are saturating the internet. Cold water plunges, humming, gargling, yawning and spiky acupressure mats are all being touted as ways to help us “regulate” and return to calm. If you’re still talking about feeling “stressed”, you’re behind the times; now, says the internet, you are “dysregulated”.

The nervous system is an integral part of being human. “It’s essentially the body’s communication and control network,” says Dr Serena Lai, consultant psychiatrist and associate medical director at London Psychiatry Clinic. “Made up of the brain and spinal cord, it communicates with the entire body through nerves, helping us to sense what is happening around and inside us. When we have that information, we can process it and coordinate a response.”

The autonomic nervous system is one part of this network, regulating things the body does automatically, including heart rate, blood pressure and digestion. It has two main branches. “The sympathetic system creates our fight or flight response, helping us mobilise resources when we need to respond to a challenge,” says Lai. “The parasympathetic nervous system – or rest and digest mode – conserves energy, slows the heart and supports recovery.”

Sympathetic activity increases during stress, whether that’s an urgent email or a family bereavement. The heart beats faster, muscles tense, digestion can change and we become more alert. These evolutionary responses help us respond to threats – but while once that might have been a predator, now it’s as everyday as seeing a celebrity death on Instagram. Perhaps it’s no surprise, then, that the idea of a nervous system reset is so appealing to so many of us – we’re overstimulated and in desperate need of ways to feel more level.

Except, as every expert I spoke to agreed, there is no such thing as “resetting” the nervous system – nor should we want to. We need sympathetic activation to exercise, concentrate, meet deadlines and respond to demanding situations. The problem is when we struggle to recover once that demand has passed, leaving us feeling wired and tired, and potentially contributing to increased inflammation and cardiovascular and metabolic problems. A healthy autonomic nervous system is not permanently calm; it’s able to adapt to changing circumstances.

Much of the conversation about nervous system regulation revolves around the vagus nerve – which is actually a pair of nerves, made up of about 80,000 fibres apiece – that starts in the brain and travels down through the neck into the chest and abdomen. Because it helps slow heart rate and plays a role in the body’s rest-and-recovery processes, it is associated with stress relief and relaxation – you might see people referring to increased “vagal tone” as a sign of enhanced vagus nerve activity.

One of the most common ways vagal and parasympathetic activity is assessed is through heart rate variability (HRV), says neurosurgeon Dr Kevin Tracey, author of The Great Nerve. “This is the time in between individual heartbeats – generally, greater variability is associated with greater vagal influence,” he explains. The higher the vagal influence, the more likely our parasympathetic system is to be dominant – cue feeling of calm. “Sympathetic activity tends to shorten the time between heartbeats.”

Learning how to work with your nervous system could make it more flexible, meaning you rise to challenges when you need to, then recover when they have passed. These simple, science-backed habits can help.

Breathing slowly has been shown to increase HRV and promote parasympathetic dominance. “One study showed that slow-paced breathing of around six diaphragmatic breaths [breathing deeply into the belly rather than just into the chest] a minute is one of the most effective ways of producing an acute change in heart rate variability,” says Lai. She recommends inhaling for about five seconds, exhaling for five, and repeating for five to 10 minutes.

Cyclic sighing is another option. It involves taking one deep inhale, followed by a second, shorter “sip” of air to fully inflate the lungs, before a long, slow, lung-emptying exhale through the mouth. In one study, practising for five minutes a day improved mood and reduced respiratory rate – an effect that became more pronounced over the course of the month-long trial.

“Meditation – where you practise bringing your attention to the present moment – is a great way to help slow down the heart rate,” says Tracey. “It’s especially good when done in tandem with paced breathing, as you can really measure your heart rate decreasing.” Apps including Headspace, Insight Timer and Calm, he adds, can make it easier to build the practice into everyday life.

Other contemplative practices, from body scanning (where you relax, close your eyes and contemplate physical sensations) to yoga, may also support parasympathetic activity. One 2018 paper proposed that many of these practices naturally slow the breath, which in turn influences vagal activity.

“Sensory quiet” in general may be important for autonomic recovery, explains Dr Vishnuraj Prakash, head of Ayurveda and functional medicine at Tulåh Clinical Wellness in Kerala, India, so practise doing nothing – no podcasts, phones or other stimuli.

“Movement is incredibly useful because it changes your state,” says somatic practitioner Nahid de Belgeonne. “For example, if you sit at a desk for a long time, your muscles are contracted and fixed and your breathing shallow. As soon as you get up and move, you interrupt that fixed state.” She advises embracing being “fidgety” throughout the day and taking regular walks.

There is plenty of evidence that regular aerobic exercise – whether walking, cycling or swimming – can improve autonomic regulation and HRV over time. Tai chi is particularly interesting because it combines movement, breathwork and meditation and it produces more parasympathetic activation than conventional exercise of the same intensity.

Crucially, more exercise isn’t necessarily better. Research has found reduced HRV in athletes who overtrain, so recovery matters too. “Simple exercises are really all that’s needed,” says Dr Karen Chung, consultant neurologist at Welbeck. “I often tell patients who are overwhelmed to get off the bus a stop early and walk a little further. ”

Moderate-pressure massage has been associated with reduced heart rate, anxiety and cortisol, as well as increased parasympathetic activity – and as little as 20 to 30 minutes seems to be enough. Pressure does matter: a very light, feathery touch could actually be more stressful than calming. Even 10 minutes of head massage can increase HRV – by as much as 66%, according to one small study.

Stimulating acupressure points, whether through touch or acupuncture needles, may also help, although, as Lai points out, the evidence is less consistent. Auricular acupuncture is one obvious route in – a branch of the vagus nerve supplies parts of the outer ear. Other commonly used acupuncture points to promote parasympathetic activity are found around the wrists, outer shins, top of the head and sternum – although which are used, and why, is best left to a qualified practitioner.

Some research suggests acupuncture can influence autonomic activity, including increasing parasympathetic action. The evidence is thinner when it comes to acupressure mats. Anecdotally, they may help some people relax, but there are cheaper and better evidenced ways to achieve the same end.

Our nervous systems respond well to regularity – consistent sleep and wake times, eating at similar times each day and resting. “For many of my patients, life is incredibly fast-paced, so mostly it’s as simple as going to bed a little earlier or taking an hour away from our phones,” says Chung. “Repeating the same behaviours daily helps the body’s ability to move from activation back into recovery,” adds Lai.

Building breaks into the working day can help too. For those spending hours on screens, de Belgeonne recommends working in focused 90-minute blocks, followed by a 20-minute break. Evenings should signal a change of pace where possible. “Reduce evening stimulation during stressful periods,” advises Prakash.

Does cold exposure work as well as social media influencers would have us believe? As Tracey explains, the body’s initial response to cold water immersion is actually a sympathetic one, triggering the release of stress hormones and increasing the heart rate. It is only afterwards, research suggests, that there is a parasympathetic rebound, which could help explain why some people report feeling calmer after a cold plunge.

You don’t necessarily need to submerge yourself. Dunking your face in cold water can trigger the diving reflex, which slows the heart rate through increased parasympathetic activity – even a couple of splashes may be enough to elicit a response. However, Tracey points out that there still isn’t enough credible evidence to conclude that cold water immersion has meaningful benefits for nervous system regulation. But if you enjoy it and find you feel calmer afterwards, great – that’s really all the evidence you need.

Surgically implanted vagus nerve stimulation is an established medical treatment for conditions including epilepsy and treatment-resistant depression. But that doesn’t mean the consumer device showcased on your Instagram feed is backed by the same evidence.

Noninvasive devices typically use electrical stimulation through the skin – often at the ear or neck – in an attempt to stimulate branches of the vagus nerve. While the US Food and Drug Administration has cleared some for specific medical conditions, such as migraines, that is very different from being approved to reduce stress, says Tracey. For the majority of wellness devices, independent clinical evidence is limited. That’s not to say they definitely don’t work, but the less exciting basics – sleep, movement, slow breathing and rest – might be a better first port of call.

One study found that just 15 minutes of walking in a forest reduced sympathetic and increased parasympathetic activity, while others have linked time in nature with lower cortisol levels. So get outside – ideally without your phone.

“Eat a balanced diet, get regular exercise, spend time in nature and with people you love, and get some hobbies,” says Tracey. “And have a plan for dealing with stress. Beyond all the elaborate reset practices, these are the things that are actually worth doing.”

The simple secrets behind great ramen

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 14:00:09 GMT

You need five things: broth, flavour-giving tare, noodles, fat and toppings. And it’s the toppings that make it really special. Here are five versions, from a Toyko classic to a new Cardiff cult hit

Watch our guide to the UK’s best ramen renegades in Feed with Jimi Famurewa

At its simplest, ramen is the balance of five elements: broth, tare (secret seasoning sauce), noodles, fat and toppings. If you understand that, this seemingly cryptic and complex corner of Japanese food culture opens right up. The first four take time, but if you pick up a shop-bought stock and some decent noodles, I won’t tell anyone. But the toppings are where the real payoff is: the fastest way to turn a midweek nothing into something worth showing off.

A universal note Spring onions should be used to top every bowl (finely diced white onion will work as a backup). Where there’s a broth, aim for 300ml, and where dashi is mentioned, instant is fine – unless you’re vegan, in which case steep 20g each of kombu and dried shiitake in one litre of cold water overnight, and keep the mushrooms for the soboro. Noodle portions are 130g unless stated otherwise, and any specialist items should be available online or at your local Asian supermarket.

None of these toppings belong to one bowl, so swap them about – and they’re all good beyond ramen: chashu in a cheese toastie, say, soboro on rice, or ajitama in a caesar salad. The tares are multiuse, too: the tantanmen tare is great in scrambled eggs; the miso tare on corn on the cob, and the shio tare will improve pretty much anything.

Ramen’s platonic ideal, and one piece of pork gives you the topping, tare and fat.

Broth 50:50 chicken stock and dashiTare 3-4 tbsp chashu braising liquidFat 1 tbsp, skimmed from chilled braising liquidNoodles medium classicToppings pork belly chashu, shop-bought menma (seasoned bamboo), ajitama

For the chashu (serves 6-8) Roll and tie 500g pork belly and brown it all over in a pan. Deglaze the pan with 150ml sake, add 300ml each of shoyu, mirin and water, 30g demerara sugar, six sliced garlic cloves and a sliced 4cm piece of ginger, and simmer gently, turning, for two hours,. Cool in the liquid to room temperature, then chill overnight. Cut into 1cm-thick slices and torch or pan-fry to serve.

Sichuan dan dan noodles, but make it ramen. Sesame, spice, and a soboro that works like a ragu.

Broth 50:50 kombu-shiitake dashi and unsweetened soy milkTare 2 tbsp tahini, 1½ tbsp shoyu, 2 tsp black vinegar, 1 tsp sugar, a pinch each of MSG and ground Sichuan pepperFat 1 tbsp rayu chilli oilNoodles medium classicToppings spicy mince soboro, pak choi

Spicy mince soboro (serves 6-7) Soften a small diced onion and 2cm piece grated ginger in oil for five minutes. Add five grated garlic cloves followed by 500g fatty pork mince – although any mince works, but vegan mince will need more water - and fry until it’s in grains, not lumps. Add three tablespoons of doubanjiang (chilli bean sauce), one and a half tablespoons each of shoyu and mirin, plus a splash of water. Cook for 15 minutes until glossy.

Japan’s most famous ramen export. Thin, straight noodles in a creamy pork bone broth, eaten fast by design.

Broth tonkotsuTare 30ml shio (30g salt, 10g sugar and 10g MSG dissolved in 70ml sake, 20ml mirin and 110ml water – makes 230ml/about 7 bowls)Fat 1 tsp sesame oilNoodles thin, straightToppings ajitama, pork belly chashu, shop-bought kikurage (wood-ear fungus), beni-shoga

Ajitama (serves 6)Warm 100ml water, dissolve 10g brown sugar in it, then add 100ml each shoyu and mirin and chill. Pierce six fridge-cold large eggs at the wide end and boil for seven minutes, stirring for the first 30 seconds to centre the yolks. Plunge into iced water, peel, and submerge in the cold marinade for 12-72 hours.

A late-night Cardiff cult classic – chicken, curry sauce and chips – our version of nagoya mazesoba. Sauce in the bowl, hot noodles on top, toss hard.

Broth none – rules are meant for breakingTare 100ml shop-bought Japanese curry roux, made thick and saltyFat 1 tbsp each butter and chicken fat (from the thighs)Noodles thick (200g)Toppings shio koji chicken, crispy onions, beni-shoga, and grated cheese, if you’re feeling cheeky

Shio koji chicken thighs (serves 4-5) Coat 500g skinless and boneless chicken thighs in 50g shio koji, 20g mirin, half a tablespoon of shoyu and one teaspoon each of grated ginger and garlic. Leave up to three hours. Add 100ml water, cover and cook over a low heat for 45 minutes. Uncover and reduce until it crisps. Shred the meat and toss through the glaze.

Usually built on pork broth and lard for Hokkaido winters, this version is plant-based, but stands up.

Broth kombu-shiitake dashiTare 60g a bowl – 100g each white and red miso with 2 tbsp sake, 1 tbsp each mirin and shoyu, 1 tsp each grated raw garlic and gingerFat 2 tbsp vegetable oil, fried with grated garlic and gingerNoodles thick, wavy, yellowToppings stir-fried cabbage and beansprouts, sweetcorn, toasted sesame seeds, and butter, if you’re not vegan

Stir-fried cabbage and beansprouts (serves 4) Get a wok very hot with a little neutral oil. Add 200g shredded cabbage and 150g beansprouts, and toss hard for two minutes – you want char, not steam. Season with a tablespoon of shoyu, a teaspoon of sesame oil and a pinch each of salt, sugar and shichimi togarashi.

James Chant is the owner of Matsudai Ramen in Cardiff. Watch him make ramen in Feed with Jimi Famurewa

There is a way to look after people, the planet – and Britain’s growth. It’s what we call the ‘wellbeing economy’

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 13:01:29 GMT

Imagine the UK with a 20-year investment plan, with green homes and fast transport. We already have the tools to make it happen

You’ve just left school. What’s your future?

I know a physics graduate making flat whites; a 30-year-old living in his childhood bedroom who feels like a failure; a lad in Blyth who turned down a job 15 miles away because there’s no bus, and for young people his age car insurance is almost £2,000 a year. Britain’s young people are our greatest resource, and we are failing them because capital markets won’t allocate investment where it is needed. Saying “hope” in a conference speech sounds warm. But people need a plan.

The first priority of any government is the security of its people. Financial markets are sending price signals that AI booms and share buybacks are more important than clean energy or warm homes. We fund aircraft carriers and artillery shells. But wind turbines and council houses are part of our national security, too. Imagine a country with a 20-year investment plan, with retrofitted homes and fast transport connections that leave nowhere behind. That’s a future filled with the potential of proud work for young people.

But four words run Britain: “We can’t afford it.” Governments call this mindset “prudence”. My response to it is Hostage Nation, my plan to fix Britain. This is a report that lays out how to source the finance, shows what we need to build – and tracks why it would make us more prosperous and resilient. I joined the Green party to achieve this vision. As we approach the party conference, I hope this will become official Green policy that we’ll fight the next election on.

Nine sets of fiscal rules have been broken and abandoned since the financial crash. Andy Haldane, a former chief economist of the Bank of England, said current fiscal rules were “far from optimal; in fact I’d go as far as to say silly”. The Institute for Fiscal Studies said in 2024 that changing policy based on fiscal headroom projections was “almost literally mad”. What if we’re not really hostages to the bond market? What if politicians have got Stockholm syndrome instead?

Bond markets are just complex betting shops. That’s their business model: guess the future, and price accordingly. That price changes when the US Federal Reserve raises interest rates or the strait of Hormuz closes. Why do we let bookies decide whether we build railway lines? Give a country nothing to build and struggling people will find someone to blame.

Businesses want customers more than they want tax cuts or light-touch regulation. I once asked the chief executive of a global engineering firm if he would invest in green hydrogen. “I’m not investing half a billion in a plant and staff unless I can sell it for 20 years,” he said. No government gave that signal.

Provide demand, and supply chains will organise themselves. When I was mayor of the North of Tyne combined authority, I moved our adult training providers from one-year to rolling three-year contracts. Employment training places rose from 22,000 to 35,000 a year on the same real-terms budget. That’s what certainty brings.

Markets are great at providing barber shops and burger vans, but markets don’t build reservoirs. The only organisation that can guarantee orders for infrastructure 20 years from now is the state. Public ownership is a must for public planning. We’re not short of need: 100,000 council homes a year; fully renewable energy with a storage grid; clean transport; insulating every home; buses and trains that run as one network and are cheaper and more convenient than cars; regenerated high streets with sports centres and warm youth clubs. What George Monbiot calls public luxury.

We can fund it with off-market finance. The government savings bank National Savings and Investments (originally the Post Office Savings Bank) has been going for more than 160 years, and 24 million of us use it. The government could offer savers national infrastructure Isas – a fair, safe return for investment in public works. The gilt market carries on; this is a separate channel insulated from tariff antics and international conflicts. No hedge fund has ever shorted a premium bond.

We invest £70bn a year in cash Isas. Our pension pools hold more than £2tn, yet less than 5% is invested in British firms. There is tax relief on both. If you want to speculate on Silicon Valley, that’s your right. But tax subsidies should be reserved for savings that build Britain.

As for infrastructure, the state can outcompete private capital. For a business, wages are an expense. For a country, wages lower the welfare bill. The state collects 40p in every pound back in tax. Money flows through high streets and pays business rates. A 2014 pilot in Sunderland showed that a £5,000 investment in insulation and energy-efficient boilers for people with COPD lowered bills and reduced hospital admissions by 25% and GP appointments by 60%. Combine retrofit and clean energy at cost and energy bills fall by 67%. It turns out the cheapest way to heat a home is also the quickest way to decarbonise a country.

This is what a wellbeing economy looks like. In the North of Tyne we judged projects on mental health, environmental impact and community wealth before a penny was released.

What about inflation? Train the workers, build the supply chains, then release the money. This creates real capacity and builds assets on the public balance sheet. We have the powers. We don’t need new treaties or quangos. We need to wake up the state machinery we already have.

In 1946 Britain was so poor we started rationing bread. The national debt was two-and-a-half times the size of the economy. That generation built the NHS. Then an average of 126,000 council homes every year for 35 years. Eight prime ministers and two parties kept building. Today our relative debt is under half that. We have machines they could only dream of. They weren’t richer than us. They were braver.

I don’t have a crystal ball, but I’ll wager the upcoming budget will tinker around the edges of these issues. Voters already know the Greens care, and with a plan to really fix Britain – and fund it – support will keep growing. Hostage Nation is backed by 134 endnotes that are there to be checked. We can start this plan tomorrow. Values win sympathy, but answers win seats.

Jamie Driscoll is a Green party councillor on Newcastle city council and former North of Tyne mayor

Andy Burnham is facing calls from the Liberal Democrats to publish details of all his meetings with Manchester City’s owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group (Adug), and declare all hospitality he has accepted at the Etihad Stadium.

The prime minister was widely criticised this week for saying he would be “really concerned” if Adug were forced to sell City after being found guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial regulations, which led to Downing Street issuing two clarifications of his position on Thursday.

Burnham also praised Adug’s investment in Manchester, having had close relations with the company, through which Sheikh Mansour bought City in 2008, during nine years as the mayor of Greater Manchester which ended when he returned to parliament this summer.

In a strongly-worded letter to Burnham the Lib Dems’ spokesperson for culture, media and sport, Anna Sabine, criticised his apparent defence of City as “extraordinary” and invoked Gianni Infantino’s aborted World Cup sell-off scheme in what she described as a difficult year for football.

“As you will know, an independent commission has found Manchester City guilty of 114 charges of breaching financial rules over a timeframe of nearly a decade, including the use of ‘sham contracts’ and schemes to disguise more than £830m of funding,” Sabine writes in a letter seen by the Guardian.

“Despite this, your response was to thank the club’s owners for their work and describe the findings as ‘contested’ and that it was ‘wrong to jump to a conclusion’. It is extraordinary that a prime minister would use his position to call into question the findings of the independent investigation, and risk undermining trust in the Premier League’s processes.

“This has been a difficult year for football’s reputation. Fifa’s conduct around the World Cup has already raised serious questions about integrity in the game we love. At a moment like this, fans expect their prime minister to stand up for the rules in place, not to appear to side with a club found guilty of breaking them.”

Sabine also told the Guardian that Burnham’s ties to Adug should be scrutinised and is planning to write to Downing Street and the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to demand details of their meetings.

“Football fans up and down the country deserve to know that the rules apply to everyone, however rich and powerful they are,” Sabine said. “When the prime minister leaps to the defence of a club’s owners within hours of a verdict, people are entitled to ask what their relationship is.

“Andy Burnham must come clean and publish details of every meeting and conversation he has had with City Football Group, Abu Dhabi United Group or UAE government representatives, going back to his time as mayor – and that includes any hospitality freebies received.”

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

Burnham, an Everton fan, has been pictured attending City games at the Etihad Stadium in hospitality areas.

The extent of that hospitality is unclear because under GMCA regulations the public disclosure of gifts is available for current office holders without the submission of a freedom of information request.

A Downing Street spokesperson said Burnham had not met City’s owners since becoming prime minister in July and that his quarterly list of engagements would be published before the end of the year.

City’s chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, visited Downing Street last month for a meeting with the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, but Burnham did not attend.

Burnham has not been to a City game since he became prime minister but has attended two Everton matches at Hill Dickinson Stadium, where he was accommodated in the directors’ box despite having a season ticket in the South Stand.

City confirmed on Friday that they had appealed against an independent commission’s verdict. They repeated their assessment that the verdict “contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe”.

‘You could have an amazing time for £30,000’: UK castles cash in on Traitors-style events

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 12:19:20 GMT

From stag and hen dos to luxury weekends, fans are spending big to create their own version of the hit show

On Thursday night, the singer-songwriter James Blunt, Love Island host Maya Jama and mathematician Hannah Fry were among the 21 Celebrity Traitors returning to UK screens for another round of deceit and detective work. Famously, contestants do not stay at Ardross Castle in the Scottish Highlands during filming, and the venue is not a hotel, so fans cannot book their own overnight stays without hiring the entire Ross-shire estate. But that has not stopped people from trying to recreate their own versions.

The show’s surging popularity has been accompanied by a bonanza in Traitors-style events across the UK. From stag and hen dos to castle conspiracy weekends, event companies now host year-round imitations for fans looking to recreate the drama of the candle-lit roundtable. The show is also proving to be a boom for the owners of Britain’s crumbling castles – with wealthy fans even hiring them out for their own private events.

“We see a huge spike in people searching for Traitors-style experiences on our pages every time it comes back on TV,” said Roger Masterson, founder of Celtic Castles, which specialises in castle stays and rentals. “We’ve got castle hotels that put together Traitors packages. A 15-bedroom castle might sleep 30, so they’ll bring in couples and organise the faithfuls and traitors over the weekend. They build a story around it and play the game. There are huge varieties with how it’s done.”

Companies organising team bonding exercises are by far the most common customers. GOTO Events, which runs tailored Traitors-style experiences, offers packages from five people to 1,000, complete with their own version of the missions that contestants play to build up the prize pot and a Claudia Winkleman-style host. A GOTO spokesperson said these had become the most popular experience they offer.

“Ever since the show launched, it’s just not died down. We keep thinking things will slow down and they haven’t,” the spokesperson said.

“Everyone pretty much takes it as a bit of fun because you know that someone is lying. In one of my first events, the big boss was one of the betrayers and got called out in the first round. It was funny. Everyone loves calling out their boss.”

But a Traitors-style experience often does not come cheap. Daylong events are a few hundred pounds, while those looking for the full castle experience pay much more. Rothes Glen castle in the Scottish Highlands is offering a three-night package from £4,388 a room for two guests for a castle conspiracy weekend in August next year. A private event will set you back even more: hiring a luxury castle for the weekend can set you back tens of thousands of pounds – and that’s before the cost of organising the game, says Masterson.

“If you were looking at an exclusive-use property, let’s say for 30 people, they might charge £10,000 a night on a bed and breakfast basis. So, a two night stay would be 20 – then add another 10 for the event. You could have an amazing time for £30,000 for the whole weekend,” he says.

The boom is also helping fund repairs to Britain’s crumbling castles, he says. “I’ve been with owners and I ask them why they’re moving into the hospitality market. And they say: ‘Well, we need £100,000 to replace the roof’.”

Since the first episode on Thursday, Traitors mania is set to take over the country once again, running until Friday 30 October. Celebrities will compete for up to £100,000 for their chosen charities.

“We are expecting another surge [with the new series]. We are ready to go,” said GOTO.

Fangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedy

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 12:00:08 GMT

He won a Bafta while only a teen, and now he’s the lead in a creepy sitcom adapted by Alan Partridge’s writers. Ahead of The Reluctant Vampire, he talks mates, mums who write him letters – and his love of David Brent

Only when absolutely badgered will Lenny Rush admit that the title role of The Reluctant Vampire, Val, was written for him: “Shane Allen, the executive producer, loved the books when he was young, and he was the exec on Am I Being Unreasonable?. So yes, the scripts were written with me in mind. I’m so happy they were so good. I’d have felt awful if they said ‘We’ve written this for you’ and …” he trails off, pulling a face of exquisite pained courtesy.

Rush likens the show to The Naked Gun and Airplane!, and it has the writing team behind Alan Partridge, so can conjure awkwardness out of thin air. But it also taps into a comic tradition that goes even further back: a delight in the ridiculous, people talking to bats and gargoyles, invisible women interjecting by surprise, a surrealism whose comedy comes from the audacity of acting it with such commitment. “In my opinion,” says Rush, “sometimes things are labelled as a family show but they’re aimed at kids. I really do get the feeling that The Reluctant Vampire is for everyone.”

The Reluctant Vampire was written in the 80s by Eric Morecambe, in a surprising digression into children’s fiction from the comedy giant. It’s about the young scion of a bloodsucking household who doesn’t have any skills: his teeth aren’t pointy, he hates the taste of blood, and it transpires that he’s not a vampire at all but a rogue human. In the hands of Neil and Rob Gibbons, it’s like watching the essence of British comic sensibility – slapstick shot through with genuine pathos.

“You’ve got Tom Davis playing a vampire, this big character, with these big movements and this big voice, that can’t not attract a younger audience,” says Rush, “but the lines are genuinely funny.” The show opens with Davis in full vampire regalia, ready to strike an elderly victim in her bed, only for Rush to derail it all by rushing in saying he needs a wee.

Still only 17, Rush has been a fixture on TV for many years, starting aged seven in CBeebies documentary series Our Family. Then, aged eight in Apple Tree House on CBeebies he played Eli, a young rascal on an estate of well-intentioned young rascals. If you have children this age, you’ll feel like you’ve known him for ever, and if you are watching the latest season of Slow Horses, you’ll know him as the foul-mouthed, ancient-beyond-his-years kid whose steel trap of a mind effortlessly vanquishes the spies.

But his breakthrough role was in Am I Being Unreasonable?, for which he won a Bafta at 14 for best male performance in a comedy – and he was nominated again for the same award this year. That role, Ollie, along with his magisterial Bafta acceptance speech, sealed his reputation as a guy who has hacked your mainframe, and could effortlessly make you laugh at any time.

You can see in Rush’s performance as Val how much he’s gorged on Mr Bean, Alan Partridge, Monty Python. “I probably watched some things I shouldn’t have when I was younger,” he says. Never mind the age-appropriateness, how he found the time is anyone’s guess, since he has spent so long watching the British version of The Office that he knows it episode by episode, and has been working – as well as going to school – since he was seven. David Brent has always been his inspiration, and he delivers the kindest reading of that character I’ve ever heard. “You think: ‘What an idiot.’ Then you think: ‘What a not very nice man.’ Then you get to the end of series two, and there’s a really big element of pity. He’s just a man! Trying to find his way! He just wants to be part of the gang. It’s actually a tragedy.”

The opening episode of The Reluctant Vampire makes a lot of his stature, his parents measuring him and wondering if he’ll ever be tall enough to be a vampire. Rush, who has a form of dwarfism known as spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita, never went into acting for his condition to be a “talking point. I never thought I could be an inspiration for disabled people or young people.” The impact of his visibility on the world around him came as a complete surprise. “When Am I Being Unreasonable? came out, I started to get messages from mums, saying: ‘My little boy’s got a disability or a form of dwarfism, he’s struggling a bit at the moment at school. But he’s seeing you on telly and it’s giving him confidence.’ It’s so mad that I can be doing what I love and making people feel like that. I’m so pleased that that’s how people have seen it.”

Actually, though, the unvampiric vampire is a metaphor for belonging that is universal to teenagehood. “Going to school, trying to fit in, trying to impress, failing miserably. I think that’s why it’s so relatable. Even though it’s about vampires. Or you could see it as someone trying to find their place in society: ‘Am I doing this right? Am I good enough?’ It shouldn’t be so awkward, but it is.”

He’s not bringing a lot of his own experience of school to the travails of Val, incidentally – he never stopped attending, but was always off filming something and must have been artlessly cool. Which also made his parents very focused on his attendance. “My mum took school really seriously – not even necessarily, to be honest, the education side; she just found it very important for me to be seeing my mates. So I’d be on the PlayStation, and go: ‘I’m working with Gary Oldman,’ and they wouldn’t even look up from the game. You can get swept away really easily, on set. You have assistant directors coming into your dressing room, asking what you want for lunch, it’s quite insane. You have to have the right people around you.”

After Am I Being Unreasonable?, Rush got two episodes of Doctor Who, even if he wasn’t exactly a devotee. “I’ve not told Russell T Davies this, but I never watched Doctor Who. I knew what it was! I knew it was an honour to get asked. I knew it was a real moment in your career, especially to get cast young – I think Andrew Garfield was in it at a young age.” He played Morris Gibbons, a 13-year-old genius and adviser in the science unit, a really smart move after the role of Ollie, in which he’s also a genius but of a more cunning, domestic kind.

Am I Being Unreasonable? sometimes seemed to hang off his every expression – the plot of that show was absolutely wild, full of the worst parenting in the world, elaborately revealed secrets, dead pets. Rush’s command of the mood was what tethered it to earth. “Ollie was the breakthrough part, and after that I saw myself as an actor. But when I’d look online, before and after, people would say ‘He’s a great comic actor’ or ‘He’s a great young comic’. And I’m really thankful for that, but I never saw myself as a comedian or a comic actor. And as much as I love comedy, I don’t want that to stick as my thing.” His mum asked him recently whether he’d ever try standup. “It’s a bit of an annoying thing about British culture, and quite sad in my opinion, that it’s easy to get pigeonholed, and if I ever did try standup, it would take me further away from the Slow Horses kind of work.”

His next role is Dobby in the Harry Potter series that’s been beset by controversy – not just about whether actors can be in it without tacitly endorsing JK Rowling’s views, but also bizarre racist death threats to cast members. Rush hasn’t started yet, definitely hasn’t had any death threats, and is tight-lipped, saying only: “It’s pretty incredible – I feel so lucky, it’s insane.” It’s casting against type, this house elf, because Dobby’s not the effortless manipulator of all he surveys: his emotional top note is craven gratitude and anxious helpfulness. Maybe Val is a useful bridging role, because as a not-really-vampire, Rush ventures into new territories of panic and pitfall.

The Reluctant Vampire has palpable ensemble chemistry, between Rush, Sian Clifford as his mother, Davis as his dad, Asim Chaudhry as a Lurch-like character. Newcomer Gabriel Nagy is a great foil as his brother, a functioning, evil vampire. “I never felt like anyone was learning from me,” he says. “I felt like I was learning from them. I never felt like number one on the call sheet, having to keep everyone in high spirits. I remember Tom telling me, it sounds obvious but it was so true and so clever – if you’re doing a comedy, you want to make people laugh at home, so your goal in that scene is to make your co-star laugh. Try and get them to break.” They’re all pros, of course, so no sign of anyone corpsing; but like every classic comedy since TV began, you can feel that they’re smiling on the inside.

The Reluctant Vampire is on BBC One on Sunday 4 October at 6.40pm.

Should we refuse to give the Bayeux tapestry back to France? Of course not! So why are we keeping the Parthenon marbles?

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 12:00:08 GMT

It is simply wrong for the British Museum to hoard what doesn’t belong to Britain. Let the squabbling end and the sculptures be returned to Greece

For the Bayeux tapestry to return to France would be a scandal. It is British, probably made in Canterbury by British women, and displays one of the greatest events in British history. The tapestry certainly does not belong in Normandy. It is right that it is now on British soil in the British Museum. Its display is so brief that the herd of visitors desperate to catch a glimpse of the medieval artwork must be jostled to keep moving, as if watching Shakespeare’s Henry V on fast-forward. So let’s keep it. Everybody knows possession is nine-tenths of the law. We can call it a long-term loan.

I am joking, of course. This is largely what I assume the British Museum is worried might happen if it lent the precious Elgin, or Parthenon, marbles to Athens. In the Guardian last month, the Greek prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, argued that the status of the Bayeux tapestry is parallel to that of the Parthenon marbles. “Both were conceived as single works, intended to be seen and understood as a whole,” he wrote, arguing it was time for the marbles to be reunited.

The British Museum director, Nicholas Cullinan, even appeared to agree. He remarked that the Bayeux tapestry loan offered a “glimmer of possibility” of a deal on the Parthenon marbles, which were acquired by the British Museum in 1816.

Cullinan’s predecessors have long come across as jingoistic hoarders, as if the museum were a lasting memorial to the British empire. In the 1980s, the then director, Sir David Wilson, had an infamous clash with Greece’s then culture minister, Melina Mercouri, who had travelled to London to appeal for the sculptures return. “I want my marbles back,” she demanded to Wilson in front of TV cameras.

The debate has since swirled back and forth. But it is as unedifying as watching grownups argue over a bag of sweets. Insofar as the public cares, a majority of Britons think the marbles should go back to Greece.

There was a refreshing breakthrough in 2022 after George Osborne became the museum’s chair and boldly opened negotiations with Athens. He even held a public debate on the matter. The objective was certainly confused. Was it a discreet exchange of some classical artefacts, or was it to be the final reuniting of the Parthenon pediments in the new Athens museum? The latter clearly made sense, both artistically and because of the significance of the Parthenon to Greek national identity.

Since then, the prospect of a possible return of the marbles has been bedevilled by politics and diplomacy. The Greek government rejects any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum’s “ownership”. But such de-acquisitioning would only be possible if the law were changed. Boris Johnson, once an ardent supporter of the marbles’ return, reversed his position when in office. For his part, Rishi Sunak refused to change the law and clearly wanted the marbles to stay in Britain.

Cut to Andy Burnham, who we may have expected to adopt a different stance. During his brief stint as culture secretary between 2008 and 2009, Burnham was reportedly a champion of the marbles’ return. In 2002, he even sponsored a private member’s bill on facilitating their transfer back to Greece. His advocacy is longstanding. As recently as 2023, Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, declared: “Send them back, no strings attached. And let’s use culture to change how Britain is seen around the world.”

But Burnham has done a Johnson and Sunak and let it be known he has reversed his position. Elgin’s ghost seems to spook the Downing Street rafters.

The bottom line is there is no agreement on the nature of what a loan could look like. And to make matters worse, the British Museum is lending two minor Parthenon fragments to an exhibition of Greek sculpture opening in November in Frankfurt’s Liebieghaus museum. This has so infuriated Athens that it has reportedly refused to lend nine fragments of the Parthenon marbles to the exhibition, as if proximity to the British ones would be contaminating. Talks are reportedly back to stalemate. This is desperately sad. I have followed this debate since first visiting the Parthenon with its then surveyor in the 1970s. The temple and its carvings must rank among the founding compositions of western culture.

Bringing their sculptural integrity back to life and on the site of its creation should so clearly be the ambition of every historian and archaeologist worth their salt. For museum leaders to go about hoarding, empire-building, nit-picking and point-scoring is frankly pathetic. Modern national museums are outrageous in how they amass collections and then sometimes prevent others from seeing them.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

When I was chair of the National Trust, we tried to persuade the Tate Gallery and others to lend us paintings from their basements that never saw the light of day. The answer was almost always: “No, they are ours, not yours!” We thought they belonged to the public.

As for leaders such as Johnson and Burnham, they demand a course of action in opposition yet lack the guts to do it in power. This has gone on long enough. Greece should drop its obsession with formal “ownership”. London should dispatch its 17 pediment sculptures on indefinite loan to Athens. Then, together, all of Europe can rejoice.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

The US midterm races that will decide control of Congress – mapped

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 11:30:41 GMT

These graphics explain what the Democrats would need to do to flip the Senate and House of Representatives

A turning point in Donald Trump’s second term will soon arrive. On 3 November, voters across the US will decide whether to keep the president’s Republican allies in control of Congress, or return Democrats to the majority.

Many indicators of voter sentiment suggest the Democrats are favored to take back control of the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate. Winning either would be a significant victory for the party and give it the power to block Trump’s legislative agenda and more aggressively investigate his administration.

These charts and maps reveal where the battle for Congress will be fought.

The 2026 midterms offer Democrats the chance to win the Senate, and in turn the ability to put a serious check on Trump's agenda – including blocking any new appointments to the supreme court or his cabinet.

Republicans currently hold a majority with 53 seats out of 100, while the Democrats and their allies hold the remaining 47.

Thirty-five seats are on the ballot this November. Senators serve six-year terms, with a third facing voters at each two-year election cycle.

But in practice, the battle for the Senate is being fought across a very small map.

The Cook Political Report, a prominent US election forecaster, currently lists seven seats as tossups: Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas.

A further two – North Carolina and Kansas – are leaning Democrat and Republican respectively.

Democrats must win at least four seats that are held by Republicans to gain a majority.

At the start of 2026, Republicans appeared well positioned in the battle for the Senate, with many seats rated by Cook as solid for the party and a host of others currently held by Democrats as tossups.

But as Trump's approval ratings fell over the course of the year amid discontent with the Iran war and rising gas prices, Cook shifted several races in Democrats' direction, as did other major forecasters.

A key example of this is Georgia, which is now rated as a likely win for the Democrats.

In a further sign of the momentum behind Democrats, Texas, a longstanding Republican stronghold, is considered to be in play this year.

Recent polls show that the party's candidate is ahead by a razor-thin margin.

Texas offers Democrats the opportunity for a historic victory.

For decades the state has voted red, and no Democrat has won a Senate race since 1988.

It has been similar in elections for the White House, too. The last time Texans voted for a Democratic president was in the era of Jimmy Carter in the 1970s.

In 2024, Trump won 56% of the vote to Kamala Harris’s 42%.

Running for this seat is state representative James Talarico.

Focusing on wealth inequality, he has called for billionaires to pay higher taxes.

"It's time to start flipping tables," is Talarico’s campaign slogan.

The Republican nominee, state attorney general Ken Paxton, has highlighted his close relationship with Trump.

The president endorsed Paxton in a video filmed in the Oval Office, in which he praised his work "defend[ing] our southern border from the Obama and Biden invasions".

"Thank you very much, President Trump. We won’t let you down," Paxton replied.

Talarico's focus on billionaires is echoed in the campaign for another Senate tossup currently held by a retiring Democrat: Michigan.

Going up against Republican Mike Rogers is Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive Democrat who has been endorsed by figures like Harris and Bernie Sanders.

The race is neck-and-neck but El-Sayed is currently polling slightly ahead.

Michigan is a swing state at the presidential level, but Democrats have a long history of victories to the Senate, while no Republican has won a seat since 1994.

Trump has repeatedly broken through there. He won Michigan in 2016 and 2024, but lost the state to Joe Biden in 2020.

Galvanising El-Sayed's campaign is his call for Medicare for All.

The former public health official calls for expanding the program for elderly and disabled people to every American.

He recently sparred with Fox News anchor Jesse Watters over the costs of such an expansion.

Polling suggests close to half of Michigan voters support the idea, though a sizeable number remain opposed.

Iowa may also prove to be a big test of Democratic fortunes.

The state has grown very Republican since it twice backed Barack Obama, and hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 2008.

This year, polls indicate Democrats may have a chance at winning its Senate seat.

Republican Ashley Hinson is neck-and-neck with her Democratic rival Josh Turek, a change from previous Senate races in Iowa.

And presidential elections show there is precedent for a blue upset in Iowa.

Iowa’s population is far more concentrated in the countryside compared to states currently represented by Democratic senators, so victory would represent a major expansion of the party's coalition.

Republicans nonetheless dominate the US's rural areas. Most of the 14 states where Cook considers the Republican candidate sure to win are rural.

Hinson has been attempting to keep the party’s agricultural base on side by championing the year-round sale of gasoline that contains a higher concentration of biofuel, which could both lower prices at the pump and financially boost farmers.

Turek, her opponent, is a two-time Paralympic gold medalist in wheelchair basketball. Recently, he released a campaign video where he shoots hoops with Barack Obama, the last Democratic president to win Iowa.

As well as these key Senate races, the US House is up for grabs. It, too, is currently controlled by Republicans.

Every seat is up for election, as members only serve two-year terms.

Overshadowing House elections is the unprecedented level of politically motivated redistricting seen in the run-up to the 2026 midterms.

After Trump set off a redistricting war last year, nine states have redrawn congressional boundaries, some to benefit Democrats, others Republicans. Analysis suggests that Republicans will gain more seats overall.

This redistricting has been subject to several legal challenges. A Democratic gerrymander in Virginia was struck down by the state supreme court, and the US supreme court rejected a Republican attempt in Missouri.

Yet the redistricting has not dashed Democratic hopes of taking the House.

The Cook Report rates more than 40 races as competitive.

Winning around half would hand Democrats a majority.

In New York City’s exurbs, Republican Mike Lawler hopes to win a third term representing his swing district by turning voters against democratic socialist mayor Zohran Mamdani.

“Socialism, communism and Marxism have no place in New York City and no place in America,” said Lawler, a top target of Democrats.

One of nearly two dozen Democrats in districts Trump won in 2024, Marcy Kaptur has represented northwestern Ohio since 1983, the longest-ever tenure for a woman in Congress.

Newly redrawn boundaries have increased her district’s Republican lean, making her re-election bid an important test of whether voters are still willing to split their tickets between parties.

The One Big Beautiful Bill is a major issue in this California district.

The Republican incumbent David Valadao voted for the Trump-backed measure, which extends tax cuts for wealthy people and corporations while slashing the Medicaid program for poor and disabled people. His constituents have some of the highest Medicaid enrollment rates in the country.

It’s possible whichever party wins the House achieves only a single-digit majority of seats, as Republicans have had for the past four years. But there’s also a chance that this year will see a “blue wave” of wins by Democratic candidates even in districts that Trump won by wide margins in 2024.

Either way, history favors the party out of power in the midterms, particularly in the battle for the House. All recent presidents have lost control of a chamber in midterm elections, including Trump, in the 2018 election.

Polling shows there has been a nationwide shift towards the Democrats in the run-up to the midterms, even in states Republicans have dominated for decades.

Many recent surveys of the generic ballot, a key indicator of voters’ intent in congressional elections, give the Democrats an edge ranging from the high single digits to the low double digits.

The events of this year – notably the Iran war and its impact on inflation – have undoubtedly changed the race, and much of the advantage seems to have swung towards the Democrats.

Across all key races, Democratic candidates have been campaigning on affordability, at a time when the Trump administration’s actions in the Middle East have pushed up prices, particularly for gasoline and diesel.

It is a reflection of just how concerned US voters are about the economy, rating it as the most important issue in surveys, far ahead of immigration, healthcare or civil rights.

Meanwhile, Trump’s personal ratings have also fallen, with Reuters/Ipsos finding only 32% of US adults now approve of his job performance.

That is worse than his previous low of 34%, recorded by Gallup at the end of his first term in 2021 after the January 6 attack on the US Capitol.

The 2026 midterms may be another brutal reckoning for the US president – the question is whether punishment from voters will lead him to change course.
