It’s true: this is my final column. You have exactly 24 hours to complain before my inbox self-destructs

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 10:00:16 GMT

Yes, after 25 years I’m signing off, and I’ve cherished every moment – especially storming the French embassy with a (toy) AK-47

Journalism 101 – a course I have yet to complete – dictates that if you have something salient to say you should get there fast. So right now, I should mention that this is my last ever column for the Guardian. I’ll level with you: I spent a long time wondering how to write it. At first, I thought it should be about all the things I’ve learned, purely because that would be a hell of a lot shorter than a column about all the things I keep failing to learn, no matter how many times I make the mistakes. For example: if you’ve got a good joke, you’d best put it in the intro. (Why is there literally no joke in this intro?)

Or: remember that people love the piss-taking until it strays into the arena of something they like, when it suddenly becomes wholly unacceptable. Take the time I wrote: “Arguing on the internet is like playing real tennis: even if you win, you’re still a twat”. This prompted an immediate missive from a member of the Cambridge University real tennis club, which appeared on the letters page under the headline “Real tennis has been served badly by this unfair slur” and began: “Like many Guardian readers, I have thoroughly enjoyed and always look forward to reading Marina Hyde’s witty and caustic commentaries on the world about us. However …” Incidentally, I told this story at one book tour event, and then at the signing afterwards, a lovely young lady came up to get a book dedicated to her father, Jeremy. And of course, she said: “I should probably mention, he’s the guy who wrote in from the Cambridge University real tennis club.” Truly, the circle of life. To Jeremy, and the many other Jeremies who have written in over the years, let me just say: we all know the real twats are rackets players.

In the end, though, this could only be largely a column of thanks. I’ve ended up covering so many things over my time at the Guardian – from World Cups to Olympic Games to just the 47 general elections – but for the past few years, my permanent berth has been here in the Opinion section. And I want to pay tribute to all the people on this hallowed desk. I have tried to be the easiest columnist to deal with … like that means anything. Columnists are very possibly the worst demographic in journalism. And as you know, that really DOES mean something. As I say, I’ve tried to keep my interventions in the editorial process very limited, but I do have to accept I have basically said three things to the Opinion desk, on repeat. 1. “So what if it’s in bad taste?” (I stand by that one.) 2. “It’s not offensive – what you’ve done is confuse the subject of the joke with the object of the joke.” (I mean … that genuinely is so obnoxious. I can only apologise.) And 3. the extremely timeworn: “why have you put a headline on this that makes me look like a – ”. And then I have to use a word that even in the Guardian you’re only allowed to use if it’s in reported speech.

The amazing editors and subeditors have borne all of that with good humour and equanimity. I don’t know what they’ve said after we’ve put down the phone to each other, but God knows they’d have been entitled to it.

I think we can all live without my retrospective, but I will say my time at the Guardian began in lively fashion, working on the Diary column. Quite soon after starting, we were given a one-off Osama bin Laden puppet by the Spitting Image creators, which I was dispatched to get photographed on the steps of the French embassy in London. (But why?) The only problem was that the latex Osama was carrying a toy AK-47, and just as I’d propped him against the door of the embassy to get the picture, it swung open and I was pulled inside by French security. Things escalated fast. In the end, the incident was attended by 10 police squad cars and five police motorcycles, and Knightsbridge was brought to a total standstill.

Again: why? Why did we do this? Genuinely the reasons for it are lost in the mists of time for me. Like so many stunts pulled by what we used to call newspapers, it made absolute sense in the context of the news cycle in which it happened, and makes absolutely no sense once ripped from those temporal moorings. But over two decades on, I would obviously like to thank the various police forces on the scene – French, Met, and diplomatic – for deciding not to press charges, which would, I sense, have made the rest of my so-called career rather tricky.

Over time, that old Fleet Street wild west gave way to the digital wild west in which we live now – a place of no less remarkable incident. One of the bizarre things that came with the advent of social media was seeing which famous people reposted your columns. Probably my favourite was when I wrote one about a new ITV show where Rob Lowe played a police chief in Brexit Britain. (I know – how did it not get a second season?) In the course of this column, I happened to digress all the way back to that time in 1988 when Rob was campaigning for Michael Dukakis at the Democratic national convention, on the eve of which he ended up making a sex tape in his convention hotel in Georgia with two girls, one of whom was 16. And then I mentioned that at my school, we were all totally thrilled and excited when that story came out, because it meant that Rob Lowe was definitely open to sex with 16-year-old girls. (cf “so what if it’s in bad taste?”)

Imagine the lift on my eyebrow when Rob Lowe only went and reposted this column, particularly bearing in mind that for the past few years his timeline had consisted of incredibly wholesome content about dropping his children off at university and so on. Did it indicate that he still had a bit of the animal left in him (my preferred reading, as I don’t think you ever truly kill it off) or had he simply not read through to the relevant bit? We will, I think, never really know – and I always enjoyed such mysteries.

While we let that one settle, it feels like a great moment to begin my lengthy thanks to the Guardian’s legal department, with whom it may not surprise you to learn I have shared many, many intense moments over the years. There was a point not so long ago when someone on the Opinion desk relayed to me that someone in the legal department had said: “really the best person at legalling Marina’s column is Marina”. First: no. But second: this honestly might be the greatest compliment I ever got. It’s like the old proverb goes: legal a woman’s column and you feed her for a day. Teach a woman to legal her own column and you feed her for a lifetime. I want to thank legal for all the incredibly nutritious masterclasses.

And, speaking directly to the department, I am very much hoping we don’t get a complaint on this last column, although that would in some ways be amusingly on-brand. Looking back over what I’ve typed so far … I feel like Rob Lowe is the most obvious vulnerability? Alas, my Guardian email address will no longer work, so – hate to say it – you guys will be on your own with this one should it materialise. What we had was simply too special to be exported over to my new inbox. (This regretful bounce-back also applies to any rackets players who may now be seeking to get in touch.)

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Finally, then: that email address, and what it has meant to me. Many people don’t believe this, but in all the 25 years I have worked for the Guardian, I never had a private email address. Thus I have been in a constant – constant! – dialogue with Guardian readers who write in about my columns. Long before all the amazing digital metrics that we now have on where and how deeply our work is read, I had multiple daily emails from Guardian readers with subject headlines like “thank you”, “screw you” and – occasionally – “shame on you”. They ran the full gauntlet from adoring to bracing to skin-flaying. I would honestly not have had it any other way.

If you write opinion on the news, ultimately you are in the audience business, and to have an ongoing back-and-forth with the one you’re serving has been as much of a privilege as it has been endlessly enlightening and stimulating. So how could I not save the most important people in this column to last? Thank you so much, dear readers – and I hope to see you down the trail. In the meantime, my very best wishes to you and yours. It has, I promise you, been an absolute honour.

Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist

She’s been making sense of the madness for the last 25 years: celebrate the end of an era with Marina Hyde’s final column collection, What a Time to Be Alive! To support the Guardian, order your signed copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply

For too long, only the right has expanded the boundaries of what governments can do. Can Burnham change that?

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 09:00:16 GMT

The PM might come across as a nice bloke but he is politically ruthless. He will need to be if he is to turn big talk into big changes

How much can a Labour government change the country? According to many voters, journalists and politicians, including plenty in the party itself, the answer to that stubbornly recurring question has always been: not that much. Labour governments can’t restructure the economy, radically redistribute wealth, truly empower the disadvantaged or adopt a genuinely ethical foreign policy without upsetting too many powerful interests, from the British rich to the US government to global financial markets.

This endlessly repeated conventional wisdom – internalised by some on the left as well as centrists and the right – has haunted many Labour governments, from the first, tentative ones in the 1920s to Keir Starmer’s diligent but failed administration a century later. Yet conventional wisdom can be wrong, especially in volatile periods such as the current one, when precedent may count for little.

At last year’s Labour conference, Andy Burnham was widely derided for what was seen as a half-launched and clumsy leadership coup attempt. Much of the media and Starmer’s cabinet reckoned his chances of being prime minister were gone for good. Yet, at this week’s unusually packed and perhaps unwisely optimistic gathering, Burnham’s can-do presence was almost as dominant as Tony Blair’s in his early leadership years: a constant point of reference, from the main hall to the merch stands to leftwing fringe events.

Moreover, Burnham appears to want to use his personal dominance – which may well be briefer than Blair’s, given Labour’s more fragile position in a more fragmented politics – to open up an array of huge issues that his party has long been advised to keep closed. Electoral reform, social care, public intervention in failing privatised utilities, the pension triple lock, even rejoining the EU: announcements about exploring or pursuing all these punctuated his conference speech, in a sequence of softly voiced political shocks.

“Change will be difficult,” he acknowledged. But he insisted: “More of the same isn’t good enough.” At an excited fringe event the night before, his ally Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, who in that job and his previous one as energy secretary has pioneered Labour’s unexpected recent interest in confronting difficult problems and dangerous interests, summed up the party’s defiant new mood. “All politics is a risk. Progressive politics is a particular risk,” he said with relish. Burnham might have similar charisma and communication skills to Blair in the 1990s, but New Labour ministers did not dare say such provocative things.

Defenders of that now remote-seeming political culture would argue that avoiding head-on clashes was one of the reasons Blair was twice re-elected. But Burnham, who served in the Blair government at a formative age, does also have a strong conciliatory impulse, such as his frequently stated keenness to cooperate with other parties. However, as with his reluctance to criticise them by name – his conference speech was almost completely free of the usual party-political attacks – this apparent absence of aggression is in one sense the opposite: a determined attempt to break with the ultra-partisan politics of the post-Brexit decade that has excited many journalists but increasingly exhausted and alienated the public.

Burnham might come across as a nice bloke but he is ruthless, wrongfooting opponents and rendering their tactics obsolete, as his supposedly formidable Labour enemies such as Morgan McSweeney learned this year. Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage’s perpetual outrage and tribalism suddenly seem rigid and unreasonable next to Burnham’s talk of hope and national togetherness, and his disarming admission this week that all politicians must do better, that “this country isn’t where any of us would want it to be”.

Labour’s modest but persistent rise in the polls suggests that sufficient voters have had enough of the old high-argument, low-achievement politics to make Labour the leading party again for a period, perhaps up to the next general election and even beyond, when many of his ambitious reforms are actually meant to take place. Of course, proposing, let alone implementing, major changes to the status quo such as loosening the triple lock will also make many voters absolutely furious (even if that policy initially appears popular), and provide regular targets for Labour’s enemies in Westminster and the media. Yet, with the electorate more divided than ever, and the bar for re-election probably set as low as winning over less than a third of voters, being controversial or unpopular matters less for a government than before – provided it holds its nerve and pleases a large enough core of supporters. Burnham’s sweeping attacks on Labour bogeymen such as the privatised utilities seem likely to achieve that. Meanwhile, his cross-party overtures and support for electoral reform may well lure voters and politicians from the Lib Dems and Greens.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Like Pedro Sánchez in Spain, another centre-left premier of similar age who has managed to stay in power for eight years, Burnham is a paradoxical politician: both frank and evasive; opposed to populism and good at populist gestures; prepared to echo the left’s critique of capitalism but also pro-business; a self-styled lone saviour who is able to work in coalitions. Photogenic and politically agile – you could say shameless – Sánchez and Burnham seem better suited to today’s world of flux, short attention spans and deep discontent than the previous generation of stiff social democrats such as Starmer. Perhaps the modern centre-left is finally working out how to govern and reshape the societies that its more popular 1990s predecessor never sufficiently reformed.

For too long, it has been the right that expanded the boundaries of what governments can do. If Burnham’s barely begun administration is to become a significant one – perhaps like that of Harold Wilson, another slippery, charming Labour leader with Merseyside connections – it will need to enact big reforms as well as talk promisingly about them.

Sixty years ago, Wilson won an election landslide, and commemorative items competed with the cult of Burnham on the merch stands at conference in Liverpool. “Wilson’s greatest hits”, said the cover of a souvenir record, “Featuring Creation of the Open University, Equal Pay Act, Abolished Capital Punishment, Race Relations Act, Abortion Act, Decriminalised Homosexuality”. Wilson’s premiership was often unpopular and struggled economically, but it lastingly changed Britain by resolving some contentious social questions. Burnham may have to settle for doing the same.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

Times Insider

Times editors explore the thinking behind our coverage of the explosive allegations that have roiled a campus and the country.

Sexual assault allegations have rocked Cornell’s campus and put the university under a spotlight. Credit... Heather Ainsworth for The New York Times

Supported by

By Megan DiTrolio and Mike Abrams

With Nikita StewartSarah Garland and Susan Wessling

Megan DiTrolio and Mike Abrams are editors on the Trust team, focusing on efforts to help readers understand The Times and its journalism.

A former sophomore at Cornell University became known to the nation as Jane Doe this week when prosecutors reopened an investigation into claims that she was raped by several men at a Chi Phi fraternity house two years ago.

Last month, Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against the university, the fraternity, her sorority and the seven men who she says assaulted her and plied her with ketamine that night in 2024. Days later, a student newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun, criticized the university for the way it had handled its internal investigation — and published an editorial identifying the men. (The men have denied wrongdoing.)

The New York Times has obtained hundreds of pages of confidential investigative files that provide more details about that night and the school’s response. In an edited conversation, Nikita Stewart, Metro editor; Sarah Garland, education editor; and Susan Wessling, Standards editor, explained how our coverage unfolded this week.

Student journalists at Cornell have been covering this story aggressively. How has this become a major story for The New York Times? And were we late to the story?

NIKITA STEWART: We reviewed the lawsuit, but we wanted to approach it with an abundance of caution. We wondered how we could find a way in, and when the local district attorney said that he would reopen the case, we seized the opportunity.

Our coverage has taken a restrained approach to identifying the men accused of sexual assault. Can you walk us through the conversations and considerations?

SUSAN WESSLING: There’s certainly a fairness concern — while these men have been accused of something terrible, they haven’t been charged with anything. And whatever we publish has to be accurate, so we’ve been working to gather the facts. A lawsuit offers only one side of a situation. As the men’s names have been relevant to specific parts of our coverage, we have published them, including in a story on Thursday describing the accounts they gave to university officials about what happened that night.

NIKITA: When the lawsuit was filed, we had concerns that the men were not public figures and not charged. There was a lot to untangle. That gave us pause. Once the district attorney said he was reopening the case, we reassessed and decided that we would use the names in context and with specificity.

Some messages exchanged over Snapchat by students — and now shared widely on social media — were obscene. We have not directly quoted a number of those messages or published screenshots. Can you walk us through our thinking, and how we decide what to show to readers?

NIKITA: We consult with Standards editors on those decisions. We have to walk the line of being transparent with our readers while making sure our publishing of the messages is not gratuitous. We are still combing through records and will make decisions on what serves the story and the reader.

SUSAN: We have a high bar for publishing obscene or offensive comments. When the words themselves are critical to understanding the story, we make the decision to tell or show readers precisely what was said. So every day we’re making judgment calls about whether the specifics of those messages are relevant to understanding each story — and in many stories, they won’t be.

The Times seeks precision, facts and details in its reporting and writing. But in some situations, we have paraphrased the students’ language. For example, in one article we reported that fraternity men were inviting members to “join in, using a crude name for female genitalia” instead of directly quoting a particular message. In a story published on Thursday, we used the lewd quote. Why now, and how did we land there?

SUSAN: In a broad overview piece, like the What We Know article that the paraphrase appeared in, we made the call that the exact language wasn’t crucial to the point we were making. In a different story, where we’re recounting the specifics of the Cornell investigation and what the men did and said, the exact language helps a reader understand their state of mind, and the atmosphere of that night.

NIKITA: In the case of our article of the men’s accounts, we felt it was important to show the language and to put the reader on campus at that time.

Are we assuming that readers either already know what we’re talking about or will find the messages themselves elsewhere?

SUSAN: We do know that people might already know what we’re talking about, but we don’t make our decisions based on those assumptions. We make judgments about what we think is right for each story. And we’re aware that not everyone will agree with those judgments, even internally. There has been real debate in the last few days about how far to go, and the risks of amplifying something offensive and off-putting versus the risks of what some see as sanitizing reality. Lots of people weigh in, and we make the best call we can.

We have over 1,000 pages from an internal Cornell report on this matter. What can you say about how you received such a highly sensitive report? Walk us through the process of examining so much material.

NIKITA: I will not discuss how we obtain information like this, but we verified their authenticity and then our Metro investigations editor took the lead in assembling a team of eight reporters to read the files.

SARAH GARLAND: We confront this kind of reporting fairly often. The Epstein files obviously come to mind. A. I. is now really helpful in guiding reporters. We have tools that can help us search for and catalog information. But it’s never a substitute for pulling in as many people as we can to just read. Having people focused on different aspects can also help, so one or two people are following a particular thread through the documents.

There’s often a rush to judgment on social media. What steps do we take to cut through that? Do we ever fall short?

SUSAN: We cut through the online rush to judgment by doing reporting. We’re after the truth, and getting at the truth involves digging below the surface. Our commitment to accuracy and fairness means we have to double-check and reach out to the people involved to try to get their side — before we publish anything. That doesn’t mean we have the full picture on the first day of any news story. But we can say what we do know, and be humble about what we don’t know and are still trying to understand. It’s often also important to say what hasn’t happened — in this case, for example, to point out that the men in the Cornell case haven’t been charged, and that the allegations in Jane Doe’s lawsuit haven’t been tested in court.

SARAH: I can’t count the number of colleagues who have come to me urging caution as we examine these allegations. We’ve had group discussions and one-on-one conversations about how to make sure we are being fair and careful about presenting the facts at every step.

NIKITA: This is one of the reasons it was so important for us to obtain the records that we did. We could examine the investigation and recollections of events, without social media speculation.

This story involves young people — both those directly involved and other Cornell students who have spoken to us about the case. What do we take into account when interviewing and writing about people of this age group?

SARAH: We are extremely careful about how we write about and quote minors, but we have similar discussions about how to write about young people, even if they’re over 18. They’re just getting their adult lives started. And if we’re talking to them for a news article, it’s often at a vulnerable moment, or about a sensitive topic. So we always try to weigh the pros and cons. We want to include their voices, but we want to do so with care.

SUSAN: We definitely weigh the pros and cons, as Sarah said. The college students are adults, but they probably haven’t thought much about dealing with reporters, or what it means to have their thoughts published in The Times.

NIKITA: In this modern age, young adults are accustomed to controlling their narratives through social media. We saw this, for example, during student protests when some said even being photographed on a public street was invasive. We want to tell their stories accurately and fairly, and our reporters have to approach many young people who are reluctant to speak to the media with sensitivity.

This case has ignited debate about sexual violence on college campuses, Greek life, Title IX and accountability at elite universities. What role does The Times play in this conversation?

SARAH: It has. And these are perennial issues. I think our role is to ask the same questions readers are asking: How do colleges respond to reports of sexual assault? Are they doing enough to prevent it? To punish it? How should it be defined? What is the role of government — the police, the federal government?

We are ideally channeling all of that to find out what the experts say, what colleges say, what students on campus say. We also want to learn about context and history — we’ve seen situations like this before and here is what happened back then. Then, my hope, my goal, is that presenting what we find to readers makes these debates more informed. I hope our coverage is helping people — whether it’s colleges, politicians or voters — decide what to do next.

We wrote a story about The Cornell Daily Sun and how the journalists there have been covering this situation since 2024. How closely do Times journalists follow college news organizations, and what do you think of their work?

SARAH: Every morning I wake up and drink my first cup of coffee while scanning through a long list of college newspaper sites. The reporting these student journalists do helps me see trends cutting across campuses and get a sense of what is important for college students right now. And fairly often, college papers are the first ones to break big news stories on their campuses, and we have to chase after them.

Mike Abrams is the deputy editor for Trust, working to help readers understand The Times and its journalistic values.

Nikita Stewart is the Metro editor at The Times.

Christa Pike Unconscious and on Ventilator After Execution Attempt

The New York Times October 02, 2026

Christa Pike’s Botched Execution

Advertisement

Supported by

Her condition raises questions about whether Tennessee could attempt to execute her again if she is incapable of understanding what is happening.

By Emily Cochrane

Reporting from Nashville

Christa Pike was unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator in a Nashville hospital as of Thursday evening, a day after surviving a botched execution attempt, her lawyers said in a court filing.

Ms. Pike, 50, was critically ill, they wrote in the Friday filing in Davidson County Chancery Court, and both of her arms were swollen, burned and blistered when she arrived at the hospital.

Her condition, some legal experts said, raises questions about whether the state could try to execute her again if she is not fully cognizant or capable of understanding what is happening. Ms. Pike, convicted of the 1995 murder of a classmate, is believed to be the first person to have survived after receiving drugs during a lethal injection attempt in the modern era of capital punishment.

The disclosure is the most detailed update on Ms. Pike’s health since she survived two rounds of pentobarbital, the drug used as part of Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol, on Wednesday evening.

“Hospital staff are working to save Ms. Pike’s life and to clear the pentobarbital from her system,” the lawyers wrote. In a separate statement, they said she was also receiving treatment for “significant injuries to both arms.”

In a statement, Luke Ihnen, who represents Ms. Pike through the Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee, said that “we are working closely with those closest to Christa to respect her wishes, safeguard her privacy and protect her rights as a patient during this extraordinarily difficult time.”

The disclosure about Ms. Pike’s condition was part of an emergency filing in which her lawyers asked a Nashville judge to order the preservation of state prison records related to her attempted execution. The records were, they wrote, evidence of “incompetent and reckless actions.”

The Tennessee Department of Correction declined to comment, citing the pending litigation. A spokeswoman for the Tennessee Attorney General, Jonathan Skrmetti, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, paused all executions through the end of the year and ordered an investigation into what went wrong Wednesday. But Mr. Lee is in the final months of his term.

The front-runner to replace him, Senator Marsha Blackburn, a Republican, said in a statement she would try to execute Ms. Pike again.

“This process has only extended the pain for the family of Colleen Slemmer,” she said. “Their family and the families of other victims deserve swift justice.”

Ms. Pike’s lawyers have asked Mr. Lee to grant her clemency and allow her to serve the rest of her life in prison, condemning what they have called a cruel and torturous execution attempt.

Two decades ago, the U. S. Supreme Court barred the execution of people with mental disabilities as a violation of the Constitution’s Eighth Amendment ban on cruel and unusual punishment. The court has also barred the execution of people who lack a “rational understanding” of the reason they are to be put to death.

“If you don’t understand you’re about to die, and do not understand you’re about to die because the state believes you have committed murder, then you may not be executed,” said Christopher Slobogin, the director of the Criminal Justice Program at Vanderbilt University.

Ms. Pike’s medical condition also presents a difficult scenario for the medical staff working to save her life: If she recovers, Tennessee might try to kill her again.

“Professionals in health care are faced with difficult moral situations all the time — this is a particularly challenging one,” said Dr. Jeff Kahn, the director of the Johns Hopkins Berman Institute of Bioethics. “I also think that they know that their job is to do the best they can for the patient in front of them and not to think about that.”

Jamie McGee and Ann E. Marimow contributed reporting.

An earlier version of this article misspelled the last name of the director of the Johns Hopkins Berman Institute of Bioethics. He is Dr. Jeff Kahn, not Khan.

Trump Directed Use of Taxpayer Money for Ads Praising His Presidency

The New York Times October 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The government-funded ads show just how much President Trump has been able to use federal money for his own aims.

By Maggie HabermanHamed AleazizShane Goldmacher and Jonathan Swan

President Trump personally instructed his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads praising him and his presidency, setting in motion a $20 million contract that used funds from the Department of Homeland Security, according to people familiar with the matter.

The ads have run across cable and network television — on Fox News, CNN and MS Now, with football games on Fox and with national newscasts on CBS, ABC and NBC, including “Meet the Press,” which Mr. Trump is known to watch.

Mr. Trump was eager to see the laudatory ads on the air and told Russell T. Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, to come up with the money from within the government, the people said. Mark Paoletta, the budget office’s counsel, and Will Scharf, the White House counsel, both said it would be legal to use D. H. S. funds. The president and Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, both spoke with Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, about the ads.

On Sept. 20, U. S. Customs and Border Protection — which falls under D. H. S. — awarded the contract to LMD, a Maryland marketing firm, federal records show.

This article is based on interviews with 12 people familiar with the president’s interest in the ads and how they came to be. They spoke on condition of anonymity to describe the president’s demand.

The taxpayer-funded ads have been criticized by Democrats and even some Republicans as a possible violation of federal laws against using taxpayer dollars for “publicity or propaganda purposes.” And they come as the president is also directing spending from his super PAC — MAGA Inc., which entered the fall with $400 million — for which he has been raising money since he won re-election in 2024.

It was not clear why taxpayer funds, and not money from the super PAC, were used for the spots.

The White House has called the ads public service announcements and said they are appropriate because there is no “call to action” to vote for any candidate. Some of his aides also noted that Mr. Trump is not running for office now, in an attempt to blunt criticism of the ads as violating federal laws about the use of public money.

When pressed by a reporter on Wednesday, Mr. Trump said: “If somebody said that that’s wrong, I’ll gladly pay the money.”

“But these are ads for the country,” he added. “You have to understand. I’m not promoting a candidate. I’m not promoting myself because I’m not running for office. I’m promoting the country.”

At least four spots have run so far, at a cost of about $5.5 million, and that is expected to grow, according to the media tracker AdImpact and people familiar with the spending. One played images of Mr. Trump to the song “Love Me” by Christian Berishaj, who performs as JMSN. (The artist has protested the use of his song.)

Another was identical to a Trump campaign video from 2024 that condemns “villains” whom the president perceives as enemies. The use of material originally made during Mr. Trump’s political campaign has given fuel to critics who reject the White House claim that the ads are simply public service announcements.

A third ad, about the Iran war, features remarks from both Mr. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Such public service spots typically say which agency paid for them. In this case, all of the ads had an unusual tagline: “Paid for by the U. S. government.”

On Aug. 7, Mr. Trump was in the Oval Office with a group of Republican strategists working with his team, along with James Blair, his top political adviser, and Ms. Wiles. Natalie Harp, his ever-present assistant and provider of positive news about himself, was there as well.

At the time, Mr. Trump’s advisers were waiting for him to sign off, finally, on spending from his super PAC for midterm candidates, after months of anxiety from Republican candidates about whether he would help them financially in tight races.

But during that meeting, the president was much more interested in looking at videos of himself.

He turned to Ms. Harp and asked her to show the group the type of imagery he favors.

Ms. Harp pulled up a series of videos made by the White House digital team on her tablet: Mr. Trump standing in front of vast crowds; Mr. Trump beside Marine One; Mr. Trump with fighter jets streaking overhead.

One video showed Dana White, the U. F. C. president, at the 2024 Republican convention, calling Mr. Trump “the toughest, most resilient person that I’ve ever met.” Mr. Trump has talked with delight about that quote repeatedly ever since.

Mr. Trump made clear he planned to travel to support candidates in the midterms, but also that his presidency needed to be promoted, front and center, in the commercials his advisers were making.

Later that month, The Atlantic reported that MAGA Inc. was planning a blitz of midterm ads, with Trump as the centerpiece.

Instead, a Trump-linked nonprofit called Securing American Greatness aired a spot featuring the Dana White quote, spending just under $60,000, according to AdImpact. The ad primarily aired over Sept. 2 and Sept. 3 around Washington, where Mr. Trump was sure to see them.

But then, weeks later, several ads glorifying Mr. Trump began appearing across the country — this time paid for by taxpayers, by way of Customs and Border Protection.

The ads included the “Love Me” spot, in which Mr. Trump says in a voice-over that “America will never be a communist country.”

As the taxpayer-funded spots began running, MAGA Inc. has spent directly to help out in one specific race, putting more than $20 million into the Texas Senate campaign. Two other new groups linked to MAGA Inc. — No Going Back PAC and Safety and Affordability PAC — were recently created and have spent and reserved more than $163 million on spots in races across the country.

But those ads feature Mr. Trump only sparingly.

Asked to comment for this story, the White House press office sent an unsigned statement saying, “These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders and abroad.”

The White House has said there is precedent for using taxpayer money for the ads. “Don’t let the Fake News get away with their lies about our epic Public Service Announcements that have been running on tv,” Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, posted on X on Sept. 27.

His office sent out an email stating that “presidential public service announcements are nothing new,” comparing the spots to efforts to promote health care policy in past administrations, or President Woodrow Wilson’s World War I propaganda campaign.

The Government Accountability Office has found likely or confirmed violations of the anti-propaganda rule before, including during the tenures of both President Barack Obama and President George W. Bush. Those cases concerned publicity campaigns related to policies, not ads focused on the presidents themselves.

The money for the ads was freed up on Sept. 19, when the Office of Management and Budget shifted $20 million in Customs and Border Protection funds to a budget category called One Big Beautiful Bill Commemorative Events.

The next day, C. B. P. awarded a $20 million contract to LMD, a marketing firm based in Columbia, Md., that federal records show had past work as a government contractor. The actual purchase of the airtime was made by a second firm, LMO, according to a person familiar with the events, who wasn’t authorized to discuss them publicly.

A spokeswoman for the Office of Management and Budget declined to comment on the reporting for this story. A spokesperson for the Homeland Security Department would only say, “D. H. S. follows all applicable rules for contracting decisions and keeps all decision makers informed. All contracting decisions are made in accordance with applicable law.” Officials with LMD and LMO did not respond to requests for comment.

The spots started out airing narrowly but soon ran in heavy rotation not just on cable channels, but on broadcast networks as well. They ran heavily on the network morning programs like “Good Morning America” and “CBS Mornings,” according AdImpact, and appeared in entertainment shows including “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” and “The Amazing Race.” One aired repeatedly during weekend football broadcasts on the Fox network.

The ads are not the first costly television campaign under Mr. Trump, nor are they the first controversial one. In 2025, Kristi Noem, the homeland security secretary at the time, appeared in a $200 million-plus government ad campaign. The ads, which showed Ms. Noem on a horse at Mount Rushmore, ultimately drew the president’s disapproval, and became the justification for replacing Ms. Noem.

The latest ads promoting Mr. Trump come as his standing with the public has dropped. His approval rating sits at around 37 percent, a number that has been low and steady for months, according to a polling tracker by The New York Times. Republicans are increasingly fearful of a Democratic sweep of both House and Senate, and losses in state legislatures.

Mr. Trump has remained a prodigious fund-raiser for his various construction projects around Washington and at the White House, as well as his future presidential library. Last month, he promised to spend “probably” $400 million to $500 million on midterm election races, but he made clear who holds the purse strings to his super PAC.

“This is my money that I control,” Mr. Trump said.

Reporting was contributed by Jim Rutenberg in New York and Luke Broadwater in Washington.

Maggie Haberman is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

Hamed Aleaziz covers the Department of Homeland Security and immigration policy for The Times.

Shane Goldmacher is a Times national political correspondent.

F. D. A. Found Cyclospora During Taylor Farms Inspection in Mexico

The New York Times October 02, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The discovery adds strong evidence that the outbreak that sickened thousands over the summer originated in the company’s fields or processing facility in northeastern Mexico.

By Christina JewettAlice Callahan and Caroline Hopkins Legaspi

The Food and Drug Administration said on Friday that it had found two samples of the cyclospora parasite during its investigation of Taylor Farms facilities in Mexico, strong new evidence that an outbreak that sickened thousands in the United States this summer came from lettuce produced by the company.

The agency sent inspectors to the company’s processing plant and nearby farms in August, about a month after Taylor Farms recalled bags of lettuce sent to retailers across the nation. Friday’s announcement disclosed the first results of that inquiry: Inspectors discovered cyclospora in water from a tank that held outgoing wastewater from the Taylor Farms de Mexico processing facility, which chopped fresh lettuce. A second positive sample was found in sediment in a drainage ditch at an iceberg lettuce farm that operates as an independent grower for Taylor Farms.

Over the course of the summer, the cyclospora outbreak linked to Taylor Farms caused nearly 13,000 illnesses, 570 hospitalizations and two deaths in 21 states. It was the nation’s largest outbreak of food-borne illness in decades. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention declared the outbreak over in September.

The F. D. A. and the C. D. C. announced in July that the outbreak was most likely linked to the processing facility in Mexico after officials in Michigan interviewed hundreds of people who fell ill and examined supply chain records from Taco Bell.

Taylor Farms ultimately recalled 236,192 cases of lettuce sold to stores, restaurants and distributors including Walmart, Subway, Jack in the Box, Taco Bell and Sysco.

The F. D. A. said it is still working to determine if the genotype of the cyclospora samples found in Mexico matched samples collected from sick patients in the United States. Cases of cyclospora are challenging to link genetically because the parasite cannot be cultured in a laboratory the way that bacteria like salmonella or E. coli can. This means that investigators cannot easily identify whether different cases of cyclospora share a common strain.

“While there is currently not enough evidence to conclusively determine how contamination occurred in this outbreak, the positive samples show that cyclospora was present in the environment where lettuce was grown and processed,” the F. D. A. said in a statement. “This adds to the strong epidemiological data and traceback convergence supporting the link between this outbreak and recalled shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico.”

Taylor Farms said in a statement on Friday that it has not reopened the processing facility since production was suspended in July “as we work with our research team to implement enhanced safety protocols from the field to the facility.”

The company also said in a statement that the independent farm where one sample was discovered is “no longer part of our supplier program.” The statement also emphasized the F. D. A.’s conclusion that there is not enough evidence to conclusively determine where the contamination occurred.

The company said it takes safety seriously: “We know trust is earned by what we do, and we will continue to learn, improve and take action to keep our food fresh and safe.”

Previously, the company said it had invested more than $200 million per year in food safety protocols and hired experts to do a thorough review of its Mexico processing center.

Cyclospora, which can cause severe diarrhea and cramping, is known to spread only through human feces. So although the F. D. A. has not concluded how, exactly, the parasite ended up in the wastewater tank and drainage ditch, the water was most likely contaminated with traces of feces from people on or near the facilities who were infected with cyclospora themselves.

Also on Friday, the F. D. A. announced a series of actions intended to prevent future cyclospora outbreaks. Those included greater surveillance of foods that have caused past outbreaks, which can include cilantro and raspberries, and outreach to growers about how to reduce the risk of produce contamination with the parasite.

It is difficult to know whether those steps will be effective at preventing future outbreaks, since the F. D. A. has not yet determined how the lettuce at Taylor Farms was contaminated, said Jim Gorny, a produce safety expert who retired from the agency in 2024.

“Aside from that,” he said, “it’s just a recommitment to employ the same strategies and tactics over and over again hoping for a different outcome.”

Bill Marler, a lawyer based in Washington State whose office represents about 500 people sickened in the outbreak, said there is still more to learn from additional analysis of the samples from the inspection and stool samples of those who fell ill.

But before next growing season, he said, it would be ideal if federal officials could invest in the development of a water test to routinely surveil water for cyclospora, which does not currently exist. He would also like to see officials enforce a federal rule requiring food companies to hand over supply chain records in 24 hours after a product is implicated in an outbreak.

The F. D. A. finalized such a rule but delayed its implementation last year, potentially slowing down the response to this outbreak, The New York Times found.

Mr. Marler added two more items to his wish list: more inspections of facilities in Mexico like the Taylor Farms processor, which before August had not been inspected since 2019. And “an answer for the roughly 7,000 confirmed cases this summer that were never tied to any food,” he said, referring to cases that health officials confirmed but never linked to a specific source.

Frank Yiannas, a top food official at the F. D. A. from 2018 to 2023, said the agency had much more work to do to determine what went wrong this summer and how to prevent future outbreaks.

“Let’s hope this summer’s incident becomes a catalyst for a stronger, more collaborative call to action across both the public and private sectors,” he said.

Christina Jewett covers the Food and Drug Administration, which means keeping a close eye on drugs, medical devices, food safety and tobacco policy.

Alice Callahan is a Times reporter covering nutrition and health. She has a Ph. D. in nutrition from the University of California, Davis.

Caroline Hopkins Legaspi is a Times reporter focusing on nutrition and sleep.

Judge Blocks Border Wall Construction in Big Bend in Texas

The New York Times October 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The ruling dealt a setback to the Trump administration’s plans for hundreds of miles of barriers that have drawn local opposition.

By J. David Goodman

A federal judge in El Paso on Friday halted border wall construction across the Big Bend region, dealing a blow to the Trump administration’s effort to erect hundreds of miles of barriers despite fierce local opposition.

The federal government “shall not build border barrier or related infrastructure, or engage in any construction or ground disturbing activities, in the Big Bend sector,” the judge, Kathleen Cardone, wrote in her order, which she read from the bench.

In a two-page order granting an injunction in the case, the judge said the federal government could not rely on waivers of environmental and other laws it had granted itself to speed up the construction, writing that it “must comply with all applicable laws.” Judge Cardone ruled that the government could not use the waivers until the case was resolved.

She wrote that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on the merits of at least one of their claims.

The lawsuit, filed in the Western District of Texas by plaintiffs including a river boat guide and a church preservation group, sought to stop U. S. Customs and Border Protection from building border barriers across a more-than-500-mile stretch of the frontier with Mexico. The plans, which include some barriers in Big Bend National Park, have been the focus of months of protests and stop-and-start construction activity.

A spokesman for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.

Outside the courthouse, river guides and environmental activists cheered after the order was issued.

“We dodged a bullet today,” said Billy Miller, a river guide who lives in Terlingua, Texas, and was one of the named plaintiffs in the suit. “It means that we can continue to introduce people to the wildness. Their plan was going to ruin the experience of anybody going out there.”

The opposition to border construction in the Big Bend region of Texas, a remote area known for its rugged wilderness, included national groups and local residents. Among the arguments made by the plaintiffs was that few illegal crossings take place in the area because of the inherent dangers posed by its remoteness. The Big Bend sector records far fewer crossings than any other portion of the Texas-Mexico border.

Federal officials have argued that barrier construction was necessary, even if crossings were currently low, because the number would increase as barriers were constructed in other parts of the border and migrants looked for new ways to get into the country.

Still, opponents considered the ruling as a significant victory.

“No constructions can continue,” said Laiken Jordahl, an advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity and a witness for the plaintiffs who was in the courtroom on Friday. “All the bulldozers have been stopped across the entire border sector.”

J. David Goodman is the Texas bureau chief for The Times, based in Houston.

California Sues to Block Trump From Weakening Fuel Economy Rules

The New York Times October 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The lawsuit is the 97th the state has filed against the Trump administration over the past year and a half.

By Brad Plumer

Reporting from Washington

Led by California, nearly two dozen states sued the Trump administration on Friday over its rollback of fuel efficiency standards for cars, arguing that the move was based on a faulty analysis and violated federal law.

The lawsuit continued an escalating legal battle between President Trump, who has sought to dismantle a broad array of climate and environmental policies, and California, which said it has now sued the administration 97 times.

The federal Transportation Department announced this week that it would sharply scale back fuel efficiency rules for new cars and light trucks, gutting one of the Biden administration’s most aggressive policies to reduce gasoline consumption and push automakers to shift to electric vehicles.

The new rules will require automakers to achieve an average fuel efficiency of 34.9 miles per gallon for new cars and light trucks in model year 2031. That standard is far below the figure of 50.4 m. p. g. set by the Biden administration.

Last year, Republicans in Congress eliminated fines for automakers that didn’t meet the mileage standards, essentially rendering them toothless.

In its lawsuit, filed in the U. S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, a coalition of Democratic-run states and cities, led by California, plans to argue that the new rules are illegal because they do not set fuel efficiency standards at the “maximum feasible” level, as required by law.

The states say that the Trump administration’s standards are less stringent than what automakers have already achieved, and that federal agencies had ignored recent advances in electric vehicle technology when setting the rules. They also contend that the administration overlooked the costs of oil price shocks and climate pollution.

“The administration can’t manipulate its analysis to reach the result it wants,” Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, told reporters on Friday.

Mr. Bonta added that Mr. Trump’s war in Iran, which has helped push gasoline prices up by more than 30 percent this year, demonstrated the need for more fuel efficiency.

“The benefits of helping Americans drive on less gas should be obvious by now,” he said.

In a statement, the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, defended the new rules, saying that the Biden administration had “illegally twisted mileage standards to create an electric vehicle mandate — jacking up car prices for American families and forcing manufacturers to produce vehicles no one wanted.”

He added, “This administration understands the freedom of every American family starts with affordable cars.”

The Trump administration’s analysis estimated that its rules would cut car prices by $1,289 in model year 2031, on average. But drivers of those cars would also pay $1,624 more in fuel costs over time than they would have under the Biden-era standards, according to the analysis.

Many automakers opposed the Biden-era rules, saying that they would have required too quick of a shift toward electric vehicles. Auto industry groups have also criticized the constantly shifting standards, which typically tighten under Democratic presidents and loosen under Republicans.

“What the industry needs is long-term regulatory stability that includes balanced, durable and achievable fuel economy standards that continue to reduce emissions and improve fuel economy,” John Bozzella, chief executive of the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a lobbying group for major carmakers, said of the new rules in a statement on Monday.

Congress created the mileage standards in 1975 in response to an oil embargo by Middle Eastern countries. Since then, automakers have steadily improved how far cars can travel on a tank of gas, while expanding electric and hybrid offerings.

Transportation is the country’s largest source of planet-warming greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide. The Biden administration had ratcheted up the mileage standards as part of its strategy to tackle climate change.

Mr. Trump, who has rejected efforts to address global warming, attacked E. V. s during his campaign to retake the White House.

Mr. Bonta said Congress’s move to eliminate penalties for not meeting the standards did not affect the states’ lawsuit.

“We think just the lack of the penalty on its own does not make this action by the federal administration lawful,” he said. “It’s still unlawful, penalty or no penalty.”

California has sued over a flurry of other Trump administration actions affecting transportation. It has joined a coalition of Democratic-led states challenging the Environmental Protection Agency for erasing Biden-era limits on greenhouse gas emissions from new cars and trucks.

The state has also sued the Trump administration over efforts to prevent California from mandating cleaner vehicles within its borders.

The Clean Air Act of 1970 gave California the authority to limit tailpipe pollution more strictly than federal standards, as long as it receives E. P. A. permission. Under the Obama and Biden administrations, the agency approved waivers allowing California to set tighter limits on pollution from cars, trucks, ships and even lawn mowers.

Mr. Trump and congressional Republicans have tried to rescind many of those waivers using a law called the Congressional Review Act. Last year, lawmakers blocked a sweeping California plan to effectively phase out sales of gasoline-powered vehicles by 2035.

The state has challenged that move and others like it in court.

Brad Plumer is a Times reporter who covers technology and policy efforts to address global warming.

By Shane Goldmacher and Theodore Schleifer

The top super PAC for Senate Republicans is canceling all the remaining ads it had booked in North Carolina as of Friday, shifting away tens of millions of dollars in a move that signals that Republicans no longer see a path to winning the state this fall.

At the same time, the super PAC, called the Senate Leadership Fund, is making its first investment of the cycle in Kansas — a sign of rising concern among Republicans in red states — with a new ad attacking the Democratic nominee there.

If Republicans lose North Carolina, it would give Democrats one of the four seats they need to flip the Senate in the fall — if Democrats hold all of their own seats.

Ad cancellations are a common, and very telling, move down the stretch of campaigns as they reveal where national operatives see their best path to a majority. The cancellation of the North Carolina ads was first reported by Semafor and confirmed by two people familiar with the decision.

The North Carolina seat is currently held by Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican who is retiring. Democrats nominated Roy Cooper, a popular former governor who had served two terms. The Republican nominee is Michael Whatley, the former chairman of the Republican National Committee.

The Senate Leadership Fund declined to comment.

“Undecided voters who break late decide the election in North Carolina and the majority of those late-breakers typically go Republican,” said DJ Griffin, a spokesman for Mr. Whatley, adding he was “confident we have the resources to highlight career politician Roy Cooper’s 40 years of failures.”

Super PACs aligned with President Trump also do not have any future reservations for airtime in the North Carolina Senate race.

In Kansas, the new reservation shows that Republicans are worried about the re-election bid of Senator Roger Marshall, the Republican incumbent, who faces Adam Hamilton, the pastor of the largest United Methodist congregation in the country.

The new ad attacks Mr. Hamilton as a “two-faced extremist.”

The full size of the Kansas spending was not clear but as of midday Friday, the Senate Leadership Fund had booked $8.2 million worth of ads in the state, according to data from AdImpact, the ad-tracking service.

Democrats have not won a Senate election in Kansas since 1932.

The Senate Leadership Fund had initially planned to spend $71 million in North Carolina. The group has spent more than $30 million of those funds, according to one of the people familiar with the decision. The group still had $18 million reserved for the final month just on broadcast and cable television, according to AdImpact.

In preparation for these cancellations, an increased number of Republican Senate candidates started their own dedicated super PACs, in part so they could insulate themselves from cuts from the Senate Leadership Fund. And yet Mr. Whatley’s dedicated group, Old North Action, previously canceled ads as well.

The court records filed in John Doe’s case show that, after a 12-day evidentiary hearing in which he faced charges of sexual assault and sexual exploitation, he was found responsible for attempted sexual exploitation.

They also show the punishments he received following the decision, including a one-way no-contact order with the woman, a requirement that he take a class about social media use and sexual harassment and an order to write a reflection paper specifically addressing his actions.

According to the filings, John Doe had gone to the room where the assault occurred after seeing a Snapchat message sent to a group chat with dozens of Chi Phi members. After an appeal of the panel’s decision to hold him responsible for attempted sexual exploitation was unsuccessful, the records show, John Doe sued the school, arguing that university officials had not sufficiently informed him of that charge.

Last week, a judge sided with Cornell, dismissing John Doe’s petition. Two days later, on Sept. 25, he filed a notice of appeal to a higher court. That case is currently pending in the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York.

Alan Sash, a lawyer for John Doe, said in a statement on Friday that he intended to appeal the lower court’s decision, saying that he aimed to hold the university responsible for the sake of his client and “every student whose future Cornell places in jeopardy.”

The extraordinary move — holding back about one-fifth of the N. S. F.’s primary research budget — is the latest sign of how the Trump administration is finding creative ways to work around Congress. Lawmakers from both parties have consistently opposed White House-led proposals to cut funding to major science agencies, including the N. S. F. and the National Institutes of Health.

Since the N. S. F. was founded over 75 years ago, the agency has spent nearly all of its budget on so-called basic research from a wide range of scientific fields, which has led to major advances in technology such as M. R. I. s, semiconductors and the internet.

The White House wants to redirect the money to a limited set of administration priorities, including artificial intelligence and quantum computing, according to two people with knowledge of the administration’s plans.

Congress appropriates money to the N. S. F. on two-year cycles, so the agency could still spend the held-over money in the new fiscal year, which began on Thursday.

But Democratic lawmakers see the strategy as more of a political power grab by the White House.

“The money should be granted as Congress intended, and essentially, they’re ignoring what Congress did,” said Representative Zoe Lofgren of California, the top Democrat on the Science, Space and Technology Committee. “It’s a dramatic attack on the science enterprise that has served us very well since World War II, when this whole system was set up,” Ms. Lofgren added.

The White House and the N. S. F. said that diverting the money was allowed under Congress’s two-year appropriation.

Mike England, a spokesman for the science foundation, said in a statement that the agency had “carried over funds to invest in agency priorities that are aligned with broader administration initiatives.”

Mr. England said the agency “remains committed to investing in meritorious foundational research across the sciences and engineering that advances American scientific leadership.”

The Trump administration’s efforts to gain more power over grants have played out across the government, where funding decisions have historically been led by experts.

Last month, the N. I. H. signed an agreement to collaborate with the Defense Department, drawing criticism from Democrats on Capitol Hill who warned that the plan could allow the Pentagon to go around Congress and gain access to billions of dollars meant for infectious disease research. The administration previously fired the N. S. F.’s independent oversight board. And it has canceled or delayed thousands of grants across both agencies as part of its quest to punish elite universities and eliminate spending President Trump and his aides view as “woke.”

Mr. Trump’s science adviser, Michael Kratsios, has criticized the agency’s system for deciding which grants to fund. In a report released in July, Mr. Kratsios wrote that the science foundation, under the Biden administration, awarded too many grants that focused on diversity and equity. He also argued the N. S. F. should issue more “fast grants,” in ways “that bypass external review panels.”

The plan to divert N. S. F. funding was reported earlier by Nature, a science journal.

Several people with knowledge of the situation described confusion inside the agency as the staff complied with White House guidance to carry over money as funding deadlines neared. Some divisions had to pull back research proposals that were recommended for funding after peer review, these officials said.

Altogether, the $1.4 billion carried over after the last fiscal year ended on Wednesday amounted to 19 percent of the N. S. F.’s primary research budget allocated by Congress. That is a far higher percentage than in either of the two prior fiscal years, when less than $175 million went unspent, according to internal data from the agency.

At an agency town hall this week, leaders stood by the plan to divert money to administration priorities while offering assurances that the N. S. F. would also remain true to its roots, according to a recording reviewed by The Times.

When an employee raised concerns about whether the N. S. F. would continue supporting basic research, an official responded that “we’re transitioning.” Still, the official said, the agency would continue to “focus on our mission of foundational research.”

Adam Sella covers breaking news for The Times in Washington.

Christopher Flavelle is a Times reporter covering how President Trump is transforming the federal government.

Irena Hwang is a data reporter at The Times, using computational tools to uncover hidden stories and illuminate the news.

U. S. and Allies Agree to Release Diesel Reserves as Prices Soar

The New York Times October 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Group of 7, which includes Britain, France and Japan, announced the release of 100 million barrels over four months, effective immediately.

By Lisa Friedman and Rebecca F. Elliott

Lisa Friedman reported from London and Rebecca Elliott from New York.

Leaders from some of the world’s wealthiest nations agreed on Friday to release diesel from their reserve stockpiles to help ease a growing crisis over record-high prices driven mostly by the war in Iran.

Under the plan, the Group of 7 countries — the United States, France, Italy, Germany, Japan, Britain and Canada — will release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from strategic stockpiles over the coming four months. That is equivalent to around one day’s worth of global oil demand. The effort will be coordinated by the International Energy Agency, a Paris-based multilateral organization.

Calling the plan “decisive, coordinated measures to stabilize immediate energy supplies” and curb price spikes, the Group of 7 said that they would also make a “substantial” release of diesel within 20 days.

The group did not specify how much of the fuel to be released would be diesel and how much would be unrefined crude oil. Diesel and related fuels make up roughly 28 percent of the world’s oil demand, according to the I. E. A. They have been in especially short supply because military strikes on energy infrastructure in the Middle East and Russia have severely damaged refineries, reducing the world’s capacity to turn oil into the fuels that consumers use.

The deal is the second time nations have come together for a major release of fuel since the United States and Israel launched military strikes against Iran on Feb. 28, triggering a global energy crisis. In March, the I. E. A. announced that world leaders would tap 400 million barrels of oil, the largest coordinated release of stockpiled oil on record by members of the energy agency.

President Trump had threatened to impose a ban on the export of U. S. diesel, a move that has drawn fierce opposition from both American oil companies and European leaders. Retail diesel prices in the United States topped $6.50 a gallon in recent weeks, the highest ever, putting pressure on Mr. Trump and Republicans to find ways to lower prices ahead of the midterm elections in November.

“Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil,” Mr. Trump said on social media of the G7 announcement.

President Emmanuel Macron of France, the current G7 chair, said that Mr. Trump had committed to not impose an export ban on diesel fuel. Mr. Macron, who convened Friday’s teleconference, said he expected the release of emergency oil and diesel to cause gasoline and fuel prices to “drop at the pump as quickly as possible.”

Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the 27-nation European Union, said the bloc supported the G7 decision not to restrict exports.

ClearView, an energy research firm in Washington, said in a note to clients on Friday that it would not “rule out export constraints governing destinations outside the G7, but odds now look lower.”

The price of diesel futures in the United States fell 6 percent on Friday. Prices that consumers pay at the pump typically follow, albeit more slowly.

Hamad Hussain, a senior economist with Capital Economics, a research firm, said it could take as much as two weeks for retail prices to fall.

“We’ll see some of the future alleviated, but it won’t be immediately obvious for consumers at the pump,” he said.

A U. S. export ban on diesel would be deeply damaging in Europe, which has become increasingly dependent on American fuel after banning Russian imports over Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The continent has closed significant refining capacity in recent years because of high operating costs as well as climate regulations. That has exacerbated Europe’s vulnerability, making it even more reliant on imported crude and refined fuels from the Middle East, the United States and other regions.

Europe imports about 1.5 million barrels a day, with a third coming from the United States, according to S&P Global, a market data firm.

“Europe has been very reluctant to let go of their stocks because they are concerned about a prolonged disruption, and they wish to hoard the supplies they have,” said Robert McNally, president of Rapidan Energy Group, a research and consulting firm in Washington.

Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser to Gulf Oil, called the G7 release “underwhelming,” and said it amounts to barely half of the levels once imported from Russia.

Russia had remained a big exporter of diesel beyond Europe, but this year banned exports after Ukrainian drone attacks damaged refineries. It renewed that ban this week.

Another factor weighing on the diesel market is China, the world’s biggest crude importer and a big supplier of diesel to other countries, especially in Asia. China recently started restricting its exports of refined fuel including diesel, something it had done earlier in the war in Iran but then eased.

Mr. Hussain of Capital Economics noted that if the release is evenly split between crude oil and diesel, it would amount to about 400,000 barrels a day of diesel entering the market. That’s not enough to fully offset fuel that was once imported from Russia, but, he said, “it’s definitely helpful.”

Mark Landler contributed reporting from Paris.

Lisa Friedman is a business correspondent covering energy for The New York Times.

Rebecca F. Elliott covers energy for The Times.

Sales of Hulking Pickups and S. U. V. s Sag as Fuel Prices Soar

The New York Times October 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Sales of big pickup trucks and sport utility vehicles have dipped as more Americans buy hybrids and smaller cars.

By Jack Ewing

High gasoline prices are beginning to push Americans away from the full-size pickups and sport utility vehicles that generate the most profits for automakers.

Big pickups like the Chevrolet Silverado are still selling well in the United States, but buyers are gravitating to the smaller versions of such trucks. And sales of hybrid cars and midsize vehicles are growing.

General Motors said Thursday that sales of the Silverado, the company’s flagship truck, were up 3 percent in the third quarter from a year earlier. But the growth came from a light-duty version of the truck. Sales of heavy-duty Silverados slumped. So did sales of the Suburban, a three-row sport utility vehicle, contributing to a 6 percent decline for all G. M. vehicles. Buyers gravitated to smaller, less expensive models like the Chevrolet Trailblazer and Trax.

That story was similar at Stellantis, the parent company of Ram and Jeep. Sales of light-duty Ram pickups rose 73 percent while sales of heavy duty trucks fell 6 percent, the company said. A newly introduced hybrid Jeep Cherokee also sold well.

It is too early to declare that the U. S.-Israeli war with Iran, the reason fuel prices have surged, is prompting Americans to fall out of love with big trucks and sport utility vehicles. Relationships that deep do not end overnight.

“Midsize is in, but it doesn’t mean we’re completely losing the full-size S. U. V. s,” said Erin Keating, executive analyst at Cox Automotive. Many Americans are reacting to higher fuel prices by driving less or cutting back on other purchases, rather than choosing smaller vehicles, she added.

But there is a clear pattern: Dealers are moving fewer humongous pickups and selling more fuel-efficient hybrids, which have engines augmented by batteries and electric motors. Cox estimates that full-size truck sales fell 2 percent in the quarter for all brands, and that sales of large S. U. V. s fell 6 percent. Sales of midsize trucks and S. U. V. s grew, according to Cox.

If these trends persist or deepen, they could hurt automakers in the United States, which generally offer fewer hybrids and smaller cars than Asian manufacturers like Toyota, Hyundai and Honda.

American manufacturers dominate the market for big trucks. The Ford F-150 pickup is the best-selling U. S. vehicle. For many Americans, the epitome of luxury is not a Mercedes-Benz or a BMW saloon. It is a $79,000 F-150 Raptor with heated seats and Bang & Olufsen speakers.

U. S. automakers have been offering fewer and fewer smaller cars, leaving them with little to fall back on if the market continues to change. Ford, which said on Friday that third-quarter sales fell 7 percent, this year stopped making the Escape, a small sport utility vehicle.

“As you become more dependent on a certain kind of car, you’re going to be at the mercy of the market,” said Michael Lenox, a professor of business at the University of Virginia. “You’re exposed if you don’t have the alternatives that people are interested in.”

Asian manufacturers appear to be benefiting from current shifts in the market. Nissan said Thursday that sales of the Frontier, a midsize pickup, soared 44 percent in the quarter. That helped the Japanese company, which has struggled in recent years, to lift overall sales by 8 percent in the quarter.

Tiago Castro, Nissan’s senior vice president for U. S. marketing and sales, attributed the increase in sales of Frontier trucks to better advertising. But he said gasoline prices had also played a role.

Fuel-efficiency will be a selling point, he said, when Nissan soon starts offering a hybrid version of its Rogue S. U. V.

“Customers are looking for more efficient vehicles, but without compromising their style of life,” Mr. Castro said in an interview. “And hybrid provides that.”

Increases in gasoline prices have not yet led to a surge in demand for electric vehicles in the United States. Tesla said Friday that its global deliveries fell to 486,500 from July to September, compared with 497,000 in the same period last year. Tesla does not report U. S. sales separately.

The decline in Tesla sales would probably have been steeper if not for the boost in electric vehicles in Europe, Asia and other markets. U. S. sales of battery-powered cars slumped after Congress repealed subsidies last year.

Instead, Americans appear to be choosing hybrids because they offer some of the fuel savings of electric vehicles but cost less.

Hyundai, which has a broad lineup of hybrid vehicles, reported, also on Thursday, a 3 percent gain in third-quarter sales, fueled by a 39 percent increase in sales of hybrids.

Toyota, which sells the most hybrids, said sales of those models and fully electric vehicles rose 29 percent in the third quarter. Overall, the company’s sales were flat.

Most auto executives agree that, even in the United States, electric vehicles will eventually replace conventional vehicles as prices come down and people get used to the technology. Rivian, for example, reported on Friday that its third-quarter sales jumped 46 percent from a year earlier after the company introduced a more affordable S. U. V.

“We are seeing a systemic shift to E. V. s in the long run,” Professor Lenox said.

Jack Ewing covers the auto industry for The Times, with an emphasis on electric vehicles.
