Powerful Wildfires Require a New Approach, California Report Finds

The New York Times October 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A report on the fires that devastated the Los Angeles area in early 2025 recommended that local governments take a broader approach to preparedness and emergency response.

By Shawn Hubler

Reporting from Los Angeles

Wildfires have become so deadly and vast that urban areas need to rethink their approach to fighting them, an investigation into the fires that devastated parts of Southern California last year reported on Friday. The study found that the protocols firefighters relied on as flames erupted in the Palisades and Altadena fires were overwhelmed by the disaster’s “speed, scale, and complexity.”

The comprehensive analysis found that while several state and local agencies fell fatally short in their preparation and response, the clearest lesson from the disaster was the extent to which climate-driven fires are outstripping modern firefighting.

“The Southern California fires got so large, so fast, that they outpaced the capabilities of the very people trained to fight them,” Derek Alkonis, a senior research program manager for the Fire Safety Research Institute, said in a recorded news briefing. “Some of the most well-trained firefighters in the world” work in the state, he said, but their training and coordination have not kept up with the mounting risk.

The review, commissioned by Gov. Gavin Newsom and conducted by UL Research Institutes, a public safety nonprofit, was the second part of a wide-ranging examination, and the latest in a series of local, state and federal post-mortems after the fires that erupted in and around Los Angeles starting on Jan. 7, 2025.

At least 12 wildfires raged over that month across drought-parched Los Angeles and Ventura Counties, driven by extreme winds. The two largest — in the coastal Los Angeles enclave of Pacific Palisades and the historic San Gabriel Valley community of Altadena — killed a total of 31 people and destroyed more than 16,000 buildings. Thousands of survivors remain displaced.

Calls for accountability have been intense. Federal authorities have attributed the Palisades fire to buried embers that smoldered for days and then rekindled after Los Angeles city firefighters declared a small Jan. 1 brush fire extinguished. A 30-year-old man has pleaded not guilty to federal arson charges in connection with that initial fire.

Los Angeles County fire investigators have traced the Altadena fire to a transmission tower belonging to the utility company Southern California Edison.

But government agencies also have been accused of failing to do all they could to pre-empt the fires after meteorologists warned of an incoming windstorm, and to control the flames once the fires started.

The Los Angeles Fire Department failed to adequately deploy firefighters and equipment ahead of time in and around Pacific Palisades despite the heightened fire risk, decisions that the department’s internal review blamed on efforts to control spending and overtime. The Los Angeles Department of Water and Power has been sued over a disastrous loss of water pressure to fire hydrants in the Palisades; survivors say the fire might have been mitigated had a critical city reservoir not been emptied.

Los Angeles County, which had jurisdiction over the Eaton fire in Altadena, has been sued over late evacuations in an area where at least 18 people died.

Friday’s report found that Los Angeles city fire officials underestimated the fire risk, failed to deploy enough fire equipment ahead of time in Pacific Palisades and disastrously opted against holding over a shift of firefighters. The city, historically focused more on urban structure fires than on wildfires, failed to adequately monitor the sites of prior brush fires as conditions worsened, underestimating reports that one may have rekindled.

In Altadena, the investigators found, the evacuations were indeed late and chaotic. Poor communication and confusion over who was in charge slowed warnings, and authorities lost track of the fire’s direction because the wind grounded firefighting helicopters and trees blocked fire-tracking sensors. Many of the residents who died had also refused to leave despite multiple warnings, orders and pleas.

The institute’s analysis, based on data from 22 agencies and an examination of nearly 900 structures, yielded hundreds of recommendations, from standardized methods to ensure old fires don’t reignite to greater use of swimming pools as a water source for fire suppression.

But the report also painted a sobering bigger picture.

Both the Palisades fire and the Altadena fire ignited in dense metropolitan communities that back up to fire-prone wilderness areas and foothills, a development pattern that has become increasingly common in California as affordable housing has become scarcer. That, fire experts say, points to an ongoing risk.

To combat it, the investigators said, local governments need to take a broader approach to firefighting, dealing with issues like preparedness and emergency response in a much more comprehensive way at a regional level.

“Incremental improvements to individual programs alone will not be sufficient to address future wildfire risk,” the report found. “Long-term risk reduction requires coordinated action that improves wildfire resilience at the community, regional, and state and federal levels.”

Shawn Hubler is The Times’s Los Angeles bureau chief, reporting on the news, trends and personalities of Southern California.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

John Sedgwick was born into an illustrious family, but privilege was only part of the story.

Credit... By Evan Richman For The New York Times

Supported by

By Penelope Green

John Sedgwick was 6 when he was introduced to the family plot in Stockbridge, Mass.

He and his siblings and cousins had been playing hide-and-seek in the town cemetery and were shooed away by a groundskeeper, whereupon John’s step-grandmother, who was leading the game, declared, “All right then, we’ll go play in our graveyard.”

That would be the Sedgwick Pie, so named for its unusual layout: graves planted in concentric circles around a central monument, a stately granite obelisk marking the plot of the family patriarch, Theodore Sedgwick. Otherwise known as the Judge, Theodore was a staunch federalist and ambitious politician who had fought in the Revolutionary War. His second wife, Pamela, was buried alongside him, under a modest urn. Nearby lay Elizabeth Freeman, also known as Mumbet, a formidable formerly enslaved woman whom the Judge had represented in a lawsuit against her enslaver; when she won her freedom, she asked to come work for his family, and she remained with them until her death.

Radiating out from that first circle were the weather-stained headstones of five more generations of illustrious, accomplished Sedgwicks — authors, editors, lawyers, politicians and eccentrics — “a whole little city of Sedgwicks,” as John told WGBH-FM years later, “taking their heavenly rest.”

At first, he was entranced. His initial foray into the Pie, through a stand of Norwegian spruce trees, was like entering a magic kingdom. But by the time he was a teenager, he found himself irritated by what he felt it represented: unseemly ancestor worship.

The plot’s nickname, it turned out, was a joke, bestowed by a sneering neighbor in the late 19th century. So was the legend that accompanied it — that on Judgment Day, the denizens of the Pie would rise up to face not their maker, but their patriarch. Sedgwicks of yore had been irritated by the slur and the fiction, but the name stuck and later generations embraced it.

Mr. Sedgwick wore his patrimony lightly and ironically, and often wrote about it, chronicling the curious family funeral tradition involving a horse-drawn cart holding a Pie-bound Sedgwick tucked into a simple wood coffin that was covered with a deep red pall. (His father, in what is perhaps an apocryphal tale, is said to have ordered such coffins by the brace so that future Sedgwicks wouldn’t be caught short.)

For an article in New England Monthly, Mr. Sedgwick described how early Pie inhabitants had been buried in their pajamas; his family, he noted, seemed to view death as a kind of slumber party. So he bought himself a silky, Hugh Hefner-style dressing gown to be photographed in for the accompanying images, lampooning his family’s quaint customs and the WASPy proclivity for tattered, moth-eaten garments by sporting a luxurious robe that, as he later wrote, was “to die for. And in.”

But when he turned 46, that patrimony had become a darker, more pernicious burden. By then, Mr. Sedgwick was a well-respected journalist and a prolific author working on his second novel, about an older society woman who has suffered a breakdown and her relationship with the psychiatric nurse who treats her at an old-line mental hospital. He modeled the protagonist on his mother, Emily Ames (Lincoln) Sedgwick, who was then in the midst of her fourth hospitalization for depression at McLean, the leafy refuge in a Boston suburb that famously treated Sylvia Plath, Robert Lowell, James Taylor and others, including a clutch of Sedgwicks, for what Winston Churchill called the “black dog.”

It was the turn of the millennium, and Mr. Sedgwick had begun to feel untethered himself. Plagued by racing thoughts and worn ragged from weeks without sleep, he was ineluctably drawn, as his mother had been, to the idea of his own demise as a cure for what was bedeviling him. Medication and therapy eventually brought him back from the brink.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

Then his half brother, Harry, called one day to reveal that he had been ensnared by the same malady, and offered some insights into the Sedgwick legacy: Woven through all that privilege, it seemed, was a parallel history of mood disorders and suicides — more than the usual family complement, according to his psychiatrist.

Think of Edie, Harry said, the beautiful, doomed Warhol muse and Vogue model who overdosed at 28, the third tragic death in her immediate family. And her erratic father, Francis, who spent time at the Austen Riggs Center in Stockbridge, Western Massachusetts’s answer to McLean; in 1921, a doctor had diagnosed him as suffering from “manic-depressive psychosis,” a relatively new entry in the psychiatric lexicon, and urged him not to have children. (He went on to have eight.) And their paternal grandfather, Henry Dwight Sedgwick, who had nearly killed himself after a love affair gone awry. And cousin Louis Agassiz Shaw II, who strangled the family maid and spent decades in a book-lined suite at Upham Memorial Hall, a building on the McLean campus known as the Harvard Club because it housed so many of the school’s alumni. And so many others.

“I think we’ve got the family disease,” Harry Sedgwick told John, who realized then that he also had the subject for his next book.

Sedgwick history was a rich topic — the first Sedgwick landed in Massachusetts in 1635 or 1636 — but it had already been amply documented. And John, unlike others in his family, was a bit embarrassed by it, until he thought about investigating that history through this dark lens.

Was the secret to the Sedgwicks’ notable successes and equally impressive downfalls more than just a natural tendency toward ambition and its perils? Could the waxing and waning of moods and fortunes be attributed to the peaks and valleys of manic depression?

“In My Blood: Six Generations of Madness and Desire in an American Family,” Mr. Sedgwick’s critically acclaimed 2007 memoir — The Boston Globe likened its epic scope to that of a great novel — was the result of his investigation.

“I was a Sedgwick, guilty as charged,” he concluded. “I could never peer into my own soul and find nothing, for my soul is not entirely my own.”

Mr. Sedgwick died on Aug. 30 at his home in Brooklyn. He was 72.

“He succumbed to the illness that he had tried so hard to understand,” his daughter Sara Sedgwick Brown said in an interview. “Like many joyful, funny people — they are that way because they know the alternative very deeply.”

She added, “To be a Sedgwick is an elusive thing. It can be a trap. All of us struggle with the idea of privilege: What does it afford us and what does it mean?”

Mr. Sedgwick liked to say that he had been raised by the “last Victorian” because his father, Robert Minturn Sedgwick, an investment adviser known as Duke, was born near the end of that era in 1899. John and his two siblings were his second family; by the time John came along, Duke was 55.

Duke was a proud, lifelong tender of the Sedgwick flame. In the 1940s, he raised $4,000 from family members to buy the Old House, the family manse that the Judge had built in Stockbridge, from a relative, and he established a trust for its upkeep. Since then, one Sedgwick or another has been in residence, paying a modest rent and making the house available for family weddings, funerals and reunions.

Duke’s favorite poem was “If—,” Rudyard Kipling’s ode to manhood, which he framed and hung on his bedroom wall. Every morning, he played “Old Man River” while doing his exercises — calisthenics drawn from the Canadian Mounties handbook. He was as devoted to his schools as he was to his family history, wearing his Groton blazer until it was threadbare and recounting plays from his Harvard football career at cocktail parties.

John, a child of the 1960s, was not exactly enchanted by these fusty behaviors. At Groton, it was hard to escape the names of relatives whose deeds were emblazoned on plaques everywhere. He rebelled with typical mischief. Instead of turning in the required essay for an assignment in a religious studies class, he submitted a single, angry sentence: “I read the book, OK?”

At Harvard, where he earned a degree in English in 1977, he boarded at Radcliffe — that’s where the girls were — and ignored an invitation to join the Porcellian Club, the college’s exclusive “final” club revered by his father, whose collection of tchotchkes featuring pigs, the club’s emblem, threatened to overrun the family’s home in Dedham, Mass.

For one of his first national magazine assignments, an article in Esquire published the year he graduated, John and the author Anne Fadiman, a former housemate, mocked the institution by conducting a textual analysis of its bathroom graffiti. They sorted their material into nine genres, including the archly titled Arse Poetica, which included this doggerel:

She offered her honor, He honored her offer, And all night long, It was honor and offer.

Mr. Sedgwick went on to contribute to GQ, Vanity Fair and The Atlantic, among other publications. A series about a private investigator written for The Real Paper, an alternative weekly in Boston, became his first book, “Night Vision,” in 1982. “Rich Kids” (1985) explored the lives of young heirs, a subject of interest, he said, because he saw himself as a “rich kid manqué,” as he put it, or someone on the margins of wealth. (During the course of his research, word got out that he was an actual rich kid, and he became the object of a few unwelcome solicitations, including one from a man who asked him to back a Broadway musical.)

“He was witty and empathetic,” Ms. Fadiman said. “He could charm anyone into talking to him. I think that’s what made him such a good reporter: Everyone wanted to be with him.”

Like most family memoirs, his book was not universally beloved by his extended clan, though many Sedgwicks had helped with the research. One cousin recalled his mother angrily scribbling corrections in the book’s margins.

“I was very pleased that it was a success,” Robert Sedgwick, John’s older brother, said in an interview. “Other people were less enthusiastic.”

Mr. Sedgwick, who was born John Shaw Sedgwick on May 5, 1954, in Boston, wrote three books of history in addition to his memoir: “War of Two: Alexander Hamilton, Aaron Burr and the Duel That Stunned the Nation” (2015); “Blood Moon: An American Epic of War and Splendor in the Cherokee Nation” (2018), a biography of two rival Native American chiefs; and “From the River to the Sea: The Untold Story of the Railroad War That Made the West” (2021).

His marriage to Megan Marshall, the Pulitzer Prize-winning biographer of Margaret Fuller, ended in 2007. He married Rana Foroohar, a columnist for The Financial Times, in 2013.

In addition to his daughter Sara and his brother Robert, Ms. Foroohar survives him, along with another daughter, Josephine Sedgwick; two stepchildren, Darya and Alex Foroohar; six grandchildren; and a sister, Emily.

At his death, he was working on what he described as a Hitchcockian novel of psychological suspense. “He was very excited about it,” Daniel Conaway, his literary agent, said.

Editors were always pestering Mr. Sedgwick to write something called “The Last WASP,” the author Pagan Kennedy said, but it wasn’t clear who, exactly, that would be.

“When he died, I thought maybe he was the last WASP,” she added. “He knew he had been documenting a culture in decline, which was what made his work so interesting. And he did it so well because he was deeply of it, but still outside of it.”

This month, Mr. Sedgwick will be buried at the Pie, with all the bells and whistles that accompany that particular Sedgwick tradition: the horse-drawn cart, the red pall and his daughters taking on the role that their grandfather once played, leading the procession from the church to the gravesite.

“I’m puzzled by what he would make of it,” his daughter Sara said. “It’s the most extreme version of the tension he carried his whole life — the deep sadness and the joy that is living, the celebration. He’d think, ‘Let’s have the best party ever,’ and be so sad he wasn’t there to say or do something irreverent.”

Mr. Sedgwick had long ago made peace with his patrimony, which he came to see as a boon rather than a curse.

“I see the oscillation of mood, the up-down-up-down, of the family as its quavering vitality,” he wrote in his memoir. “Nothing in life remains static, or it is not life at all. It is like music: The sound requires vibration; the music dies when the string is still.”

If you are having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or go to SpeakingOfSuicide. com/resources for a list of additional resources.

Penelope Green is a Times reporter on the Obituaries desk.

Why Were 4 Pilots Aboard FlyDubai Flight 1073?

The New York Times October 02, 2026

FlyDubai Attack

Advertisement

Supported by

After the co-pilot stabbed the captain, two pilots who were seated in the cabin intervened alongside passengers and safely landed the Boeing 737 in Saudi Arabia.

By Karla Adam

FlyDubai Flight 1073 was carrying four pilots on its journey from Dubai to Tel Aviv. After a co-pilot stabbed the captain, two pilots who were seated in the cabin took control and safely landed the Boeing 737 Max 8 jet in Saudi Arabia.

Why were there extra pilots on board?

For the most part, airlines do not intentionally staff shorter flights with a backup flight crew simply as a precaution, because paying two sets of pilots is expensive. However, pilots routinely hitch rides on flights they are not operating — a practice known in the industry as “deadheading” — to position themselves where they are needed next.

In a statement, FlyDubai confirmed that “on-duty FlyDubai crew traveling on the flight” safely landed the plane. Because deadheading pilots are on company assignment, they are technically considered on duty, receive pay and are forbidden to consume alcohol. Wearing a uniform is optional.

John Cox, a retired airline captain and aviation safety consultant, said the extra pilots were most likely being moved to where they needed to be for their next assigned flight. “We move pilots all around the world,” Mr. Cox said.

Mr. Cox was skeptical that an airline would deploy additional pilots on a relatively short flight simply as routine insurance against potential delays. “Pilots are expensive,” he said. “They are highly trained, but also highly compensated. From a business standpoint, you want the right number of pilots at the right place at the right time. You don’t want to be paying for more than you need.”

Another possibility is that FlyDubai needed a second crew to fly the plane on its return leg to Dubai because the operating crew would have exceeded its legal duty limits and required mandatory rest, aviation industry experts said.

The airline declined to answer questions about the flight, including about the presence of the extra pilots on board the flight to Tel Aviv.

While a 3.5-hour flight would not normally require extra pilots, analysts said regional conditions have created unique scheduling demands. Major Persian Gulf-based carriers have repeatedly suspended, canceled or rerouted flights as conflicts in the region have flared.

A pilot’s regulated working time isn’t just hours in the air — it begins when the pilot reports for duty at the airport, incorporating taxi time, delays and ground turnarounds. Unforeseen detours or holding patterns can cause a primary crew to exceed its daily limit, known as timing out.

Richard Levy, a retired airline captain, praised the heroism of the crew and passengers aboard FlyDubai Flight 1073. He said it was remarkable that the wounded captain managed to unlock the door and send an emergency signal while under attack, and that the backup pilots managed to land the plane.

Mr. Levy added that it was astonishing that the aircraft stayed intact. “The rudder was ripped off,” he said. “It’s a miracle that the plane was still flyable.”

Sally Leivesley, an aviation security expert, said that having a backup crew on board shorter flights could make sense given regional tensions. In light of the ballistic missiles being fired in the region, “you really do not want your plane in that vicinity,” so flights can be delayed until the danger is cleared, Dr. Leivesley noted.

Dr. Leivesley said she saw no signs that the off-duty pilots were on board Flight 1073 because of a specific security warning. Passengers responded to the cockpit attack before the off-duty pilots did, she noted, reasoning that if the pilots had expected it, they would have reacted ahead of the passengers who rushed the flight deck.

She estimated that it would have taken only about five more seconds before the plane passed the point where it could no longer be pulled out of its descent and recovery would have been impossible.

The Mother’s Scream That Sent Passengers to the Rescue

The New York Times October 02, 2026

War in the Middle East

A badly wounded Indian pilot managed to unlock the cockpit door. Four Israeli men teamed up to overwhelm an attacker and avert disaster.

A badly wounded Indian pilot managed to unlock the cockpit door. Four Israeli men teamed up to overwhelm an attacker and avert disaster.

A FlyDubai plane carrying Israeli passengers who had earlier been aboard another FlyDubai aircraft that made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia approaches Ben Gurion International Airport near Tel Aviv on Wednesday. Credit... Ohad Zwigenberg/Associated Press

Supported by

By David M. HalbfingerNatan OdenheimerAdam RasgonJohnatan Reiss and Aaron Boxerman

The reporters interviewed more than a dozen passengers on Flight 1073.

Five-year-old Nina Manes, flying home to Tel Aviv with her family in business class, needed to use the bathroom.

Her mother, Tali, stood waiting for her outside the plane’s lavatory, when she suddenly heard frightening shouts and loud bangs coming from behind the closed door to the flight deck.

What unfolded next was a harrowing chain of events that led the passengers aboard FlyDubai Flight 1073 to think that they were all about to die in a terrorist attack — but instead turned into a tale of heroism on the part of an Indian pilot and a handful of Israelis.

Hearing what sounded worrisomely like a melee, Ms. Manes, 46, said she pulled a backup pilot, seated in his uniform nearby, by the hand and prodded him to investigate.

He pulled open the cockpit door — which had been unlocked from the inside — onto a horrific scene.

There was blood all over the flight deck.

And the first officer was stabbing the captain, again and again and again.

Four Israeli passengers aboard Wednesday morning’s flight from Dubai are being hailed for racing unarmed into harm’s way, overpowering the first officer, giving the captain first aid, and making it possible for a second backup pilot to take over and land the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.

Yaniv Hayoun, in Row 11, a plumber who liked to watch a television show about air-crash investigations.

Asaf Rajuan, in Row 7, a financial planner who had narrowly escaped death last year, when an Iranian missile slammed into the apartment building next door to his own.

Tzvika Manes, in Row 1, a banking executive returning from an exhilarating two-week family vacation in Japan, the early fulfillment of his 11-year-old daughter’s wish for her bat mitzvah.

And Shota Musaev, a dentist in Row 13 who was returning from China with his wife after a weeklong trip.

But it was Mr. Manes’s wife, Tali, whose horrified screams upon witnessing the carnage in the flight deck had served as the alarm that propelled ordinary passengers into action.

And it was the plane’s pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, who, pushing himself to unlock the cockpit door even as he was on the floor fighting for his life, had made it possible for those passengers to save all 182 souls on board.

This article is based on interviews with more than a dozen passengers on Flight 1073 and the accounts that other passengers gave to Israeli television stations, as well as an account that Captain Machchhar gave to his country’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, on Friday.

Some of the Israelis said they remembered feeling the kind of beleaguered helplessness that they felt on Oct. 7, 2023, during the Hamas-led attack on Israel, and how ordinary Israelis had rushed to defend themselves and each other when the government failed to protect them.

Some also said the situation called to mind the 9/11 attacks, and propelled them to act without hesitation, much like those on United Flight 93 who had raced forward to confront that doomed plane’s four hijackers.

Nearly all the passengers were Israelis making their way home from far-flung trips across Asia or Africa to a nation at war. Some said they had occasionally felt the sting of anti-Israel sentiment or antisemitism abroad, felt the need to hide Star of David necklaces, or told people they were from another country. Waiting to board her flight in a Dubai airport lounge, Ms. Manes said her eldest daughter, Daniella, heard a television report about Israeli settler violence, got upset and took a seat in a far corner of the room.

But the connecting flight to Ben-Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv — on an airline that had continued flying to Israel when many others hadn’t — meant being surrounded by fellow Israelis, fellow Jews, fellow Hebrew speakers.

It should have been possible, at last, to let one’s guard down.

The three-hour flight began uneventfully. Almog Itali, 52, returning from Japan with his wife and two teenage children, chose a film from the seat-back video system: “Send Help,” a horror film about the aftermath of a plane crash on a remote island.

Miryam Ochayon, 24, in a middle seat in Row 6, was on her way home after 10½ months of solo traveling around Asia, from Mongolia to the Philippines, on the sort of post-military odyssey that is an Israeli rite of passage.

She was returning home in part because she had been scheduled for reserve duty in the coming weeks, and also to attend her family’s memorial service on Sunday for her brother, Evyatar Ochayon Abukasis, a sergeant who was killed at Kissufim on the Gaza border on Oct. 7, 2023, just before his scheduled discharge.

Raised in an ultra-Orthodox family in Jerusalem, Ms. Ochayon had left that lifestyle behind as a teenager. She still made a habit of saying the Jewish traveler’s prayer before takeoff but for some reason, she didn’t think to recite it when lifting off from Dubai, just after 7 a. m., she recalled.

Ms. Ochayon said she quickly fell asleep, her head on her seat’s tray table.

The Manes family, sitting in the first two rows, were exhausted from their all-night journey back from Tokyo, but still savoring what had been a particularly sweet trip.

Daniella, who had developed an obsession with Japan at age 6, had made a visual presentation with the Canva app to persuade her parents to make the trip and specifying everywhere the family should go: “culinary experiences” like sushi, cotton candy and matcha, “fashion highlights” like Brandy Melville and other stores in the Shibuya district of Tokyo. (The 7-Eleven was overhyped, but everything else was a hit, her mother said.)

A French toast breakfast was served around an hour into the flight, but Tali Manes slept through it. About an hour later, a little after 9 a. m. Dubai time, she was on her feet, waiting for her Nina, a few days shy of 6, outside the bathroom just behind the flight deck and galley.

Suddenly, Ms. Manes said she heard “a noise you don’t usually hear” coming from inside the flight deck — “something knocking on the door.”

She turned to a backup pilot sitting a few feet away and told him something was wrong. “He was on his iPad and didn’t understand what I wanted,” she said. “I said to him, ‘Go check.’ I pulled him by the hand. I’m not an impolite person, I mean I would never do something like that. But there was this apathy.”

The man reached for the flight deck’s door. “It wasn’t locked,” Ms. Manes said. “That was our great luck.”

“What we saw there,” she said, “was absolute horror.”

Ms. Manes said she saw one of the pilots stabbing the other, with a knife of some kind, though she could not describe it in any detail.

The victim collapsed, and the attacker “kept stabbing him and stabbing him,” she said.

She said she started screaming: “He’s stabbing the pilot!”

Inside the flight deck, Captain Machchhar, a 17-year flight veteran — on the floor, badly wounded and still being attacked — could feel the plane plunging to earth.

“I was so badly hurt that I had fallen to the ground,” he told Mr. Modi in the video released by the prime minister’s office. “But I knew I had to act,” he added. “I could feel the aircraft was going down.”

He reached for the door. “I was doing it to save myself, but I also knew I couldn’t let all of them die,” he said.

“I told myself, ‘this is the last push, Smit, do it. The door is right there.’ And then I somehow opened it.”

Mr. Hayoun, the plumber, 50, heard Ms. Manes scream “He’s stabbing him!”

His first thought, he said, was that one passenger was attacking another.

“And at the very moment I stand up and step out of my seat, the plane banks — banks very sharply to the left — and then levels out again,” he told Kan 11, Israel’s public broadcaster. “That shook me.”

The lurch of the plane made him connect the plane’s behavior to Ms. Manes’s screams, he said. He told his wife and daughters to buckle up tightly. And he ran forward to the flight deck.

Before he reached there, he said, the plane went into a steep dive that threw him sideways, onto the seats and against a cabin wall. “There was an insane G-force,” he said. “I couldn’t lift myself up.”

Josh Holder/The New York Times

Ms. Ochayon said that when the plane started to dive, it wasn’t so much the angle of descent as the plane’s acceleration that was unbearable. “It felt like 10 times a roller-coaster,” she said. “Our faces — melted.”

At one point, she heard a loud cracking sound coming from the rear of the plane.

Hila Evron-Cohen, 48, was sound asleep in Seat 26C, across the aisle from her husband, when the jolt of the plane woke her. She was returning with her husband and two teenage boys from Zanzibar and Tanzania, on the last leg of a five-flight trip home that had begun Tuesday morning in the Serengeti.

As the plane nose-dived, she said, she felt her mind and body separating — and felt a fear she hadn’t experienced since Oct. 7. “It floods you,” she said. “It paralyzes you.”

At the front of the cabin, Mr. Hayoun felt the plane level off slightly. Regaining his balance, he made his way to the flight deck door.

The backup pilot was standing there, holding the door handle but doing nothing, he said. Other passengers corroborated this, saying it appeared that the backup pilot was too stunned to act.

Mr. Hayoun said he pushed past him and saw the captain on the floor just inside the door, and the first officer leaning with his knees on the instrument panel.

He said he grabbed the first officer by the throat, put him in a chokehold and pulled him backward — all while shouting for help.

Ms. Manes said her husband, Tzvika, 48, had fallen to the floor next to her from the force of the plane’s motion. “We looked into each other’s eyes, and I will never forget that look,” she said. “And he stood up to help.”

He grabbed their daughter from the bathroom, returned her to his wife, and joined the fray.

Mr. Rajuan, 44, ran forward, too. “We acted on pure instinct,” he said. “You don’t think.”

Mr. Musaev, 47, said he had started to shoot video with his phone, thinking the plane was experiencing extreme turbulence, but quickly realized it was some kind of attack and ran to the front of the plane.

In her seat, Ms. Ochayon took out her phone and started recording videos. The first was time-stamped 9:23 a. m. Dubai time — 52 minutes before the plane was scheduled to land in Tel Aviv.

Terror had taken hold throughout the cabin.

Ms. Ochayon turned to the woman next to her and said, “I can’t die, I can’t die — I can’t do this to my mother, who already lost my brother.”

Ms. Evron-Cohen said that her 13-year-old son, Hillel, began shouting to her: “Mom, I love you! Mom, I love you!”

She understood then that she and her children were going to die.

“You spend your whole life trying to protect your children,” she said. “That they don’t get hurt, that they aren’t cold, that they aren’t hot, that they’re always comfortable, that they have food and clean things.”

Now she had no way to protect them. “That helplessness is something you cannot explain in words,” she said.

If the moment seemed to drag on forever for the passengers, in the flight deck, the struggle was quick.

The passengers overwhelmed the first officer and dragged him out the door into the galley.

“We jumped on him,” Mr. Manes said. “Three guys.”

At one point, Mr. Rajuan, blood streaming down his face from a laceration, walked back into the passenger cabin and shouted, “We won!”

Mr. Manes said that someone brought wired headsets to tie up the attacker’s wrists and ankles, and a crew member brought heavy-duty zip ties.

Mr. Musaev, the dentist, said he attached an oxygen mask to Captain Machchhar’s face and tried to stanch his bleeding, pressing on his wounds with a shirt. “He had a deep head wound, his hands were all cut up and he had minor injuries on his body,” he said. “He lost a lot of blood.”

The pilot was conscious but his pulse was weakening. Mr. Musaev said he told a crew member, “We have to land as quickly as possible, because he won’t survive.”

Mr. Hayoun remained inside the flight deck along with the backup pilot. Mr. Hayoun told Israeli interviewers that he pulled back on the controls of the plane for a few seconds, before the backup pilot, by now roused from his seeming paralysis and also bleeding from a hand wound sustained during the struggle in the cramped flight deck, took control.

Outside the flight deck, the other Israeli men guarded the cockpit door, refusing to let anyone pass, until a second backup pilot persuaded them to let him in.

In a matter of a minute or two, several realizations had swept over the Israelis on board that were nearly as jarring to their states of mind as the plane’s horrifying dive, twists and recovery had been to their bodies.

The initial threat, and the terror it had caused, were over. But they also could not be sure that they were in the clear. Israelis accustomed to being ever vigilant in unfamiliar settings now became hypervigilant. They said they trusted no one.

“There was a great deal of fear that he might have accomplices,” Mr. Musaev said of the flight officer. “That’s what we were afraid of. We started telling people to spread out around the plane, so that nobody could pull out a knife and stab us, the women or the children.”

With a new pilot flying the plane, Mr. Rajuan said that those fears did not dissipate.

“We didn’t know if the pilot was with us or not, we didn’t know who was against whom. We even started suspecting the flight attendants,” he said.

“Underneath us was only desert,” he added. “We were afraid we were being taken to a hostile country.”

Eventually, the passengers quieted down. “There were no screams, no panic, no shrieking,” Mr. Rajuan said. “Everyone understood the situation we were in and what needed to be done, and everyone did what was necessary.”

The new pilot steered the plane to a safe landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, at around 9:45 a. m., despite the fact that much of the plane’s rudder had apparently broken off in midflight.

Videos showed the passengers bursting out in songs of gratitude and pride: “Hashem Yitbarach,” or “May God be praised,” and “Am Yisrael Chai,” or “The people of Israel live.”

Pragati K. B. and Pranav Baskar contributed reporting.

Ukraine Reports First Combat Use of Its Own Ballistic Missile

The New York Times October 02, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

While the missile fired on Thursday has a limited range, Kyiv is developing a larger weapon that could strike Moscow.

By Andrew E. Kramer

Reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine

President Volodymyr Zelensky said late Thursday that Ukraine had fired a domestically made ballistic missile in combat for the first time. It is a breakthrough in Kyiv’s push to field a powerful weapon that Russia has used against Ukraine to devastating effect.

Mr. Zelensky trumpeted the launch with a post on social media that included a video of a missile blasting off. “Ukrainian tactical ballistics. FP-7. First combat use,” he wrote. The post did not say what was targeted, and Mr. Zelensky’s office declined to comment.

The FP-7, produced by the Ukrainian company Fire Point, is a short-range missile that can reach only border regions inside Russia. The weapon is not expected to significantly shift what has become an escalating air war between the two countries.

But Fire Point is also developing a larger ballistic missile, the FP-9, that would be able to reach Moscow and strategic defense industry targets. Ukraine says that missile, which analysts think has a greater potential to change the dynamics of the war, is expected to be ready later this year.

Ballistic missiles stand at the top of the weapons hierarchy for air attacks. They are hard to intercept, fly quickly to targets and can carry a heavier payload than most of the exploding drones that Ukraine now uses.

The launch of the FP-7 returns Ukraine to a small group of countries producing ballistic missiles.

Decades ago, when Ukraine was part of the Soviet Union, it had a large military aerospace industry. Factories there built several models of intercontinental ballistic missiles. Those production lines were shut down after the Soviet breakup in 1991, and the industry has since mostly withered.

Russia has been firing an array of ballistic missiles at Ukraine since the start of its full invasion of the country in 2022, including an intermediate-range missile designed for nuclear explosives but fired with dummy warheads.

Ukraine has fired American-made ATACMS tactical ballistic missiles at Russian forces in occupied areas of Ukraine and into areas of Russia close to the border.

The FP-7, the missile whose launch Ukraine announced on Thursday, has a range of 155 miles and can carry a payload weighing 440 pounds, according to Fire Point.

Military analysts say that a likely use for the missile will be counterattacks on Russian missile launchers, rather than strikes on strategic targets like defense factories inside Russia.

“It will be a specialized weapon,” said Serhiy Hrabsky, a retired colonel and a commentator on the war for the Ukrainian media. “Ukraine cannot produce dozens of them daily.”

But the missile could help tip the economics of the missile and drone war more in Ukraine’s favor. Targeting Russian missile launchers is more economical than trying to shoot down Russia’s ballistic missiles in flight with American-made Patriot interceptors, Mr. Hrabsky said. Patriot interceptors cost millions of dollars each and are in short supply globally.

Fire Point has said it is restarting ballistic missile production in Ukraine from scratch. It says it is relying on new technologies adapted from modern consumer goods, such as a type of carbon fiber originally intended to make bicycle frames.

The war has increasingly turned to the skies as Ukraine has essentially fought Russia to a standstill on the ground.

Russian missile and drone strikes are intended to cripple Ukraine’s economy and raise the cost to European allies of supporting the country. The attacks also aim to demoralize the population with electrical blackouts.

Ukraine’s own long-range strikes, largely with drones, have focused on oil refineries, oil ports and oil tankers to harm Russia’s economy.

Russia now has the upper hand in the drone and missile war, launching far more of both types of long-range weapons than the numbers of exploding drones that Ukraine has fired back.

In Ukraine, the FP-7 has been nicknamed the Pelican. On Sept. 20, Mr. Zelensky said in a statement that Ukraine had fired a weapon called the Pelican into Russia. Confusion followed as Mr. Zelensky’s office later said he had been referring to a drone, not a missile.

Fire Point declined to comment after that launch. It has referred to its ballistic missiles as “ballistic drones” for legal reasons, because Ukraine is a party to a Cold War-era pact, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, that limits the range of ground-launched missiles.

Both Russia and the United States have withdrawn from the treaty. Mr. Zelensky’s post on Thursday referred to a use of “tactical ballistics,” seemingly distinguishing the weapon from more destructive strategic missiles.

Andrew E. Kramer is the Kyiv bureau chief for The Times, who has been covering the war in Ukraine since 2014.

Trump Is Getting Desperate. It Shows.

The New York Times October 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Liz Oyer

Ms. Oyer was the Department of Justice pardon attorney from 2022 to 2025.

When the deputy attorney general personally announces an indictment from Justice Department headquarters, it signals a matter of national importance. So when Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter announced that he would hold his first news conference, observers rightly expected a major case.

Instead, Mr. McCotter announced an indictment of a rogue postal worker for improperly disposing of mail. The Utah mail carrier, Damon Matai Seei, was apparently covering a colleague’s delivery route at the time. By his own admission, he was feeling “overwhelmed,” and sought to “lighten his workload” by discarding a batch of undelivered mail in a church dumpster. In an interview with federal law enforcement, he admitted this was a “poor decision” made out of “frustration” and “laziness.”

Mr. Seei claimed that he believed the discarded mail was advertising material. But according to prosecutors, it also included 300 mail-in ballots for a primary election. He was charged with a single felony count of delay or destruction of mail, which is one of several commonly prosecuted postal crimes.

Mr. Seei had no apparent intent to interfere with an election. But that did not stop the Justice Department from offering him up to the public as an election saboteur. The deputy attorney general called Mr. Seei — a 34-year-old with no prior criminal history — “a danger to the public and to the integrity of the electoral system.” Mr. McCotter and his boss, Attorney General Todd Blanche, each appeared on Fox News to shore up the story.

Their chest-thumping highlights how desperate Justice Department leaders are to substantiate the president’s claims of election interference, and how miserably they are failing. At the news conference, Mr. McCotter admonished reporters: “Remember, folks. Voting fraud is real.” In other words: We may not have much proof, but trust us.

Recent polling shows that President Trump’s baseless claims about mail-in voting fraud are persuading few people outside his base. Still, the officials who surround him remain doggedly committed to proving otherwise — much like the ministers who refused to tell the emperor he was wearing no clothes. After Mr. McCotter’s news conference, a top Justice Department spokeswoman lashed out at a correspondent who characterized Mr. Seei’s prosecution as “a case about a tired mailman.” On its official X account, the department posted a highly produced video in which Mr. McCotter insists weakly, and without evidence, that the case is “just the tip of the iceberg.”

These actions are reminiscent of the aftermath of the 2020 election, when a rogue Justice Department official sent a letter to Georgia election officials falsely claiming that the department had evidence of “significant” irregularities in the state’s election. His plan was stymied only because the rest of the Justice Department’s senior leadership threatened to resign if it went forward. The acting attorney general, Jeffrey Rosen, reportedly told Mr. Trump he could not “change the facts” of the election.

What’s different and scarier now is that the Justice Department’s leadership is working together to validate the president’s election lies from the top down. Turning fiction into fact is now part of the job description. A refusal to concede that Mr. Trump lost the 2020 election has become a litmus test for all his political appointees.

Initially, Mr. Trump’s justice system targeted specific individuals who had angered him — such as Senator Mark Kelly or the former F. B. I. director, James Comey. Now, it has adopted a dragnet approach, trawling to find perpetrators on whom to pin conspiracies cooked up by the president. Ordinary citizens are being ensnared.

David Hearn, a man from Maryland, was one of them. In June, U. S. Park Police officers and National Guardsmen were deployed to patrol the reflecting pool, under pressure to prove the president’s claim that “SICK, DERANGED PEOPLE” intentionally destroyed its lining. Mr. Hearn, passing through the National Mall on his bike, stopped to put his hand in the water. He was arrested on the spot and later charged with felony destruction of property.

The case against Mr. Hearn crumbled when prosecutors were forced to substantiate it with evidence. Jeanine Pirro, the U. S. attorney for the District of Columbia, had to dismiss the indictment — earning the ire of the president — but only after Mr. Hearn was thrust into the national spotlight and painted as an enemy of America. In a news release, Ms. Pirro had said Mr. Hearn’s “deliberate acts of destruction” were “an affront to our shared history and the dignity of our national heritage.”

Most Americans didn’t fear for our personal safety when the Justice Department came for James Comey, Mark Kelly and Letitia James, the New York attorney general. These were professional political actors who chose to be in the national spotlight. Of course, no one should be subjected to a frivolous or vindictive criminal investigation. But they were people the president viewed as enemies. Now, he’s getting desperate and targeting civilians.

So far, the courts have consistently rejected Mr. Trump’s politically motivated prosecutions. Most Americans can see these cases for what they are: flimsy and pathetic — a sign of Mr. Trump’s weakness. As Mr. Hearn and Mr. Seei experienced firsthand, the president’s control of the levers of justice has the potential to do great damage, even if the charges ultimately don’t stick.

The solution is for those in Mr. Trump’s orbit to stop enabling him. That’s unlikely to happen. Mr. Trump is now relying, to an unusual degree, on a revolving cast of opportunistic political appointees. The flagging career work force has been increasingly marginalized, as leadership is demanding total loyalty and is aggressively squashing dissent.

Mr. McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general, warned that “the actions of even one malicious actor” can undercut the security of our democratic elections. He’s not wrong — but what his news conference illustrated is that the malicious actors are the ones inside our government.

Ultimate loyalty of the D. O. J. to President Trump and every attorney within that Department who supports these types of prosecutions is in violation of the Code of Professional Ethics; bringing a frivolous case before the Court can and should result in sanctions, if not referral to the respective State Bar Associations.

Liz Oyer writes about the rule of law in her newsletter, Lawyer Oyer.

Airlines Set to Bring Israelis Back From U. A. E. After FlyDubai Cockpit Attack

The New York Times October 02, 2026

FlyDubai Attack

Advertisement

Supported by

The attack, on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, halted the only direct service between the two cities since the war in Iran disrupted air traffic.

By Johnatan Reiss

Reporting from Tel Aviv

Several Israeli airlines on Friday were preparing special flights to bring Israelis back from Dubai, after a midair cockpit attack this week on a FlyDubai flight to Tel Aviv halted the only direct service between the two cities.

Thousands of Israelis are estimated to have remained in Dubai since the attack on Wednesday, according to David Sasi, a spokesman for Miri Regev, the Israeli transportation minister.

FlyDubai suspended its service between Dubai and Tel Aviv after the attack. Etihad, another Emirati airline, operates flights to Israel out of Abu Dhabi, the Emirati capital. Israeli airlines stopped flying to the United Arab Emirates at the onset of the U. S.-Israeli war against Iran in late February.

Two Israeli airlines, Israir and Arkia, said Friday that they had obtained “the required permissions” to land at Dubai’s airport. Arkia said it planned to operate one flight to Dubai on Friday and another on Saturday.

El Al, Israel’s flag carrier, said that it had been “prepared to operate the special rescue flights” on Friday but that authorities had “suddenly” canceled its permission.

El Al planes were already set to take off from Tel Aviv for Dubai when their landing slots at the Dubai Airport were revoked, according to a representative for the airline. El Al said it was working to obtain new permissions to operate flights on Saturday night.

The Dubai International Airport did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Investigators are still trying to understand what prompted the attack on Wednesday, during which the co-pilot stabbed the pilot on FlyDubai Flight 1073. Israeli passengers confronted the co-pilot and subdued him, according to witnesses and Israeli officials. The aircraft lurched and descended so violently during the tumult that its rudder was damaged.

The United Arab Emirates has said that it is taking the lead in investigating the attack. In a social media post on Friday, Anwar Gargash, a senior Emirati official, called the incident a “dangerous terrorist act.”

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said in a video statement on Friday that the co-pilot, an Omani national, “underwent Islamist radicalization” and that he “intended to crash the plane with all of its passengers.” He did not provide further details or offer any proof of his claim.

Mr. Netanyahu said that the authorities were investigating whether the co-pilot, whose identity has not been made public, had carried out the attack on behalf of another party.

The wounded pilot and co-pilot have been transferred from Saudi Arabia, where the plane made an emergency landing, to the Emirates.

The pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, said in his first public remarks about the attack that he was “fighting” for his life when he opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and overpower the attacker.

“I was so badly hurt that I had fallen to the ground,” he said on a video call from his hospital bed with Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, according to footage of their conversation released by the Indian government on Friday.

“But I knew I had to act,” Captain Machchhar added. “I could feel the aircraft was going down.”

Captain Machchhar has been hailed as a hero for fending off the assault. Mr. Modi said on Friday that he had “made the entire country proud.” Mr. Gargash, the Emirati official, said Captain Machchhar “embodied the meaning of bravery and responsibility.”

Adam Rasgon contributed reporting.

‘I Couldn’t Let All of Them Die’: Pilot on FlyDubai Flight Recalls Sudden Attack

The New York Times October 02, 2026

FlyDubai Attack

Advertisement

Supported by

Capt. Smit Machchhar, who was stabbed by his co-pilot midair between Dubai and Tel Aviv, said he “had to act” to prevent a crash despite serious injuries.

By Pragati K. B.

Reporting from New Delhi

The Indian pilot who was attacked during a FlyDubai flight this week said on Friday that he opened the cockpit door despite grievous injuries, allowing passengers and crew members to overpower the co-pilot who had assailed him.

“I was fighting for my life,” Capt. Smit Machchhar said on a video call from his hospital bed with Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, in his first public remarks since the attack. Video of their conversation was released by the Indian government.

“I was so badly hurt that I had fallen to the ground,” said Captain Machchhar. “But I knew I had to act,” he added. “I could feel the aircraft was going down.”

The attack, on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying about 170 passengers, sent the aircraft into a terrifying plunge. Israeli officials have said the co-pilot appeared to have tried to crash the plane after stabbing Captain Machchhar, although investigators are still trying to understand the assailant’s motives and how the attack unfolded. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination” but did not elaborate.

Passengers were able to overpower the attacker, while two people aboard with flying experience helped land the plane in Saudi Arabia.

Captain Machchhar, who said he had 17 years of flying experience, including 11 as a captain, said he knew instinctively what was happening to the aircraft, even as he lay injured on the cockpit floor. The Boeing 737 Max 8 he was flying plummeted more than 16,000 feet in 30 seconds during the attack.

Captain Machchhar told Mr. Modi that he recalled telling himself: “Smit, this is the last push, just do it. The door is right there.”

“I was doing it to save myself,” he said, “but I also knew I couldn’t let all of them die.”

Captain Machchhar, who was hospitalized in Saudi Arabia then transferred to the United Arab Emirates, told Mr. Modi that he was receiving good medical care.

The episode has made him a hero in India.

“Your courage and presence of mind — you made a decision within a fraction of a second, and saved so many lives,” Mr. Modi told the captain during their conversation. “You have made the entire country proud.”

Mr. Modi’s office put out the video of the split-screen conversation on a day of nationwide protests in India, including in the capital, New Delhi. Protesters are demanding the resignation of the country’s chief election officer for trying to rig voter rolls in the favor of Mr. Modi’s party.

Captain Machchhar grew up in Mumbai and entered aviation almost by accident after attending a seminar on flying. He later became a captain and a trainer of aspiring pilots. In a podcast interview last year, he described flying as something he felt “blessed” to do and emphasized the importance of pilots being rested and prepared to perform under pressure.

Suhasini Raj contributed reporting.

Pragati K. B. is a reporter for The Times based in New Delhi, covering news from across India.

Whatever AI Safety Is, It’s Not This

Wired October 01, 2026

Here’s a fun history lesson for you. Don’t worry, we’ll make it quick! In 1966, nearly 51,000 people died on US highways. The overwhelming evidence suggested that many lives could have been saved with modern seat belts, which by then had been around for several years. The automotive industry responded by rallying together, and, in a triumph of self-regulation, voluntarily put the safety feature in every new vehicle that rolled off the line.

Kidding! Of course they didn’t do that. In the fall of 1966, Congress established the Department of Transportation and then passed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act as well as the Highway Safety Act, giving the federal government sweeping new authority to set safety standards. By 1968, seat belts were required in every new car. Despite a massive increase in highway traffic in the last 60 years, far fewer fatalities happen on the road today.

I was thinking about this while watching various AI CEOs huddle around US president Donald Trump on Tuesday, congratulating themselves and each other on having signed an AI safety accord. My colleague Maddy Varner wrote about the specific stipulations here, but the short version is that it’s largely up to the AI labs to keep themselves in check.

Or, as Trump put it even more succinctly in the Oval Office on Wednesday: “They’re gonna police, and they’re gonna police each other, and they’re gonna self-police, they’re gonna police themselves. It’s going to work out very well.”

So this is the current state of AI safety regulation. On one side are the AI executives, employees, and tech luminaries, who are all saying that there need to be clear, thoughtful, tactical rules introduced to avoid potential disaster. (Bill Gates, for instance, has been on a media blitz playing Cassandra about an AI apocalypse.) On the other side is Trump’s magical thinking that if you say something enough times, it must be true.

That’s not to say any of this is simple or easy. The question of how to properly “pace the frontier,” as some of those same executives like to say, remains open. Even if all of the major AI labs were to agree to a slowdown, there’s no good way to keep them to their word, and China would likely continue on its own path regardless. The US economy is increasingly propped up on the AI industry, which itself has become an ouroboros of financing deals and circular investments; any meaningful crackdown risks major instability that reaches well beyond Silicon Valley.

The automotive industry is also admittedly an imperfect analogy for all kinds of reasons. There’s no seat belt equivalent for AI, no straightforward solution that can demonstrably reduce risk overnight. (It also took decades for the majority of states to pass laws mandating that people actually wear them.) The potential harms are less certain and less quantifiable. AI doomers will tell you the technology could result in human extinction in a decade; skeptics argue that’s sci-fi marketing malarkey.

We’ve talked about various AI risk scenarios before, but no one can say for certain what’s going to happen next. If you’re looking for data points to calculate your own personal p(doom), I’d point to a recent CNN report about how the US military supposedly nearly boarded a Chinese ship in part because a false AI-generated report said it was carrying nuclear materials. What, if anything, does the AI accord accomplish to prevent similar incidents from happening in the future? Unclear.

The correct answer to all this uncertainty surely isn’t “I guess we’ll find out.” But that’s exactly what self-regulation encourages. To its credit, OpenAI has delayed and even canceled the release of its most advanced models over security concerns. But not before they went on various, extensive hacking sprees, new details about which are still trickling out at a steady pace.

In an interview with TIME published on Thursday, Trump suggested that the Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation were sufficient “guardrails” for the artificial intelligence industry. Are they? It’s far from clear if AI companies can even be held legally responsible when their models go rogue. And it’s not like AI agents themselves are being served subpoenas.

The truth is, no one knows how to solve for AI safety right now. It’s going to take massive amounts of coordination, resources, and regulatory authority to develop the right framework and enforce it, which is exactly the kind of thing governments are designed to provide. Instead of even attempting to work through any of that, the Trump administration is getting out of the way and telling everyone to step on the gas. Don’t bother buckling up.

This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Tim Heidecker Is Bringing His Joe Rogan Parody Show to The Onion

Wired October 01, 2026

As satirical news outlet The Onion continued to wage a legal battle to acquire the assets of Infowars out of bankruptcy this summer, it launched a streaming program that spoofed the brand and its bellowing conspiracist ringleader, Alex Jones.

Comedian Tim Heidecker took the reins of the operation, adopting Jones’ guttural and paranoid bluster as he investigated, among other unconfirmed reports, whether Jones himself had exploded in his car after eating too much Whataburger.

But Heidecker wasn’t about to stop there in his quest to transform the Infowars brand into a gonzo comedy network along the lines of Adult Swim. Now he’s taking aim at another high-profile target: Joe Rogan, the bro podcaster whose rambling, misinformed conversations with everyone from Vice President JD Vance to [checks notes] Yakov Smirnoff have somehow kept his long-running series, The Joe Rogan Experience, at the top of the charts for years. Heidecker’s companion show, The Tim Heidecker Podcast, premieres at 8 pm ET on Thursday night, and WIRED can exclusively reveal that the debut episode includes lots of complaining about pronouns, wildly dumb speculation around AI, and plugs for a supplement called “Crab Salts” that makes your “head hurt” and causes you to shout.

A representative for Rogan did not immediately return a request for comment.

Heidecker first lampooned Rogan’s discursive and disorganized interviews in 2021, with a viral 12-hour podcast (in reality, one hour of footage looped a dozen times) covering topics including psychedelics, cancel culture, and whether Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson would run for president. His guests for that show, comedy duo and Onion contributors Rajat Suresh and Jeremy Levick, return for the new episode, offering their “expert” takes on hot-button topics. (The pair have essentially perfected the art of fake celebrity web content and once even got Justin Theroux in on the joke for a mock Hollywood Reporter-style actors roundtable.)

“What is essentially happening is, in place of Christianity, we have the 10 commandments of woke,” Levick says during a discussion of DEI policies on the first episode of The Tim Heidecker Podcast. The chat veers into concerns that bearded men are dressing as princesses to visit Disneyland. Heidecker then abruptly informs the boys that he’s planned a weekend trip to Glasgow “for Scotch wrestling.”

In 2026, it’s more difficult than ever to exaggerate the absurdities of the right-wing media ecosystem, with its fact-free moral panics and bizarre alternative medicines. Though if anyone is up to the task, it’s the endlessly inventive Heidecker—who will have no shortage of grifters and lunatics to go after once he’s done with his run as a Rogan type. Luckily for him, few of those potential impressions are as rough on the voice as Alex Jones.

Amazon Alexa Devices Are Already on Sale, but the Deals Aren’t All as Good as They Look

Wired October 01, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Amazon's Prime Day has returned for its fall edition, and the Amazon Alexa-powered devices are already on sale. But are the sales actually any good?

There's already the question of whether you want Alexa in your house, and now it's a question of whether the sales are more of a mind game than a real discount. That's thanks to Amazon raising prices across its device categories at the end of August, leaving us with the same product lineup but a worse case to recommend it. Some devices are already on sale right now ahead of Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days for $40 off, but went up in price by $20 just a few weeks ago, cutting that discount into something that feels barely worth the spend.

If you're interested in Amazon's device sales but want the real picture of what the discount is and which devices are worth it, I've got you covered. I've been testing Amazon Alexa speakers since they launched in 2012, and I am also WIRED's resident Kindle tester, which gives me almost too much insight into the price games Amazon plays with these devices. Here's my full breakdown.

Right now, Amazon's Alexa-powered Echo speakers and Fire TV sticks are currently on sale ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days next week (October 6-7). These devices saw price hikes at the end of August, so some of the deals aren't as good as in the past. They do seem to be permanent price changes, though, so if you're certain you want one of these models, this is the best time to buy.

So far, most Kindles aren't on sale yet, but all three Kindle Kids models (the Kindle Kids, the Kindle Paperwhite Kids, and Kindle Colorsoft Kids) are already on sale. (Amazon also announced new versions of these Kindles today, along with the rest of its lineup, so it's up to you whether you want the current on-sale model or to preorder the new one!) If you're looking for a Paperwhite and Scribe, they aren't on sale yet as of this writing. Neither are Eero routers.

But I expect most of those models will be discounted once the event begins. Both Kindle and Eero products also saw price hikes at the end of August, so I recommend buying them only on sale (even if the sales aren't as good as they used to be, since they're similar discounts but on higher prices).

Not all deals are great, especially given the recent price increases. If you're set on getting a new Amazon Alexa-powered speaker, though, here are the discounts (and devices themselves!) that are still worth it.

Amazon

Amazon

Best Buy

The best deal in Amazon's early device deals is easily the second-gen Echo Spot, revived in 2024. It's 50 percent off its new price, and it's still a solid discount off its original price of $80. I really like this fun little smart speaker. It works great as a bedside alarm, shows when your next alarm is set, and can display the weather or your calendar details when you ask Alexa. Best of all, you get the fun benefits of a screen without a camera to worry about.

Amazon

Amazon

The only new Amazon Alexa speaker that didn't get hit with a price change is the second-gen Echo Studio. It still sits at $220, which is not only its original price, but also the original price of the first-gen model. It's a nice thing to see. Its discount isn't huge for Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days, but it's $40 for powerful, room-filling sound that could extend across great rooms without getting muddy.

Amazon

Amazon’s New Kindle Lineup Is Lighter, Thinner, and More Metal

Wired October 01, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The Kindle will turn 20 in 2027. Amazon says it plans to celebrate the milestone throughout the year, but to kick things off, it's starting with an entirely refreshed Kindle lineup.

On Thursday, the company introduced a handful of new Kindle models: a new 6-inch base Kindle, a 7-inch Kindle Paperwhite, and a 7-inch Kindle Colorsoft. You can buy Signature Editions of the latter two and Kids versions of the entire range, which include artist-designed kids cases, a year of Amazon's worry-free guarantee for damage, and a year of Kids+, the company's subscription service that offers unlimited access to ad-free, child-appropriate books.

The highlight is Amazon's use of aluminum for the Kindle's construction rather than traditional plastic. The starting tier is plastic, but you can upgrade to an all-aluminum model (Amazon uses 80 percent recycled aluminum) if you prefer that Kindle model and you just want something more robust.

It can get a little confusing with all the different SKUs, so here's a quick rundown:

The base Kindle, the aluminum version, and the Kids Kindle are on sale starting today. The Paperwhite and Colorsoft are available for preorder on a rolling basis and will launch at the end of October.

The Kindle's screen offers 30 percent faster book opening than its predecessor, Amazon says. The build is a whole millimeter thinner at 6.8 mm, and Amazon cut the weight by around 18 grams to 140 grams. The Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft are both similarly lighter (204 grams) and thinner (6.8 mm), retain the waterproof design, and feature adjustable warm reading lights. Like before, the screen has a higher pixel density that makes text appear sharper.

Amazon says the new Kindles are also compliant with the European Union’s new battery regulations, meaning the batteries should be easier to remove and replace.

Upgrading to the Signature Edition for the Colorsoft and Paperwhite nets you the aluminum build, an ambient light sensor that adjusts brightness automatically, and an accelerometer that lets you turn the screen to landscape orientation and have the pages adjust accordingly. The upgrade also adds the ability to use a double-tap gesture to turn pages.

Uniquely, the Signature Editions feature pogo pins that let you charge via Amazon's new $60 dock, which props the device up as it charges. There's also a new Page-Turn Cover ($80)—a case with physical page-turn buttons that magnetically attaches to the back of the devices and pairs via the pogo pins, which Amazon says offers page-turn buttons to the vocal minority that still loves them (around 5 percent of Kindle users) without adding unnecessary bulk to the device.

Don't worry, you don't need the case, the Signature Edition, or even a new Kindle if you just want page-turn buttons. Amazon is debuting its own Kindle Click, a $35 page-turn accessory that pairs over Bluetooth for the non-Signature (and older) Kindle models.

The Kindle business is booming. Amazon's Kevin Keith, vice president of devices, says Kindles have seen double-digit growth over the last three years, with 2025 being the highest sales year in more than a decade. He says 60 to 65 percent of people buying new devices have never had a Kindle before, with Gen Z, millennials, and even Gen Alpha driving the lion's share. This past January saw the highest single-month Kindle reading volume in history.

At the same time, Kindles are more expensive than ever. “Memory pricing is a little bit crazy,” Keith says, referring to the memory shortage behind the general price bump on all electronics. Amazon upped prices of existing Kindles earlier this year; the new devices match those prices.

Part of the redesign aims to lower overall manufacturing costs and standardize the hardware. Take the refreshed display on the base Kindle—Keith says many of the improvements trickle down from the development of the Kindle Scribe. For the first time, the base Kindle has a display that sits flush with the body, just like its pricier counterparts. (It previously had a raised plastic bezel around the screen.) That whole front panel is also available in a new color: Ube (purple).

While Amazon has made Kindles with colorful fronts (like the matcha green Kindle from 2024), it hasn't done this with flush displays. That's because simply coloring the front would make the Ube color, for example, scatter around the screen as the frontlight reflects it, casting a purple hue on the display. To counter this, Keith says Amazon developed a new “edge-to-edge” color technology that prints two different colors under the cover lens: the Ube color backed by a layer of black. The black absorbs the light, which solves the problem. Amazon says it perfected this tech in the Scribe and ported it down here.

Color is important. Keith says alternative colors typically make up just 15 to 20 percent of sales—the rest being classic options like black or white—but the matcha green model captured a surprising 55 percent. Amazon also chose that color because, at the time, it noticed a general increase in the popularity of matcha in drinks and sweets (it also noted that folks on #BookTok are reading in coffee shops). Hence the new ube color, which is based on the popular purple yam of the same name.

“We've been tracking food trends, and two years ago, ube just exploded—ube was growing 200 percent year over year,” says Chris Green, Amazon's vice president of design. “We expect it to do far better than the matcha.”

For the aluminum housing, instead of milling the device's frame from a block of aluminum and using a lot of water in the process, Amazon stamps a flat sheet, which then goes into a forge that presses down to create the backplate and sides. The process supposedly takes seconds compared to the hours it can take to machine a single aluminum device frame (like an iPhone or MacBook), saving material and energy. It helps lower the Kindle's carbon footprint, which is now equivalent to 11 hardcover books.

Green says these improvements bring down the device's density. The density of the average human body is around 1 gram per cubic centimeter; an iPhone is around 2.2 grams per cubic centimeter. The new Kindles are around 1.2 grams. Lowering that number can help make the hardware “disappear” during prolonged use.

“I truly want people to never think about the Kindle,” Green says. “I just want them to think about the magical world that the author has created inside of this device.”

For Green, who has designed nearly all of Amazon's hardware in his 19-year tenure at the company (and yes, he says he's embarrassed by the Fire Phone), chasing that 1.2-grams-per-cubic-centimeter target is all about getting the gadget out of the way so the Kindle can mimic the analog calm of physical print.

“More people are reading on paper, more people are reading on Kindles,” Green says. “Is it a backlash to AI? Probably. People are trying to find things more authentic—we're in a crisis of authenticity.” Surveys have shown that overall leisure reading is down across the US, but the people who are reading are buying more than ever.

As for the 20th anniversary of the Kindle in 2027, Keith says the company may roll out a significant refresh to the Kindle's user interface, though he didn't share more. Expect special anniversary editions of some Kindles. When I asked whether we could expect the return of the Kindle Oasis—an asymmetrical e-reader with physical page-turn buttons—Green chuckles.

“The first Oasis was one of my passion projects,” he says. “I loved that. I really, really loved that product. But I was a vocal minority on that—most of the people wanted slabs.”

So, probably not.

Correction on October 1, 2026 at 2:30 pm: We've updated this story to correct an incorrect statement about page-turn speed that Amazon initially provided (along with Kevin Keith's title).

I Found the Best Kindles to Take Your Library Anywhere

Wired October 01, 2026

Amazon

Amazon (16 GB)
