Asus

Whether you’re away from home for work or on vacation, a travel router could come in very handy, and the dual-band, Wi-Fi 7 Asus RT-BE58 Go is faster and offers greater range than the TP-Link Roam 7 (BE3600) it replaces here, though it is a bit bigger. Connect your devices at home, and a travel router provides convenience on vacation. I took it on a recent trip, and it was nice to simply hook it up to a source to have pre-paired Wi-Fi on everyone’s devices without being asked for the login again and again (as usually happens). You can plug in an internet source via Ethernet, connect to public Wi-Fi, or employ USB tethering. It’s especially handy when you want to connect multiple devices to hotel Wi-Fi, which limits your device connections.

Despite its small size, it does a decent job delivering reasonably speedy connectivity, especially at close range. There are two fold-out antennas, and it will easily fill a hotel room or vacation apartment. Although there’s no built-in battery, the USB-C power port on the back works just fine with a power bank for complete portability. There is VPN support, it can serve as an AiMesh node if you have an Asus mesh, and you can plug in storage via the USB port to share files or back up locally.

Netgear

Amazon

Netgear

Lenovo

After testing several 5G routers and mobile hot spots, I recommend the Netgear Nighthawk M7. Pop in a 5G SIM (it works with AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon) or sign up for an eSIM (Netgear offers plan for 140 countries), and you have a dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router to use on the go. It has a smart design, a handy 2.4-inch color screen, and a battery that’s good for up to 10 hours of use (I got 9 hours before having to charge). I combined it with a power bank to last even longer. You can connect up to 32 devices via Wi-Fi and expect a range of up to 2,000 square feet. Many other 5G routers I tested became unstable and warm with multiple devices connected, but the M7 handled it just fine.

Previous Netgear hot spots, while excellent, have been very expensive, so I’m happy to trade in some ports and a touchscreen to get a more affordable device. It only has a USB-C port, but it’s capable of 2.5 Gbps speeds if you snag Netgear’s USB-C to Ethernet Adapter ($32) and plug in a device with an Ethernet cable. While it covers several popular 5G bands, there’s no mmWave support, but it also covers a good range of LTE bands. I love that you can set it to fall back onto Wi-Fi when available, such as when you return to the hotel at the end of the day.

This is how the throughput compares on different bands averaged over multiple devices and tests in the same room with a clear line of sight to the routers.

I have tested many other models and have several more in the queue. These aren’t as great as the picks above, but they are worth considering.

Fortify Router (GL. iNet with ExpressVPN) for $200: A home router with built-in VPN service is a tempting idea, even more so when it’s built on GL. iNet’s Flint 2 platform and includes one year of ExpressVPN service (redeemable with the order ID). VPN service set up at the router level means every device that connects is protected, and ExpressVPN is in our best VPNs guide. Now, you could set up a VPN of your choice with most routers (all of our Asus picks above), but the Fortify Router makes it easy. Beyond that, this is a decent dual-band Wi-Fi 6 router (it’s essentially the GL-MT6000) with a 2.5 Gbps WAN, a 2.5 Gbps WAN/LAN, four Gigabit LAN ports, and a USB 3.0 port. Performance-wise, this router will suffice for average family homes with 1 Gbps or lower connections and modern construction (you’re limited to around 900 Mbps with VPN service, but likely slower). Speed and stability are very good, and latency on the 5-GHz band is low. But it struggled to fully cover my old thick-walled property. Configuration is easy via the web interface, and it supports various apps and plug-ins, including AdGuard, Tailscale, and Tor.

TP-Link Archer BE600 for $250: This standalone router supports Wi-Fi 7. I don’t love the design, but the six adjustable antennas allow for tinkering, and TP-Link has been very generous with the ports (one 10 Gbps, four 2.5 Gbps, and a USB 3.0), though it’s a little annoying that the USB is on the side. This model also offers excellent close-range speeds on the 6-GHz band, and solid speeds on both the 5-GHz and 2.4-GHz bands, though TP-Link’s dual-band BE260 slightly outperformed it on those two bands. But it does offer a pretty expansive range (up to 2,600 square feet).

TP-Link Roam 7 (BE3600) for $130: This dual-band, Wi-Fi 7 travel router was my pick, but the Asus RT-BE58 Go above is a slightly better performer for around the same money. This is still a good, portable device, capable of keeping you online in your hotel room or modest apartment. It also supports mobile tethering, VPN, and can serve as a Wi-Fi range extender. There’s a USB-C for power that works with portable chargers, and a USB-A for file sharing or backup.

TP-Link Archer BE260 for $125: This dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz) Wi-Fi 7 router runs close to our top pick on performance and is a solid alternative. This router offers a slight upgrade over the BE230 above, with improved 5-GHz performance, an extra antenna, and a coverage boost up to 2,400 square feet. It also sports a 2.5-Gbps WAN, a 2.5-Gbps LAN, three Gigabit LAN, and a USB 3.0 port. Throw in EasyMesh support and a relatively low price, and the BE260 is a tempting option. But if you want enhanced security and parental controls, you have to subscribe, which takes the shine off the value.

Asus RT-BE86U for $250: The new Wi-Fi 7 version of the Asus RT-AX86U, this dual-band (2.4- and 5-GHz) router is similar to the Asus RT-BE88U below. It lacks the 6-GHz band but brings all the other improvements that Wi-Fi 7 offers. The RT-BE86U proved reliable in my tests and performed extremely well on the 5-GHz band, matching the slightly more expensive RT-BE88U. It is slightly smaller but still has one 10-Gbps and four 2.5-Gbps Ethernet ports, alongside a USB 2.0 and a USB 3.0 port.

AVM FRITZ!Box 5690 Pro

AVM FRITZ!Box 5690 Pro for £462: AVM has dominated the German router market for years and is expanding across Europe and the UK, so I tested the FRITZ!Box 5690 Pro. AVM’s range is distinctive in white and red plastic, but there’s a focus on functionality. This tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router boasts a 2.5-Gbps WAN/LAN, four gigabit LAN, and a USB 3.1 port. It’s fast, scoring mid- to high-table results in my tests, and it proved reliable. It also has DSL or fiber-optic modems, an integrated DECT base station for cordless phones, built-in storage (NAS), and support for Zigbee to connect smart home devices. You don’t need an account to set it up or configure it. There’s a firewall and guest network option in the straightforward web interface (you can use the mobile app if you prefer). AVM’s routers are developed and manufactured in Europe, making them an interesting, privacy-focused alternative to routers from China or the US. The company also has a strong track record of supporting its products for years after release. Folks in the UK and Europe looking to upgrade to Wi-Fi 7 should consider this router. My fingers are crossed that AVM expands into the US next.

Asus RT-BE92U for $287: After a simple setup and a trouble-free week of speedy, stable internet across the 2.4-, 5-, and 6-GHz bands, I can recommend this router. It has Wi-Fi 7 benefits like MLO and 320-MHz channels, support for a guest network, VPN services, free security software, and parental controls. It also boasts a 10-Gbps WAN/LAN, a 2.5-Gbps WAN/LAN, three 2.5-Gbps LANs, and a USB 3.2 port. This tri-band Wi-Fi 7 device came perilously close to claiming the midrange spot above, but was a smidge slower on the 5-GHz and 6-GHz bands and had a considerably shorter range. However, if your home is around 1,500 square feet and you’d rather avoid a subscription, the RT-BE92U is an excellent alternative. Customer reviews suggest some folks have had trouble with this router, but the latest firmware was rock solid for me.

Asus RT-BE88U for $350: This dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router is an odd prospect because it does not offer the 6-GHz band at all, just 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz. But you can still combine those bands with MLO and enjoy features like 4K QAM, and this router will be fast enough for the average home. It has ports galore (two 10 Gbps, four 2.5 Gbps, four Gigabit, and one USB 3.0). It outperformed several more expensive routers on the 5-GHz band, and that’s likely what most of your devices are using most of the time right now. Asus also offers free security software and parental controls with its routers, so there’s no need for subscriptions. But when I consider that you can snag the Netgear Nighthawk RS300 listed above for less, I find it tough to recommend this router to folks in the US. If the 6-GHz band is unavailable or nerfed in your country, the RT-BE88U is for you.

Netgear Nighthawk RS700 for $600: Although I had setup issues that required a factory reset, there’s no hiding the top-notch performance of this router. It’s a Wi-Fi 7 tri-band router with two 10-Gbps Ethernet ports, four gigabit ports, and a USB 3.2. The tower design is new for the Nighthawk line, and it looks great. This router will blend in far better than our bulky Wi-Fi 7 pick above from Asus, and it was slightly faster on the 6-GHz band, though not the 5-GHz or 2.4-GHz bands. It mainly misses out on a recommendation because it is more expensive. We’re already seeing discounts on the RT-BE96U, and Asus offers free security software and parental controls. If you get the Nighthawk RS700S, the “S” at the end denotes a free year of Netgear Armor, which costs $100 a year thereafter. If you need parental controls, that’s another $70 a year.

TP-Link Archer BE800 for $500: With a fresh design that’s more desktop PC than router, the BE800 tri-band beast came out high up in my tests on the 2.4-GHz, 5-GHz, and 6-GHz bands, proving impressively swift for file transfers and downloads. It also boasts speedy ports galore, a cool but kind of pointless customizable dot-matrix LED screen, and the Tether app offers a guest network, IoT network, VPN server or client, EasyMesh, QoS for device prioritization, and remote management.

Netgear M3 for £450: I was very impressed by this mobile 5G router. Slip a SIM in there, and it connects to 4G or 5G networks to deliver Wi-Fi to your devices. It’s a dual-band Wi-Fi 6 model that’s speedy on the 5-GHz band. The M3 had no trouble handling multiple connected devices (up to 32) and served a stable internet connection for around 10 hours. You can charge via the USB-C port, and there’s a 2.4-inch LCD color screen for configuration. It’s a solid hot spot for business or personal travel. Sadly, the M3 doesn’t seem to be available in the US, but folks in the UK can save some money and snag this instead of the M7 above (it’s frequently discounted).

Firewalla Gold SE for $519: This quirky portable device is perfect for people who worry about security and privacy. It offers comprehensive tools for monitoring all traffic in and out of your house, robust and detailed parental controls, ad-blocking, and enhanced security with a built-in firewall and VPN option. It serves as a router, but you will want to pair another router in access point mode for Wi-Fi in your home. It’s expensive and may prove intimidating for inexperienced folks, but it offers deep insight into your network and an impressive depth of security features without an additional subscription. The Gold SE has two 2.5-Gbps ports and two gigabit ports and is suitable for folks with up to 2-gigabit connections. If your internet is only one gigabit, try the more affordable but slightly less capable Firewalla Purple ($319).

While I recommend buying a Wi-Fi 7 router if you’re upgrading, there are loads of Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 6 routers that will serve the average family well. With Wi-Fi 6E you still get the faster 6-GHz band. The bulk of household traffic still likely uses 5 GHz, and you can save a lot of money by sticking with Wi-Fi 6 for a bit longer.

Netgear Nighthawk RAXE300 for $285: The curvy spaceship design in matte black is a little more stealthy than your average gaming gear, but those wings contain antennas for a strong signal throughout your home. The Nighthawk RAXE300 is a tri-band router with Wi-Fi 6E support, covering the 2.4-GHz, 5-GHz, and 6-GHz bands. It served seamless, speedy Wi-Fi during two weeks of testing, with zero issues while handling a revolving mix of four simultaneous gaming and video streams. A single 2.5-Gbps WAN/LAN port, five gigabit LAN ports, and a USB-C 3.0 port will be enough for most folks.

The Nighthawk app is excellent and offers band splitting, guest network options, and a host of analytical tools. The Premium Smart Parental Controls ($8/month or $70/year) and Netgear Armor ($100/year) are slick, but the extra expense is hard to swallow when many competitors offer cheaper or free alternatives with similar features. This is discontinued, but a few places still have stock, and it’s still a great router.

TP-Link Archer AX55 for $100: This affordable Wi-Fi 6 router is still a decent pick for the average home. The slick black finish is attractive, and there are four antennas to direct Wi-Fi to every corner (it is worth tweaking and testing different positions). Performance was solid throughout my two-floor, 1,600-square-foot home but dropped off slightly in the back garden. Stability was excellent over a couple of weeks of testing, and this router ticks many feature boxes (MU-MIMO, beamforming, WPA3). It has four Gigabit Ethernet LAN ports, a single Gigabit WAN port, and a USB 3.0 port on the back, which is enough for most people.

I’m a fan of TP-Link’s Tether app, where you can review traffic, split bands, create a guest network, schedule reboots, set automatic updates, and even tell the LED to turn off at night. TP-Link’s basic free HomeShield tier offers network scanning, QoS (Quality of Service) for device prioritization, and basic parental controls so you can filter and blacklist websites and set the same bedtime every day. If you want a variable schedule, time limits, downtime, and real-time security protection, you must upgrade to HomeShield Pro (30-day free trial, then $6 per month or $55 for the year). If money is tight, you may even consider the next system down, the TP-Link Archer AX21 ($90). Performance is slightly weaker, but the experience is broadly similar.

These are the internet routers we had issues with or can’t recommend for one reason or another.

Acer Connect X6E 5G: This is an interesting Wi-Fi 6E model with a 5G SIM card slot capable of keeping you online using a mobile network should your main broadband connection fail. It has two Gigabit Ethernet ports, a WAN/LAN, LAN, and an RJ-11 port for a phone line. It’s easy to set up and offers an NFC connection option, so you can just wave your phone over it to connect. This unusual blend of features could be good for business travelers. Performance was solid when it worked, and you can get a very fast connection at close range on both the 6-GHz and 5-GHz bands. Sadly, the range was limited, and the Connect X6E 5G was intermittently unstable during my testing, dropping devices randomly and cutting out repeatedly.

D-Link AX3000 DBR-330: This lightweight, rectangular travel router from D-Link is aimed at business professionals who travel for work. It’s a dual-band Wi-Fi 6 router that can also serve as a hot spot, with a connection via USB. There’s even a potentially handy microSD/TF card slot for up to 2 TB of storage for file sharing or backup. Setup via the browser is easy, and there’s built-in VPN support. It proved nice and fast at close range, but it dropped off quickly, and I couldn’t get a signal two rooms away. It will work fine for a hotel room, though. You can get our TP-Link travel router pick above or the Asus RT-AX57 Go for similar money, and I prefer both of them.

Netgear Nighthawk RS200: The RS200 is Netgear’s dual-band (2.4- and 5-GHz) router and the cheapest in its Wi-Fi 7 lineup. After the tri-band RS300 won a recommendation, I expected this router to perform decently, but I encountered several issues, including random drops and poor range. After turning the router off and on again, many devices, including my Pixel and iPhone, struggled to reconnect. Perhaps I have too many devices in my home for it, though Netgear suggests it can handle up to 80. It has two 2.5 Gbps ports, three gigabit Ethernet ports, and a USB 3.0 port. Test results were OK, but significantly slower than the RT-BE86U.

TP-Link Archer AX5400 Pro: This dual-band Wi-Fi 6 model is almost identical to the Archer AX73, except for the 2.5-Gbps WAN port. It delivers relatively fast speeds on the 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands and boasts a 160-MHz channel width on 5 GHz. The range is good, easily covering my home and garden, but the performance was inconsistent. It was also relatively slow at moving files locally. There’s support for TP-Link OneMesh, VPN, and QoS, but you only get basic parental controls and network security unless you subscribe.

What Features Should I Look for in a Router?

My How to Buy a Router guide answers a lot of questions on the terminology you’ll come across when shopping for a new router. Still, here are a few other considerations.

Wi-Fi Standards: All my main picks are now using the latest Wi-Fi 7 protocol. That doesn’t mean Wi-Fi 6 or Wi-Fi 6E routers aren’t worth having, necessarily. But with cheaper dual-band Wi-Fi 7 routers available, there’s not much reason to buy anything older. Only Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 routers offer extra bandwidth and faster speeds on the 6-GHz band, but devices like phones and laptops must also support Wi-Fi 6E or 7 for you to take advantage. The 6-GHz band is also short-range compared to the 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands.

Internet Speeds: Your maximum internet speed is set by your ISP and depends on your internet plan. It will likely fluctuate, depending on the time of day. Some ISPs guarantee a minimum download and upload speed. While your router can’t provide an internet connection that exceeds that speed, it can potentially go faster when you stream from a server in your home or move files from one device on your local network to another.

Coverage: It’s worth checking a prospective router’s coverage and speed, but understand that your home Wi-Fi mileage may vary. Construction materials in your house, your neighbors’ activity and Wi-Fi networks, your devices, and the position of your router are just a few of the factors that will impact your wireless performance.

Ports: Ethernet ports offer stable connections and are essential for some smart home setups that require a hub for lights or security cameras. Some network-attached storage (NAS) for backups or media will plug into your main router via USB. Ensure that the model you are considering has all the ports you need.

What Is the Difference Between a Modem and a Router?

A modem (modulator-demodulator) connects your home to your internet service provider (ISP) and the external internet. A router connects the devices within your home to that internet connection wirelessly via Wi-Fi or with Ethernet cables. Check out my Router vs. Modem guide to learn more.

Can a Single Wireless Router Cover Your Entire Home?

Manufacturers usually suggest a coverage range for a router in square feet, but every home is different, and the real-world range is likely to be shorter. Walls and other obstructions will weaken and block wireless signals. Ideal placement would be in the center of the home near the ceiling of the ground floor without any obstructions. A well-placed single router is generally enough to cover a typical two-floor home up to 2,000 square feet. For larger homes, it's worth considering mesh systems to create a reliable home network.

Where Should You Put Your Router?

Physically moving your router can make a real difference to Wi-Fi speeds. It should be central, out in the open, and high up. Walls, cupboards, and even bookshelves can interfere with your Wi-Fi signal, as can fish tanks, TVs, or microwaves. Even changing the angle or moving the antennas can impact the strength of the Wi-Fi around your home, so don't be afraid to experiment with different positions.

Can I Add Routers or Extenders to Make a Mesh?

Many manufacturers allow you to create a mesh network by adding more routers or devices like Wi-Fi extenders, but check what is supported before you buy. For example, Asus AiMesh enables you to link multiple routers, while TP-Link’s OneMesh only allows you to add power-line adapters or range extenders. EasyMesh is a standard certification by the Wi-Fi Alliance that hopes to allow the mixing and matching of devices from different manufacturers to form a mesh, but few devices support it so far. You can also buy single mesh routers, like an Amazon Eero, and then add more later if you find that you need them. Based on my testing, a mesh is always better than an extender.

How Do Ethernet Cables Compare?

Running an Ethernet cable to create a wired connection between your home router and device will provide a faster and more secure link than Wi-Fi. But running Ethernet cables everywhere can be tricky. Read my Ethernet guide to learn more. Wireless connectivity makes life easy and is often fast enough for most tasks, such as browsing the web or streaming video.

What About the US Ban on Foreign-Made Routers?

The Federal Communications Commission has banned new consumer internet routers manufactured outside the US because of national security concerns. The ban doesn’t affect any routers already in American homes or currently on sale in the US, but all new routers aimed at the consumer market must be approved.

The way the ban is described, it applies to every new Wi-Fi router, because there are no companies manufacturing routers or the components they are assembled from in the US. But companies can apply for exemptions.

All new models of foreign-produced routers will require Conditional Approval from the Department of Defense and the Department of Homeland Security before the FCC can clear them for sale in the US. Read “Everything You Need to Know About the Foreign-Made Router Ban in the US” to learn more.

What About Firmware and Security Updates?

While the FCC initially published a waiver covering software and firmware updates until March 1, 2027, it has now extended that waiver “at least until January 1, 2029.”

What happens after that date is not clear, but if the FCC were to block further updates for the routers folks already own, it would exacerbate the very issue it is trying to address. The majority of routers that are compromised and used in cyberattacks are usually older devices that no longer receive security updates.

Should You Buy a Router Now?

If you live in the US and need a router or a mesh, you should buy one. Asus, Netgear, Eero, and a few others have been granted Conditional Approval already. All the major manufacturers I asked who responded or have released a statement, including TP-Link and Synology, are confident about getting exemptions, but whether they will is impossible to say for sure. An FCC spokesperson told me, “We expect approvals to be granted in a timely manner.”

The problem with waiting is that prices are likely to go up. I’ve already seen some price creep on systems from TP-Link, Netgear, and Eero, though this could also be due to the AI-driven RAM shortage.

How I Test Routers

To find the top Wi-Fi routers, I use each one for at least a week (usually longer) in a busy family home of four with lots of video streaming, gaming, and video calls. I also test the mobile apps and web interfaces to see how easy it is to change settings, set up parental controls, and access security features. My priority is to learn how well the router works in real-life rather than a lab, but I do also run a set of standardized tests, so that I have numbers to compare.

I run speed tests (downloads and uploads). I transfer files on the network on multiple devices (including iPhones, Android phones, Windows PCs, and MacBooks) from different spots around my home. I use NetSpot to survey signal strength throughout the house and create heat maps for comparison. I run the TamoSoft Throughput Test. I turn the power and modem off and on to find out how each system recovers.

How Did I Select Products to be Reviewed

I try to test as many routers as I can. It’s not possible to test every device, so while I will typically test flagship releases, I also call in more affordable routers and try to find models to suit the average family home in terms of budget and performance. We are brand agnostic, so we will test routers from any manufacturer, provided we can get ahold of them. But we do lean toward testing more systems from the most popular brands. All the routers we test are provided by the manufacturers or their PR companies.

Most are loaned for a month or so and then returned. A handful of our recommended picks are kept for longer term testing. The remainder are donated to charities. I recently dropped off a batch to Reusing IT and have donated several devices to Oxfam and Shelter.

The Real Threat to the Midterms Is Regular Americans Thinking Violence Is the Answer

Wired October 01, 2026

The attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021, was not conducted mainly by extremists or fringe militia groups. It was, according to the data, the work of normal Americans.

That is the conclusion Robert A. Pape lays out in his new book, Our Own Worst Enemies: America in the Age of Violent Populism, citing data about those who were arrested and charged following the attack.

While Proud Boys and Oath Keepers gained most of the headlines, data collected by Pape as part of his work as founding director of the Chicago Project on Security and Threats (CPOST) found that the vast majority (90 percent) of those charged with crimes arising from the attack held no affiliation with militias or militant organizations.

Pape’s analysis found that 22 percent were business owners, and almost 30 percent held a college degree. Among the defendants were doctors, engineers, CEOs, and government employees. Nearly 40 percent held white-collar jobs, while just 8 percent of participants were unemployed.

The findings are key to understanding the warning that is central to Pape’s book: Americans do not understand that the threat of political violence is coming not from the fringes, but from the mainstream.

“As the 2026 midterms approach, US elections are entering a danger zone in which state power, protest, and political legitimacy increasingly collide,” Pape writes in the book. “For most Americans, political violence is still understood as episodic—shocking when it erupts but destined to fade. That assumption is reassuring. It is also increasingly dangerous.”

WIRED spoke to Pape about his book, his concerns about violence in the midterms, why it is so important to understand the attack on the Capitol, and what, if anything, gives him hope that democracy will win out.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

DAVID GILBERT: Your book is centered on the idea of violent populism. What is it, and why is it on the rise in 2026?

ROBERT A. PAPE: Violent populism is a dangerous political climate where substantial segments of the public increasingly accept physical force as a legitimate tool to gain, preserve, or defend political power. It is on the rise due to a profound cultural clash over the nature of American identity and citizenship, exacerbated by elite rhetoric that frames politics as an existential struggle between enemies. This structural dynamic transforms ordinary, mainstream citizens into active participants in political aggression.

You call the midterms “a stress test of whether American competition can remain bounded by nonviolence.” Are you concerned about the political violence around this election?

Yes, the level of concern for this election cycle is at an unprecedented high, surpassing anything seen since the deep social upheavals of the 1960s. With national anxieties amplified by a highly combustible domestic climate and global instability like the ongoing war with Iran, elections have increasingly become dangerous potential flashpoints. This dynamic represents a direct, critical test of whether our foundational institutions can still successfully enforce peaceful political transitions.

Heading into the midterms, a lot of people are focusing on possible action from extremist groups, such as militias. Is this the wrong thing to be worried about?

Focusing exclusively on fringe militias misdiagnoses the primary danger facing American democracy today. The real threat is that political radicalization has broken out of the fringes and fully migrated into the mainstream electorate. Our primary worry should be the tens of millions of ordinary Americans who now passively accept or actively endorse violence to achieve their political goals.

You write that Americans are misreading the warning signs of political violence, again. What are those warning signs?

The primary warning sign is the broad public normalization and passive acceptance of aggressive political acts as standard features of daily political life. This is signaled by an explosion of violent symbolism across the entire media spectrum and elite rhetoric that strips legitimacy away from opposing factions. When ordinary citizens begin to view political opposition as an existential, hostile force, the ground is fully prepared for real-world conflict.

You write in the book that the January 6th attack on the Capitol was a rubicon crossed between "routine political conflict and civil war." Why was it such an important turning point?

The January 6th attack shattered the all-important democratic norm that power changes hands through ballots rather than raw displays of physical coercion. It demonstrated that an electoral outcome could be violently challenged not by foreign adversaries, but by a massive crowd of American citizens targeting their own legislative body. This crossed line signaled that internal political disputes were no longer reliably bounded by a shared commitment to nonviolence.

The narrative around the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol is that it was driven by extremist groups on the fringes of American society. But that's not what the data shows, right?

CPOST data completely disproves the fringe narrative by showing the remarkable mainstream geography of those involved in the insurrection. The vast majority of the actors were not isolated radicals or card-carrying militia members, but “normal” political activists with stable homes, jobs, and 401(k)s. Only 1 in 10 were militia members. Nearly half were doctors, lawyers, CEOs, business owners, US State Department appointees—and some even attended the White House Christmas party the year before. Most represented a cross-section of middle-class America acting on a shared, mainstream belief that democratic institutions were no longer legitimate.

Why do you think the prevailing narrative around the January 6 attack on the Capitol has been so wrong for so many years?

The narrative has been wrong because public institutions and media outlets initially relied heavily on imperfect law enforcement databases that naturally isolated the most prominent, organized fringe actors. And they did not update their readers and viewers as the bulk of the data came in. This approach ignored the underlying, broader structural dynamics of public opinion and extensive survey research. By focusing strictly on the visible, oddball characters, analysts missed the massive wave of passive, mainstream support that actually fueled the event.

My reading of this book is that most people have a fundamental misunderstanding of political violence in America in 2026. Is that accurate?

That is completely accurate and is the central, urgent argument of the entire book. The greatest threat to the United States is not an out-of-control group of radical extremists, but the reality that millions of otherwise ordinary citizens now accept violence as a regular political tool. Once political violence is normalized by the mainstream, old institutional solutions cease to function effectively.

You compare the current embrace of violent populism by middle-class white America to the expansion of the second Ku Klux Klan in the 1920s. Do you think people will be shocked by that comparison?

Many readers will likely be shocked, because the modern imagination associates the Klan strictly with regional, low-income hate groups rather than a massive social movement. However, the historical data shows that the second KKK of the 1920s was a highly mainstream, middle-class organization driven by a cultural clash over American identity. Drawing this explicit parallel highlights how easily normal, institutionalized communities can slide into systemic intolerance when they feel their cultural dominance is threatened.

Do you think readers of the book will be surprised that defense of political violence is not solely the preserve of the right, but that people on the left also reinforce your thesis of violent populism?

Yes, readers who expect a one-sided partisan critique will be surprised to see that the call for political violence comes from both sides of the aisle. [Confessed health care CEO assassin Luigi] Mangione and the recent [accused] Trump assassin at the April White House Correspondents’ Dinner reflect political violence from the left, and they are far from alone. Original CPOST surveys reveal that violent style, aggressive symbolism, and the demonization of political opponents are heavily utilized by figures across the entire political spectrum. This multisided reality proves that violent populism is a systemic, societal failure rather than an isolated partisan phenomenon.

You say that it is not yet determined if the current transitional phase of American politics will “culminate in democratic renewal or deeper political breakdown.” Do you have a sense of when we might have an answer to this question?

We need to lean into the “good news” in my book: that 70 percent of Americans abhor political violence. This is the large, untapped resource that we need to lean into. My book is essentially for the 70 percent and a call to action for what they can do—beyond voting. The 70 percent are the heart of our democracy. Leaning into them is how we save our democracy and avoid a much deeper, systemic breakdown of American governance.

What, if anything, gives you hope that violent populism can be overcome?

Hope lies in the data that can give new active optimism to vast majorities of ordinary Americans on both the left and right that still share a fundamental desire for stability and governance. By recognizing that our enemies are not really each other, but the normalization of violence itself, we can deliberately choose strategies of restraint to rebuild our vital democratic norms—and find productive new solutions.

Review: Tractive Cat 6 Mini

Wired October 01, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

7/10

As the pet tech industry expands rapidly, pet owners are more eager to adopt technology that tracks health metrics, similar to human wearable devices like smart rings, smartwatches, and fitness trackers.

I've been testing smart collars for the better part of the year, previously testing the Fi Mini and Tractive Smart Cat Tracker on my cat Basil, which monitored his location, movement, and sleep.

The Tractive Cat 6 Mini was released this spring, and I tested it on Basil for a month, comparing how this new-and-improved smart collar made specifically for cats with improved health features, like heart and respiratory rate, stacked up against other models.

This new model had surprisingly accurate health and activity stats that helped me understand Basil's routine and baseline a bit more than the previous models I've tested. I think these new health features would be especially helpful for people with aging cats or cats in poor health. (If you have an outdoor cat that roams, I'd go with the Fi Mini because it's more compact with a longer battery life.)

I valued the Cat 6 Mini's new AI-powered weekly reports and comparisons to similar cats to know if Basil is healthy. However, the collar itself died quickly, was a pain to charge, and GPS location accuracy could be hit-or-miss. Whether this smart cat collar is the right fit for you largely depends on your and your cat's needs.

Tractive Cat 6 Mini

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The Tractive Cat 6 Mini cat tracker is available in three colors: black, brown, and lavender. Unlike the previous Fi Mini and Tractive Smart Cat Tracker models I tested, which used an attachment that fits on the cat's existing collar, this device is the collar itself, and the entire thing needs to be taken off the cat to charge on its proprietary magnetic charger. (It takes about three hours to fully charge.) To set it up, all you need to do is download the Tractive app, choose a subscription plan, and set up your pet's profile.

For the 6 Mini model, there is one plan, but you can choose between one-, two-, and five-year contracts. One year is $10 per month, or $120 annually; two years is $7 per month, or $168 annually; and five years is $5 per month, or $300 every five years. The smart collar also has a two-year manufacturer's warranty. All plans include a 30-day money-back guarantee as well as family sharing, LTE cellular coverage, 365-day location history, and GPS data export.

Tractive Cat 6 Mini

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The tracker weighs only 1.1 ounces and is suitable for cats weighing 6.6 to 17.6 pounds, to ensure the breakaway collar opens when it should. Basil is 17 pounds, and the Cat 6 Mini fits him well with room to spare. This smart collar fits necks between 7.5 and 9 inches, whereas the previous Tracker Mini model could fit virtually any neck size because it attached to your existing collar.

Tractive claims the collar's charge lasts up to seven days for indoor cats and that it needs to be charged nearly daily if your pet roams outside. When I tested the smart collar on my indoor-only cat Basil, the battery needed to be charged by the fourth day of use.

Because the device itself is the entire collar, I felt like I was taking Basil's collar off more often than I'd like in order to charge—I didn't like that he was collarless while it charged. My anxiety told me that in this brief moment of his nakedness, he would escape. Also, because charge time took several hours, there were a few times I forgot to put it back on him until the next day.

Another gripe I had was that it was very difficult for me to remove the collar and adjust its diameter. I'm physically disabled and have reduced grip strength and fine-motor function. The collar has a simple looped clasp, but the thick material was difficult to slide under the plastic buckle; it often fell too long or too short, and I couldn't take off the collar without pulling it to trigger the breakaway feature, which was stressful for Basil—especially since the collar needed to be charged every four days.

I would've preferred the clasp to open by easily squeezing the top and bottom to release. Again, this would probably not be as big of an issue if I were able-bodied, but it is a potential issue for other pet owners who may have reduced motor function.

Tractive Cat 6 Mini

Rating: 7/10

Once you've picked a coverage plan, you'll create your pet's profile, set your home's location so the device enters power-saving mode when at home, and set up a virtual fence so you'll be alerted if the pet leaves the safe area. Using the stats I provided, Tractive compared Basil to cats of similar age and weight to set a personalized daily activity goal and compared his health stats to those of similar cats.

The Tractive app lets you track activity daily (by the hour) and over time, recording minutes to compare your cat's activity and sleep patterns. Each week, the app provides an AI summary of the previous week's activity and health stats. This pretty much always said Basil slept and relaxed a lot, but noted that he is more active than cats of similar age and breed. There's also average activity per day, which was around four hours for Basil, and average calories burned per day, which was helpful for knowing how much Basil should be eating.

Tractive estimates the cat’s daily calories burned by factoring in your pet's biometric info like weight, size, age, and spay/neuter status to create a baseline. The device contains a three-axis accelerometer that “continuously records the orientation and intensity of your cat’s physical movements,” while algorithms filter out minor movements like stretching to try to prevent false stat inflation. When the sensor detects physical acceleration, like running or playing, it logs these as the “active” minutes and converts them into daily activity time.

Tractive Cat 6 Mini

Sleep metrics break down the data by day and week and classify sleep into night sleep, day sleep, and “calm” time (when a cat is awake but not active). Each day's stats are compared to the average, which helped me track Basil's habits throughout the week. Similarly to how the device tracks activity, the built-in accelerometer motion sensor tracks when the cat is still and translates that into sleep and calm time, respectively, based on micro-movements.

You can opt out of Tractive using your cat's data for their anonymized global database and leaderboard comparison features. The device continuously syncs health metrics to the app via cellular networks, but you can request a full copy of what data has been gathered or request the permanent erasure of your data.

Tractive Cat 6 Mini

This model's new health metrics for cats include heart and respiratory rates. Basil's resting heart rate was consistently lower than that of cats of similar age and weight. On one day, it was 92 bpm, compared with the normal range of 105 to 168, according to the app. This was a bit alarming to me, and I plan to bring this data up the next time we visit the vet. The app also listed “potential reasons” for the low heart rate, including “fitness and conditioning” and “cold temperatures."

As with the heart rate, the app tracked respiratory rate over time by day and compared it with Basil's historical stats and those of similar cats. His daily average was 20 breaths per minute, which was within the normal range of 15 to 30. This number closely aligned with my personal tests using visual evidence and a timer on my phone.

Tractive Cat 6 Mini

Live and historical location services weren't as useful for Basil since he's indoor-only. Like the earlier Tractive model, the 6 Mini features a built-in SIM card, similar to what’s on your phone, which uses nearby mobile networks for location updates. You can set up to five virtual fences through the app, which will notify you when your pet enters or leaves these zones. However, similar to the previous model, the default virtual fence was too small around my apartment, so I had to expand it to cover my entire complex. This is concerning because if Basil escapes but stays near my building, I wouldn't receive an alert.

Tractive Cat 6 Mini

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Since my cat is indoor-only, I ran some experiments to track location accuracy. I had my roommates take the collar with them when they left to run errands, and I timed how long it took to receive an alert that Basil had left the “safe zone." I also took the tracker with me along with my phone, and tracked how long it took to receive a notification via Bluetooth.

When I took the tracker outside the safe zone with my phone, I was alerted via a notification on my home screen that Basil had left the “safe zone” almost immediately after exiting it. It provides an approximate location rather than pinpointing the exact spot on the street where he'd be, but it is still more helpful than randomly searching in the event he did get out. If I were to engage it in lost mode, the battery usually dies within four hours, so there is also a bit of a time limit in the event he did escape.

The alerts when the tracker was away from my phone were less precise. I tested it three times—once I was notified within a minute, the next time took about eight minutes, and the last time it took about five and a half minutes to alert after exiting the allotted safe zone. I should note that I get very poor cell phone service near my home, which could affect tracking and notification timing. Tractive also falsely alerted me that Basil had left the “safe zone” about once a week (during one week of testing, it alerted me four times). Each time, he was sitting in my home with the smart collar still on. I noticed it tended to send me false notifications more often when the battery was low or while it was on the charging dock.

Overall, the Tractive Cat 6 Mini provides valuable health insights that I appreciate—I love that I can track averages and detect any changes in Basil's health or habits even earlier. I just wish the battery didn't die so damn fast and that the collar had a universal design that was more accessible.

Neurable’s First Brain-Scanning Headphones Want to Fine-Tune Your Focus

Wired October 01, 2026

Neurable unveiled its very own pair of brain-scanning headphones on Thursday, the Neurable One. The company claims that wearing them helps you concentrate on whatever you’re doing—working, studying, or playing a video game.

When I spoke to Neurable earlier this year, the company said it planned to license its brain-scanning technology to power a flood of gadgets that were ready to enter the market. But it decided to launch its own hardware first.

“We wanted to take the product in-house,” Ramses Alcaide, Neurable’s cofounder and CEO, tells WIRED. “There were a lot of areas where we wanted to improve the product, and we wanted to move at a much faster rate. It also puts a little more capability for us to be able to show off what’s possible with the technology.”

The Boston company has until now relied on other brands to showcase its brain-scanning technology in their products, all of which promise to help people improve focus and provide data about your brain activity in a companion app. It began a few years ago by building its tech into some Master & Dynamic headphones. At the start of this year, Neurable showed off a gaming headset with HP's HyperX featuring two electroencephalography (EEG) sensors built in.

Like the original M&D MW75 Neuro headphones, the Neurable One features 12 EEG sensors in the nylon earpads that are used to monitor brain waves. The headphones cost $499 and will be available in October from Neurable’s website.

The EEG sensors live in the specially designed earpads.

Alongside the new headphones is a new app (the old app will continue to exist for now for older hardware), which Alcaide says tracks eight brain metrics:

The biggest hardware and software change with the Neurable One is that you no longer have to start a session in the app to capture brain activity. Instead, the Neurable One passively monitors your brain as soon as you put the headphones on—Alcaide likens it to wearing a Fitbit.

Read More

At that point, the sensors begin monitoring your brain activity to measure your focus. When it detects that you’re getting distracted, the headphones play a ping to get you back on track. If it thinks you're burning out instead, it’ll recommend a break so you can come back later fully recharged.

The headphone-app combo works similarly to help you fall asleep and to meditate. For example, with meditation, you can follow a guided session, and when the headphones detect you’re in the flow, the guide will stop talking so you stay in that zone. If it detects you’re drifting away, it’ll start guiding you back again. For sleep—designed for naps rather than proper bedtime—it can, over time, lower the headset volume of guided naps or soundscapes as it detects you falling asleep. (You can also turn off the EEG sensors and just use them as regular headphones if you want.)

Alcaide says when the app tells him his brain battery is low for the day, he’ll go to the sauna and go to bed early to help him recover. It can tell him when his peak brain speed hours are, allowing him to rejigger his schedule so he does his hardest work during those times. There’s also a check-in system called Cognitive Snapshot; when you trigger it, the app shows your current brain state and offers recommendations to improve it. That could be a guided meditation or small games to exercise those parts of your brain. The app also provides weekly or monthly reports to track your brain activity over time.

Neurable doesn’t have any new research or data to share that can speak to the effectiveness of its latest headphones. That research is in the works, but it will take time. So Neurable still points to previous research with the Mayo Clinic, which showed a 30 percent increase in focus in individuals using Neurable's headset versus people using Pomodoro techniques or other types of focus-sustaining systems. The study also saw a drop of about 10 percent in end-of-day burnout and an increase in end-of-day happiness.

The product isn’t categorized as a medical device, and Neurable says it isn’t designed to diagnose, treat, or monitor any conditions. The company also promises not to sell any of the data it collects about your brain—which could become very valuable in the future—and says it doesn't use that data for advertising. Alcaide says enterprise customers buy its headsets in bulk to help employees focus, but they’re not buying the headsets to monitor the workforce.

“It's because we know we're going to get higher productivity per employee; they're going to be happier, they're going to feel less burned out, it's a win-win for everybody,” he says. “It's like how sometimes companies get gym memberships for their employees.” He stresses that each user’s data stays with them.

Alcaide says the company partnered with an audio brand to help with the non-brain-scanning bits of the hardware, though he wouldn’t share the name. These cans have the “same premium sound” as the earlier M&D collaboration, with 40-mm beryllium drivers, six microphones, active noise cancellation, a transparency mode, and 22 hours of run time—12 if you have those EEG sensors running. It supports Bluetooth 5.2, and both AAC and aptX codecs. Neurable’s app is available on both Android and iOS.

Review: Apple Mac Studio (M5 Ultra)

Wired October 01, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

9/10

The Mac Studio has a new calling in life. For awhile, it seemed like overkill for just about anyone, regardless of profession.

But these days, computers with over 64 GB of RAM and tons of GPU performance have an entire playground of on-device AI tools to exclusively explore. With a Mac Studio, you can have a full-on agentic AI framework, generate high-end video all on-device, or run the latest foundation-level large language models (LLMs). The Mac Studio is relatively unique among the available options—at least, for now.

But beware: If you're tired of hearing about AI, turn away now.

Apple has always catered to a high-performance crowd, and with the surge of interest in local AI, its systems are uniquely set up to excel in that area. But first, the box itself. It's about as tall as a coffee mug, but it's a 7-inch-square footprint. I bet most people have never seen a Mac Studio in person, and if you get the chance, you might be surprised by how large it actually is.

The Mac Studio remains the only Mac to keep USB-A ports around. That alone's worth the souped-up $11,000 model, right? (That's a joke). Here, you get two, along with four, Thunderbolt 5 ports, Ethernet, HDMI, and a headphone jack. You can connect up to four 5K external displays at 120 Hz using the Thunderbolt and HDMI ports, if that's your jam. Interestingly, as compared to the Mac Mini, the Studio swaps the front-facing headphone jack with a full SD card slot. Photographers and videographers will appreciate that.

Apple Mac Studio (M5 Ultra)

Rating: 9/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

I do wish the Mac Studio came in more than one color, such as Space Black. Still, the Mac Studio comes in two distinct versions. The M5 Max model starts at $2,499, which comes with 36 GB of memory and 512 GB of storage. This is the reasonable configuration, designed for content creators, game developers, and media professionals. One way to think about it: It delivers the same performance as the MacBook Pro with M5 Max, but for substantially less money. There's a $1,250 difference in price even when similarly configured. The other benefit is that Apple offers more expandability in storage and memory options on the Mac Studio than on a MacBook Pro.

Apple Mac Studio (M5 Ultra)

Rating: 9/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

But that's not the model I tested. The configuration I was sent for review is that aforementioned $11,000 model, with the M5 Ultra processor and unified memory maxed out to 256 GB. That's definitely the most expensive computer I've ever had on my desk, but it's not even the priciest Mac Studio configuration you can get. The M5 Ultra is the most singularly powerful chip Apple has ever made (yet), and its first quad-die chip. It's absolutely massive. Over its high-speed interconnect, it essentially stitches together two M5 Max chips, for a total of 36 CPU cores. Think of this as the equivalent of Apple's $3,299 Studio Display XDR in terms of use case. It's extremely targeted.

Regardless of the configuration, the Mac Studio's true power comes from its obscene number of GPU cores and unified memory. You can configure it with anywhere from 36 GB to 256 GB of memory (a 512 GB model is coming in October), and up to 80 GPU cores. Let's be real—only AI enthusiasts and AI developers need more than 64 GB of memory. If that's you, there's reason to be excited about this version of the Mac Studio. While you've always been able to configure it with up to 256 GB of unified memory, the M5 Ultra adds unprecedented GPU performance to the mix. It has twice as many GPU cores as the M5 Max, the same amount as the previous M3 Ultra.

Don't think of the M5 Ultra as providing the same uplift as upgrading from the M5 Pro to the M5 Max, which is a more modest upgrade that focuses primarily on GPU performance. But two generations of GPU improvements in the Ultra chips have made each core more powerful, in both gaming and AI. Notably, each GPU core now includes a Neural Accelerator, a feature of the entire “M5” family of chips that further enhances AI workload performance.

The astounding part about the Ultra is that, in some cases, it really doubles performance over the Max. While single-core benchmarks don't show much difference, the doubled CPU cores allow the M5 Ultra Mac Studio to outperform the M5 Max (as tested in a 16-inch MacBook Pro with an 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU, plus 48 GB of memory) by 51 percent—as tested in Cinebench 2026. I'm still a bit shocked by that. The GPU performance doesn't scale quite as perfectly, but it was 32 percent faster than the M5 Max. Gaming tests put these two scores together and really show how vastly superior the M5 Ultra is. The industry-standard 3DMark Steel Nomad benchmark put the M5 Ultra at a 41 percent higher score than the M5 Max.

Apple Mac Studio (M5 Ultra)

Rating: 9/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

But it's in actual games where the Mac Studio really impresses. It can run Cyberpunk 2077 at 160 frames per second on the M5 Ultra, which is 61 percent faster than on the M5 Max. The happy-medium preset I landed on was running it at 2560 x 1400 resolution on Ultra. The game looks incredible, especially on an HDR screen. (I just so happened to be testing it with a Studio Display XDR). It can even run the game natively in 4K at 53 fps at this same preset, though I found myself most comfortable in 1440p on Ultra. Having options on how you want to tweak a game is always ideal, and for the first time, the M5 Ultra is fast enough to do just that. It's no RTX 5090-powered gaming PC, but this is as close as a Mac has ever been.

No one is buying a Mac Studio for gaming, of course. And while it's a useful test of performance, I really wanted to see how the system could handle on-device AI workflows. This Mac Studio configuration offers huge amounts of memory, but the bandwidth is another major benefit the M5 Ultra Mac Studio has over the M3 Ultra (Apple skipped the M4 Ultra). It's 1.2 TB per second compared to 89 GB per second, which is crucial for running models on-device.

I set up a simple agentic AI task in LM Bionic to summarize a dozen local files, running on a fairly small 9-billion-parameter Qwen 3.5 model; it completed the task in 2 minutes, compared to almost 10 minutes on the M5 Max MacBook Pro. But here's where I got sufficiently impressed. I loaded up a much larger, 122-billion-parameter version of Qwen 3.5, and I was blown away by the speed. It felt very much like using a frontier-class LLM right on my computer, completely offline and without accessing the cloud. And, of course, being local means it has access to your machine. So I set up the same simple agentic task using this much more expansive model, and it still finished in under 2 minutes (with much more accurate and useful results, too).

Apple Mac Studio (M5 Ultra)

Rating: 9/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Over in Draw Things, I ran some on-device image and video generation to really see what an 80-core GPU can do. Using the MiniMax H3 model, it took over 11 minutes to generate a 15-second video completely on-device. There's a long way to go before this feels like a viable alternative to cloud-based options or needing a high-powered discrete GPU like an RTX 5090 or 5080 for this kind of task. Obviously, paying this much to run AI locally is a niche endeavor. But as models get more efficient and quality improves, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio's capabilities should improve over time. We're still in the early days.

During these AI tests, in particular, I noticed how warm the Mac Studio gets when it's fully under load. You definitely don't want to touch it or set anything on top of it. You also want to leave some room behind it, since it blows a lot of hot air out of the vents. The fans can spin up quite loudly too—though, like all modern Macs, it takes a couple of minutes for the fans to really get going. The front-facing ports stay cool, though, thanks to the vents in the thermal system sitting right underneath the Mac Studio.

The Mac Studio is certainly unique. Because mini Windows PCs typically use laptop chips, they don't typically support more than 64 GB of RAM. That's where this top-end M5 Ultra Mac Studio really feels unbeatable (and even earns its sky-high price from that perspective). Add the upcoming option for 512 GB of memory (and the ability to connect four Mac Studios and use them as a single computer), and you have something extremely niche—but wholly unrivaled.

The base M5 Max Mac Studio does have stronger competition, though. For $2,399, you can get a Geekom A9 Mega Mini PC with 64 GB of RAM, 1 TB of storage, and AMD's new Ryzen AI Max+ 388. That's more memory and more storage for less money. Importantly, that AMD chip uses unified memory the same way Apple Silicon does, which is crucial for running local AI workloads. We'll hopefully be getting the Geekom A9 in for testing to see how it stacks up in real-world tests.

More competitors are coming soon, too. Nvidia's RTX Spark “superchips” are the main upcoming rival, offering up to 128 GB of unified memory in both laptops and mini PCs. They still can't do 256 GB of memory like the Mac Studio, but these will hopefully turn up the heat on the Windows and Linux side.
